entries.question: Ari has searched their library this turn with [Bog Glider]. During their end step, Nico casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Mission Briefing lets Nico cast Archive Trap from their graveyard and the trap’s alternative {0} cost applies because Ari searched their library.
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Ari is an opponent of Nico, Nico can cast Archive Trap this turn for {0} instead of its printed mana cost of {3}{U}{U}. Mission Briefing lets Nico cast an instant or sorcery from their graveyard "this turn" [Mission Briefing text], and since Archive Trap is an instant, normal timing rules let Nico cast it any time they have priority, including during the end step (Mission Briefing's grant doesn't restrict timing for instants — that timing restriction only matters for sorceries, per [Mission Briefing ruling #3]).

Archive Trap's own text says, "If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may pay {0} rather than pay this spell's mana cost." This is an alternative cost (governed by [118.9a] and [118.9b]), and per [Archive Trap ruling #5], it only checks that an opponent searched their library this turn — it doesn't matter whether that search actually found a card. Ari activated Bog Glider's ability, which explicitly instructs them to "Search your library for a Mercenary permanent card with mana value 2 or less," so that counts as a search of Ari's library regardless of whether Ari found anything (and per [Bog Glider ruling #0], Ari wasn't even required to find a card even if one was present). So as long as Ari qualifies as an opponent of Nico, the condition is satisfied for the rest of the turn.

When Nico casts Archive Trap, they announce during casting whether to use this alternative cost in place of the mana cost [601.2f], and if they do, the total cost becomes {0} generic mana — there is no colored mana left to pay, since the alternative cost fully replaces the mana cost rather than just reducing it. Nico could instead choose to pay the normal {3}{U}{U} cost if they wanted, per [Archive Trap ruling #4], but there's no reason to if the alternative cost is available.

One caveat: this all assumes a game structure where Ari is specifically an opponent of Nico. In a two-player game this is automatic. In a multiplayer game, the same logic still applies as long as Ari and Nico are opponents of each other (which is true unless they're on the same team) — the rules text just requires 'an opponent,' and nothing here changes between two-player and multiplayer play.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mission Briefing allows Nico to cast Archive Trap from their graveyard, without any other restrictions on how it's cast. Nico can choose to pay the alternative cost of {0}.

entries.question: In a game of Two-Headed Giant, Antonio activates the last loyalty ability of [Chandra, Hope's Beacon] with X=1. Could they target both Nico and Noah?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Antonio may target Nico and Noah separately with Chandra's −X ability (X=1) because each teammate is a distinct player and legal targets.
entries.answer:
Yes. As long as Nico and Noah are legal targets (for example, no protection or hexproof stops it), Antonio's activation of Chandra, Hope's Beacon's −X ability with X=1 can name both of them as the "up to two targets," dealing 1 damage to each.

Chandra, Hope's Beacon's last ability reads "−X: Chandra deals X damage to each of up to two targets," and its printed text places no restriction on those targets being opponents, teammates, or any particular team — the card's own wording controls here, so any combination of legal targets (including two players, whether they're on the same Two-Headed Giant team or on opposing teams) is allowed. The only built-in restriction is that the two targets must be different objects/players; Antonio can't point both instances of damage at the same person.

Once the ability resolves, the 1 damage to Nico and the 1 damage to Noah are each applied individually to that player, and then folded into their respective team's shared life total — so if Nico and Noah are on the same team, that team loses a total of 2 life; if they're on opposing teams, each team loses 1 life. This follows from how Two-Headed Giant handles damage to individual team members (rule 810.9d) within the two-team, two-player-each structure of the variant (rule 810.1).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each member of a team is a separate player and is targeted independently.

entries.question: Avalyn has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Avalyn cannot draw (so Keranos's reveal triggers do not occur) and Avalyn loses the game when state-based actions are checked before the next time a player would receive priority.
entries.answer:
Avalyn attempts her mandatory draw for the turn, but since her library is empty there's no card to draw, and therefore no card for Keranos, God of Storms to reveal - its reveal-and-trigger ability simply does not fire. Then, the next time any player would receive priority, the state-based action for attempting to draw from an empty library causes Avalyn to lose the game.

Step by step: At the beginning of the draw step, the active player draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [504.1]. This happens automatically, before state-based actions are checked and before any player gets priority [703.3]. Because Avalyn's library has no cards in it, this counts as 'a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it' [121.4][104.3c] - no card is actually drawn.

Keranos, God of Storms's triggered ability says 'Reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns.' Since no card was drawn (the draw attempt failed because the library was empty), there is nothing to reveal, so the reveal-and-damage/reveal-and-draw ability doesn't trigger at all. Its rulings confirm the ability only cares about what is actually revealed from an actual draw (e.g., drawing a land off the reveal causes another draw) [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #9], but that presumes a card was drawn in the first place - here none was.

After the draw-step turn-based action resolves, the game proceeds to check state-based actions before anyone gets priority [704.3][405.6f][117.5]. Because Avalyn attempted to draw from an empty library since the last state-based action check, the state-based action in rule 704.5b applies: she loses the game the next time a player would receive priority [121.4][104.3c][704.5b]. This happens automatically and doesn't use the stack, and no triggered ability from Keranos is involved since none triggered.

This answer assumes a normal turn structure with no other replacement or prevention effects on the draw. It also does not change based on player count - the empty-library loss condition (704.5b, 121.4, 104.3c) and the turn-based/state-based action framework apply the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game; the only multiplayer-specific nuance would be how other players' priority/turn order proceeds afterward, which isn't addressed by the rules provided here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Avalyn can't draw a card, so no card is revealed and neither trigger triggers. Avalyn loses the game before they would next get priority.

entries.question: Abdullah casts [Telemin Performance] targeting Nico. In response, Nico casts [Veil of Summer]. Abdullah responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate declines to rule whether Telemin Performance fizzles after both Veils resolve, whereas the reference states it fails to resolve due to Nico having gained hexproof, so the final conclusions differ.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Both Veil of Summer spells resolve before Telemin Performance does (the stack resolves last-in, first-out), so Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first, then Nico's Veil of Summer, and only after that does Telemin Performance try to resolve against Nico. Here's exactly what each spell does, and where the provided rules run out.

Stack order: Abdullah casts Telemin Performance targeting Nico (bottom of stack). Nico responds with Veil of Summer (middle). Abdullah responds with a second Veil of Summer (top). A cast spell "becomes the topmost object on the stack" and "remains on the stack until it resolves" [601.2a], which is why the most recently cast spell — Abdullah's Veil of Summer — resolves first.

1. Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves. Per Veil of Summer's text, it checks "if an opponent has cast a blue or black spell this turn." Abdullah's opponent is Nico, and Nico's only spell this turn (Veil of Summer) is green, so Abdullah does not draw a card. The other two effects still happen unconditionally: "Spells you control can't be countered this turn" (this now protects Telemin Performance, still on the stack, from being countered for the rest of the turn) and "You and permanents you control gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn," so Abdullah gains hexproof from blue/black [Veil of Summer]. Note that Veil of Summer "has no effect until it resolves" [Veil of Summer ruling #1], so none of this happened while it was sitting on the stack.

2. Nico's Veil of Summer resolves next. Now Nico's opponent is Abdullah, who did cast a blue spell this turn (Telemin Performance), so Nico draws a card — only one card, even though only one qualifying spell was cast [Veil of Summer ruling #0]. Nico's spells also can't be countered this turn (moot, since Nico has no other spell on the stack), and Nico and Nico's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn [Veil of Summer].

3. Finally, Telemin Performance tries to resolve, still targeting Nico, who by now has hexproof from blue (and Telemin Performance is a blue sorcery). Here the provided rules stop short of a full answer: they tell us hexproof means Nico "can't be the target[] of blue... spells... opponents control" going forward [Veil of Summer], but none of the rules given to me state whether a spell already legally targeting a player is rechecked for target legality at resolution and fails if the target has since become illegal. That specific rule (the general target-legality check performed when a spell resolves) is not among the rules provided here, so I can't confirm from this rule set whether Telemin Performance fizzles against Nico or still goes through. I don't want to guess at that mechanic without a supporting rule.

What I can say for certain: Abdullah's Veil of Summer does not net a card draw, gives Abdullah hexproof from blue/black and protects Abdullah's spells (including Telemin Performance) from being countered this turn; Nico's Veil of Summer nets Nico one card draw and gives Nico hexproof from blue/black. Whether that hexproof stops the already-targeting Telemin Performance is the one piece this rule set doesn't settle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves first. Then Nico's resolves and draws them a card. Then Telemin Performance tries to resolve and fails, since it has an illegal target.

(Abdullah's Veil of Summer didn't accomplish anything useful.)

entries.question: Athena controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nicholas flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Athena's turn. Can Nicholas activate its abilities this turn?
entries.reason: The candidate allows activating The Wandering Emperor's loyalty ability after it was flashed in, whereas the reference says casting it on Athena's turn is prevented by Teferi, so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nicholas can activate one loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn, at instant speed, because The Wandering Emperor's own text overrides the normal timing restriction — and Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability doesn't stop him, since that ability only restricts casting spells, not activating loyalty abilities.

Normally, loyalty abilities (rule 606.1, 606.2) can only be activated "any time [the controller] has priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn" (rules 606.3, 209.2). Since Nicholas flashed The Wandering Emperor in during Athena's turn, this turn isn't a main phase of Nicholas's own turn, so that default rule wouldn't normally let him activate anything until his next turn.

However, The Wandering Emperor's printed ability states: "As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant." This is card text that specifically overrides the general timing restriction of rule 606.3/209.2 (card text beats a general rule it contradicts). Because instants can be cast on any player's turn, this permission lets Nicholas activate a loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor right away on Athena's turn, as long as he otherwise has priority (rule 117.1b) — for example, in response to something, or whenever priority passes to him.

Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability ("Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery") restricts Nicholas's ability to *cast spells*, not his ability to *activate abilities*. Activating a loyalty ability is not casting a spell, so this restriction simply does not apply here. The Teferi, Time Raveler ruling about "precedence" only concerns situations where an effect tries to let an opponent cast a spell as though it had flash (i.e., actual spellcasting) — it's not about activating a permanent's abilities, so it doesn't extend to block The Wandering Emperor's loyalty-ability permission.

One caveat: per The Wandering Emperor's own ruling, Nicholas may still only activate one of her loyalty abilities during the turn she entered the battlefield (consistent with the "no player has previously activated a loyalty ability of that permanent that turn" restriction in rule 606.3/209.2). So he gets exactly one activation this turn, but he can do it at instant speed rather than waiting for his own main phase.

This answer assumes Nicholas is an opponent of Athena in a two-player game; the rules given are all framed for a single active player's main phase and don't specify anything different for a multiplayer table beyond that any player with priority may act, so the same reasoning would apply in a multiplayer game as well.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nicholas cannot cast The Wandering Emperor on Athena's turn due to Teferi, Time Raveler's effect.

entries.question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, how much life does each team begin the game with?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that each Two-Headed Giant team starts with a single shared 30 life total, matching the reference.
entries.answer: Each team begins a Two-Headed Giant game with 30 life, shared between the two players on that team. This is a single shared life total for the team, not 30 life per individual player [810.4]. Two-Headed Giant is played with two teams of two players each [810.1], and this shared total replaces the normal individual starting life total of 20 [103.4a][119.1a]. Note that a larger variant like Three-Headed Giant increases a team's starting life total by 15 for each player beyond the second on that team [810.11], but for the standard two-player-per-team version, 30 life is the starting total.

entries.question: Aldo casts [Lumithread Field] for its morph cost. If Nico wants to counter it with [Spell Burst], what is the mana value of the Lumithread Field on the stack?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the morph-cast Lumithread Field is a face-down spell with no mana cost and thus has mana value 0.
entries.answer:
The mana value of Lumithread Field on the stack is 0. Aldo is casting Lumithread Field using its morph ability, which is an alternative cost (rule 118.9c). Normally, paying an alternative cost doesn't change what a spell's mana cost is for other purposes (118.9c) — but morph is special: rule 702.37c states that when you cast a card using morph, it becomes 'a face-down creature card with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost' and it goes on the stack 'as a face-down spell with the same characteristics.' Since the face-down spell has no mana cost at all, its mana value is 0 per rule 202.3a ('The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0'), unless it's the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent/spell or a melded permanent — neither applies to a morphed Lumithread Field, since morph just makes the same card face-down rather than making it a different DFC back face. So while face down, Lumithread Field's mana value is 0, not 2. If Nico casts Spell Burst choosing X=0, it can legally target the face-down Lumithread Field spell (mana value 0) and counter it, per Spell Burst's text 'Counter target spell with mana value X' and the ruling that X's chosen value determines the mana value being checked against.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. A morphed spell is a 2/2 creature with no mana cost. Since the spell has no mana cost, its mana value is 0.

entries.question: Alfonso controls [Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass] equipped with [Glaive of the Guildpact] and no Gates. Does it have vigilance and menace?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference that Glaive of the Guildpact grants vigilance and menace regardless of how many Gates you control, with only the +1/+0 bonus depending on Gates.
entries.answer:
Yes. Glaive of the Guildpact's text states that the equipped creature "gets +1/+0 for each Gate you control and has vigilance and menace," and the granting of vigilance and menace is not conditioned on controlling any Gates — only the +1/+0 bonus scales with Gates controlled. As the official ruling for Glaive of the Guildpact confirms, the equipped creature has vigilance and menace even if you control no Gates. Since Alfonso controls no Gates, Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass equipped with Glaive of the Guildpact simply gets +0/+0 from the Gate-counting clause, but it still has vigilance (letting it attack without tapping, per rule 702.20b) and menace (meaning it can't be blocked except by two or more creatures, per rule 702.111b).

entries.question: Ainsley casts [Tandem Takedown], granting their two [Devoted Hero] +1/+0. Can each Devoted Hero deal damage to a different one of Nolan's creatures?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling: Tandem Takedown has a single recipient target so both Devoted Hero must deal their damage to the same chosen creature/planeswalker/battle.
entries.answer:
No. Tandem Takedown has three targeting slots total: up to two target creatures you control (the sources) and a separate, single "another target creature, planeswalker, or battle" (the recipient). Because the phrase "another target creature, planeswalker, or battle" uses the word "target" only once, only one object can be chosen to fill that role — the same single target must be shared by both Devoted Hero. So if Ainsley controls two Devoted Hero, both of them will deal damage to the *same* one of Nolan's creatures (or planeswalker/battle), not to two different ones.

This follows from how targeting works: rule 115.3 and 601.2c explain that the same target can't be chosen multiple times for one instance of the word "target," but a spell *can* reuse the same object for two different instances of "target" if it says "target" more than once (e.g., "Destroy target artifact and target land" could hit the same artifact land twice). Tandem Takedown's recipient clause is only one instance of "target," so there's no second recipient-target slot to point at a different creature — Ainsley must pick one recipient when casting the spell, and both Devoted Hero (assuming both remain legal targets and get +1/+0) deal their damage to that single chosen creature, planeswalker, or battle.

Note: if that single recipient becomes an illegal target by the time Tandem Takedown resolves, per Tandem Takedown's own ruling, nothing deals or is dealt damage at all (even if both Devoted Hero are still legal), since the damage-dealing target failed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Tandem Takedown specifies that they each deal damage to another target creature, meaning one single other creature.

entries.question: Aaden has 3 [Witch's Familiar] in their graveyard and casts [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed]. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Nyla activates [Sentinel Totem] to exile all cards from Aaden's graveyard. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Izoni's ability checks the graveyard at resolution and, since the graveyard was emptied before resolution, zero tokens are created.
entries.answer:
Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability will create 0 Insect tokens. The ability's effect ("create a 1/1 black and green Insect creature token for each creature card in your graveyard") requires information from the game — the number of creature cards in Aaden's graveyard — and that number is determined only once, at the moment the ability actually resolves, not when it was put on the stack. Since Nyla activated Sentinel Totem and exiled all cards from Aaden's graveyard (including the 3 Witch's Familiar) before Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's triggered ability resolves, the graveyard is empty at the relevant moment, so the count is zero and no tokens are created. This is not a 'looks back in time' exception (those apply only to specific trigger types like leaves-the-battlefield abilities), and it is not the kind of effect described in 608.2i that ignores an object no longer meeting prior criteria — Izoni's ability is checking a game-wide count (creature cards in a graveyard) at resolution, not tracking a specific previously-identified object.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The number of tokens to create is determined when the ability resolves, by which point the graveyard has no creatures in it.

entries.question: Atlas casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nicole's lands but not cast any spells. Can Atlas do this?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Piracy lets Atlas tap Nicole's lands for mana but doesn't force spending that mana, so Atlas may tap them and choose not to cast any spells.
entries.answer:
Yes. Piracy's own text says "Until end of turn, you may tap lands you don't control for mana. Spend this mana only to cast spells." That first sentence is a permission — it lets Atlas tap lands Nicole controls for mana even though Atlas doesn't control them, which overrides the normal rule that only a permanent's controller can activate its abilities (a card's own text overrides a general rule it contradicts). The second sentence, "Spend this mana only to cast spells," is only a restriction on what the mana may be used for — it does not require Atlas to actually cast anything. Per rule 118.3c, activating a mana ability is never mandatory, and nothing in Piracy or the general rules obligates a player to spend mana just because they generated it. So Atlas may tap all of Nicole's lands for mana under Piracy's permission, and then simply decline to cast any spell. The mana produced would just go unused (since it can only be spent on casting spells, and Atlas isn't casting any), but tapping the lands themselves is fully legal and doesn't require follow-through with a spell.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Piracy creates a restriction on what Atlas must spend the mana on, but does not prevent them from not spending the mana.

entries.question: Annie controls [Heliod, Sun-Crowned] and casts [Essence Feed]. Can they choose to put Heliod, Sun-Crowned's +1/+1 counter on one of the tokens created by Essence Feed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that the tokens are created during Essence Feed's resolution before Heliod's triggered ability is put on the stack, so Annie may target one of those tokens with the +1/+1 counter.
entries.answer:
Yes. When Essence Feed resolves, it causes Annie to lose... to gain 3 life and create three 0/1 Eldrazi Spawn tokens as part of a single resolution of that one spell; the tokens are already on the battlefield by the time Heliod, Sun-Crowned's triggered ability ("Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature or enchantment you control") is put on the stack, since a triggered ability isn't put on the stack until after the source of the trigger (here, Essence Feed) finishes resolving. Because the Eldrazi Spawn tokens are creatures Annie controls at that point, they are legal targets for Heliod's triggered ability, and Annie may choose one of them to receive the +1/+1 counter.

Note that the life-gain from Essence Feed ("You gain 3 life") is a single life-gain event, so Heliod's ability triggers only once for this spell, not once per point of life gained or once per token created — Annie gets one +1/+1 counter to assign, and she can put it on Heliod itself, on the Eldrazi Spawn tokens, on any other creature/enchantment she controls, or even on Heliod's own body if it's a creature (devotion permitting). This assumes the life gain and token creation from Essence Feed happen together as effects of the spell resolving before Heliod's ability is placed on the stack, which is the normal order of events for a single resolving spell; there's no indication in this scenario that anything interrupts that resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Annie creates the tokens, then gains life as part of the resolution of Essence Feed. After Essence Feed has resolved, Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger will be put on the stack. At that point Annie can choose a token as their target.

entries.question: Aleah casts [Clash of Titans], can Aleah choose Nixon's [Storm Crow] for both targets?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: "another" in the spell's text requires the second target to be a different creature, so both targets cannot be the same Storm Crow.
entries.answer:
No. Clash of Titans's text is "Target creature fights another target creature," and the word "another" explicitly requires the second target to be a different creature from the first. Aleah must choose two distinct creatures — Nixon's Storm Crow can only fill one of the two target slots, not both.

Normally, when a spell uses the word "target" multiple times, the same object can be chosen for each instance of "target" as long as it fits the targeting criteria (rules 115.3 and 601.2c). But Clash of Titans's second instance is worded "another target creature," and that word "another" is part of the targeting criteria for that instance — it excludes whatever was already chosen as the first target. So the general multiple-target rule doesn't let Aleah pick the same creature twice here; she needs two different creatures. Note that Clash of Titans can still target two creatures controlled by the same player, per its ruling — it just can't target the same creature twice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The word "another" here retains its normal English meaning, and means that both targets cannot be the same creature.

entries.question: Alejandro controls [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider] and two [Blight Mamba]s. If Alejandro deals combat damage with both Blight Mambas, how many poison counters will Nico get?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nico gets four poison counters because each 1-counter event from the two infect Blight Mambas is doubled to 2 by Vorinclex controlled by Alejandro.
entries.answer:
Nico will get 4 poison counters. Each Blight Mamba is a 1/1 creature with infect, so combat damage dealt to Nico by a Blight Mamba doesn't cause life loss — instead it causes that Blight Mamba's controller (Alejandro) to give Nico that many poison counters, i.e. 1 poison counter per Blight Mamba (rules 120.3b, 702.90b). Since Alejandro controls both Blight Mambas, it is Alejandro who is 'putting' those poison counters on Nico. Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's first ability says 'If you would put one or more counters on a permanent or player, put twice that many of each of those kinds of counters on that permanent or player instead' — 'you' here is Alejandro, Vorinclex's controller, and Vorinclex's own ruling confirms it cares about who is doing the putting to decide which of its two counter-doubling/halving abilities applies. Since Alejandro (not an opponent) is the one putting the counters, the doubling clause applies rather than the halving clause. Each Blight Mamba's combat damage is a separate event, and a replacement effect like Vorinclex's only applies once per event (rule 614.5), so each 1-poison-counter event is independently doubled to 2 poison counters. With two Blight Mambas dealing combat damage, that's 2 events of 1 counter each, doubled to 2 counters each, for a total of 4 poison counters given to Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two damage will be dealt to Nico and they will get four poison counters. ([702.164c], [702.90b])

entries.question: Andre casts [Abrupt Decay] targeting Nico's 5/5 Horse creature token, then responds by targeting it with [Arcane Denial]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Arcane Denial can't counter Abrupt Decay (its other draw effects still occur) and Abrupt Decay then resolves and destroys the 5/5 Horse token.
entries.answer:
Arcane Denial resolves first (it was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack), targeting Abrupt Decay. However, Abrupt Decay's own text says "This spell can't be countered," and that printed text overrides the general effect of Arcane Denial's "Counter target spell" instruction. So when Arcane Denial resolves, Abrupt Decay is NOT countered — but Arcane Denial's other effects still happen: Nico (Abrupt Decay's controller) may draw up to two cards at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep, and Andre (Arcane Denial's controller) draws a card at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep. This mirrors the official ruling on Abrupt Decay: a spell that counters spells can still legally target Abrupt Decay, and when it resolves Abrupt Decay isn't countered, but any additional effects of the countering spell still occur [Abrupt Decay ruling #1].

After Arcane Denial finishes resolving, Abrupt Decay remains on the stack and is now the top object, so it resolves next. During its resolution, Magic checks whether its target — the 5/5 Horse creature token — is still a legal target under rule [608.2b]: it must still be a nonland permanent with mana value 3 or less. A token's mana value is 0 unless something has changed it, so unless some other effect has altered the token's characteristics or removed it from the battlefield, it remains a legal target, and Abrupt Decay resolves normally, destroying the 5/5 Horse token.

Note: this assumes Andre cast Arcane Denial as a response while Abrupt Decay was still on the stack (i.e., before Abrupt Decay resolved). If instead Arcane Denial were cast after Abrupt Decay had already resolved and left the stack, there would be no spell left for Arcane Denial to target, and Andre would have to choose a different (legal) target for it, per the normal targeting requirement in [608.2b] that a spell needs a legal target when it resolves.

This analysis is not dependent on player count — nothing about choosing a defending player or turn order among more than two players is relevant here, so the outcome is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Arcane Denial resolves but can't counter Abrupt Decay. During Nico's upkeep, Andre draws one to three cards, based on their choice.

entries.question: Arabella controls [Yixlid Jailer] and casts [Ever After] targeting [Dearly Departed] and [Fugitive Wizard]. Will Fugitive Wizard enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Fugitive Wizard does not get the counter because Yixlid Jailer removes Dearly Departed's graveyard ability, so it cannot grant the +1/+1 as Ever After resolves.
entries.answer:
No. Fugitive Wizard will enter the battlefield without a +1/+1 counter, because Dearly Departed's graveyard ability is turned off by Yixlid Jailer.

Dearly Departed's ability ("As long as this creature is in your graveyard, each Human creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it") is a static ability that functions only while Dearly Departed is in the graveyard (this is the zone in which the ability says it operates, per rule [604.2], which ties a static ability's continuous effect to the permanent/card being in the zone the ability specifies). However, Yixlid Jailer's static ability says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," which strips Dearly Departed of that ability for as long as Dearly Departed is a card sitting in the graveyard.

When you apply Ever After, both Dearly Departed and Fugitive Wizard are returning from the graveyard to the battlefield simultaneously. To figure out what replacement/static effects apply to Fugitive Wizard as it enters, you check the game state and continuous effects that exist as the event happens — this includes checking whether Dearly Departed's graveyard-based ability was actually active. Since Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield the whole time, Dearly Departed never actually has a functioning "grant a counter" ability while it's a card in the graveyard — Yixlid Jailer has already removed it. Dearly Departed ruling #1 confirms you look at "what the creature will look like on the battlefield" and "any effects affecting a creature entering under your control" when deciding whether it gets the counter; here, the relevant effect (Dearly Departed's own ability) simply isn't there to grant anything, because Yixlid Jailer's card-text override ("Cards in graveyards lose all abilities") beats Dearly Departed's printed text while Dearly Departed is in the graveyard.

So neither Fugitive Wizard nor any other Human you control gets a +1/+1 counter from this instance of Dearly Departed as long as Yixlid Jailer continues to affect the graveyard. If Yixlid Jailer were removed from the battlefield before Ever After resolves, Dearly Departed's ability would be live again and Fugitive Wizard (a Human) would get the counter.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Dearly Departed has no abilities while in the graveyard.

entries.question: Nicholas controls [Solitary Confinement]. Addilyn attacks with [Ranger of Eos] and casts [Skullcrack] targeting themselves. Does Nicholas lose life?
entries.reason: Both say yes — Skullcrack makes "damage can't be prevented this turn," so Solitary Confinement can't prevent the combat damage and Nicholas loses life.
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Ranger of Eos is unblocked and attacking Nicholas, Nicholas loses 3 life from Ranger of Eos's combat damage. Solitary Confinement's damage-prevention ability is turned off for the rest of the turn by Skullcrack's text "Damage can't be prevented this turn," so it can no longer shield Nicholas.

Here's why: Solitary Confinement reads "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you," which is a prevention effect under rule [615.1] — it works like a continuous shield watching for damage events. Skullcrack's second sentence, "Damage can't be prevented this turn," is a blanket statement that shuts off damage prevention for the entire turn, for all damage, not merely the 3 damage Skullcrack itself deals. This mirrors how Skullcrack's first sentence ("Players can't gain life this turn") makes life-gain impossible game-wide for the turn, per [Skullcrack ruling #1] and [Skullcrack ruling #2]. Because Solitary Confinement's card text says to prevent damage, and Skullcrack's card text overrides that by making prevention impossible for the turn, Skullcrack's more specific/overriding effect controls (card text overriding general rule application) — Solitary Confinement's shield simply fails to do anything for damage dealt this turn, including Ranger of Eos's combat damage to Nicholas.

Skullcrack itself, however, deals its 3 damage only to its chosen target — and the question states Addilyn cast Skullcrack targeting themselves (Addilyn), not Nicholas ([Skullcrack ruling #0] confirms Skullcrack only targets the named player). So that 3 damage from Skullcrack goes to Addilyn, not Nicholas, and (per rule [120.3a]) would normally cause Addilyn to lose 3 life since damage from a source without infect dealt to a player causes life loss — and since damage prevention is off, nothing stops that either.

Separately, once combat damage is dealt, rule [120.3a] confirms that damage dealt to a player by a source without infect (Ranger of Eos, a normal creature) causes that player to lose life equal to the damage — 3 life for Nicholas if the full 3 power connects unblocked.

One timing/setup assumption: I'm assuming Ranger of Eos is unblocked and is attacking Nicholas (the question doesn't state blockers), and that this is a two-player game between Nicholas and Addilyn. If Ranger of Eos were blocked, or if a third player were the actual defending player in a multiplayer game, Nicholas might take no combat damage at all — the rules given here are framed for two-player interactions, and no multiplayer-specific rule was provided for this attack scenario, so a multiplayer table could differ if Nicholas isn't the defending player.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Skullcrack says that damage can't be prevented, so Solitary Confinement doesn't prevent it.

entries.question: Armani casts [Hangarback Walker] with X = 3. Can Neriah counter it with [Thoughtbind]?

entries.question: Avery casts [Sram's Expertise]. As it resolves, they would like tap the tokens it created to cast [Collective Effort] escalated twice. Can they?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling: Sram's Expertise creates the Servos before allowing the free cast, so they can be tapped to pay Collective Effort's escalate (an additional cost not waived by Expertise).
entries.answer:
Yes. Sram's Expertise resolves by following its printed instructions in order (rule 608.2c): first it creates the three 1/1 Servo tokens, and only afterward does its second effect let Avery cast a spell with mana value 3 or less for free. Because the tokens are already on the battlefield, untapped, and under Avery's control by the time the free-cast permission is applied, they are legal creatures to tap for Collective Effort's escalate cost.

When Avery casts Collective Effort during Sram's Expertise's resolution, rule 608.2g says that casting follows the normal casting steps in rules 601.2a-i (just without anyone receiving priority afterward). That means Avery goes through the full casting process from rule 601.2h, including choosing modes (escalate lets you choose more than one mode by paying its tap cost for each mode beyond the first) and paying all costs, including additional costs like escalate's 'tap an untapped creature you control.'

Collective Effort's own ruling confirms that any untapped creature you control can be tapped for escalate, even one you haven't controlled since the start of the turn (Collective Effort ruling #0), so the freshly-created Servo tokens qualify even though they just entered the battlefield moments earlier. Avery has three untapped Servos, so tapping two of them to escalate twice (choosing all three modes) is legal, and one Servo would remain untapped afterward.

One caveat on cost: Sram's Expertise says Avery may cast the spell 'without paying its mana cost' — that only waives the {1}{W}{W} mana cost, not the escalate cost, which is an additional cost, not part of the mana cost, so Avery still must tap creatures to pay it if they want extra modes.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. The instructions of a resolving spell are carried out in the order written, so the tokens will be on the battlefield at that time. Tapping creatures for escalate is an additional cost. ([702.120a]) Avery may still pay an additional cost for Collective Effort while casting it for the alternative cost given to it by Sram's Expertise.

entries.question: Nikolas controls [Mindcrank]. Ari casts [Vampiric Tutor]. Will the card Ari put on top of their library get milled?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same ruling — Mindcrank's trigger is created after Vampiric Tutor finishes resolving and will mill the card Ari put on top of their library.
entries.answer:
Yes — the card that Ari searched for and put on top of their library will end up being milled by Mindcrank's trigger. Here's why: Vampiric Tutor's resolution happens in this order — Ari searches their library for a card, shuffles, and puts that card on top; only after that does Ari lose 2 life. Losing life is the event that triggers Mindcrank ("Whenever an opponent loses life, that player mills that many cards"), but that life-loss event occurs *during* the resolution of Vampiric Tutor. Per rule [704.4], a triggered ability whose trigger condition happens during the resolution of a spell doesn't go on the stack until that spell finishes resolving — it isn't checked or inserted mid-resolution. So Mindcrank's ability is put on the stack only after Vampiric Tutor has completely finished resolving, meaning the tutored card is already sitting on top of Ari's library by the time Mindcrank's trigger is created. When Mindcrank's ability then resolves, Ari mills 2 cards from the top of their library, and since the tutored card is still on top at that point (barring some other effect moving it), it will be the first of the two cards milled. Since Vampiric Tutor's card-selection and shuffle already happened before the life loss (and thus before Mindcrank's trigger even exists), rule [701.24b] about excluding the found card from a shuffle isn't relevant here — the tutored card is simply sitting on top and gets milled like any other top card would. This assumes no other player or effect gets priority and manipulates the library between the life loss and Mindcrank's resolution; if something else changed what's on top of Ari's library in that window, the specific tutored card might not be the one milled, though a mill of 2 would still occur.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mindcrank triggers during the resolution of Vampiric Tutor and will be put onto the stack after Vampiric Tutor finishes resolving. (Ari can cast an instant before the trigger resolves.)

entries.question: Does Nicole have a chance to cast [Surgical Extraction] after Addison has drawn for turn but before they have a chance to cast a sorcery?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: after the draw is performed players receive priority and Nicole may cast an instant (Surgical Extraction) before the main phase, while sorceries cannot be cast then.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Addison draws for turn, priority passes to Nicole before either player reaches the main phase, and since Surgical Extraction is an instant, Nicole can cast it in that window even though no one could cast a sorcery yet.

Here's the sequence: drawing a card for turn is a turn-based action, not something that uses the stack — it happens automatically at the start of the draw step [504.1][703.4d]. Only after that turn-based action is dealt with does the active player, Addison, receive priority [504.2]. If Addison has nothing to do and passes priority, priority moves to the other player, Nicole [117.1][117.1c]. Because Nicole has priority at that point, she may cast an instant like Surgical Extraction — a player with priority can cast any spell whose timing restrictions permit it, and instants have no phase restriction, unlike sorceries [117.1][117.1c].

By contrast, a sorcery can only be cast when a player has priority during a main phase of their own turn with an empty stack [307.5]. The draw step is not a main phase, so at this point in the turn neither Addison nor Nicole could legally cast a sorcery yet — the main phase hasn't started. So the window where Nicole gets priority right after Addison's draw is exactly a window where an instant (Surgical Extraction) can be cast, but a sorcery cannot.

One timing note: this assumes Addison passes priority during the draw step without casting anything first (if Addison instead cast a spell or activated an ability, the stack would need to resolve or players would keep getting priority in turn per rule 608.1 before Nicole's opportunity arises, though the same instant-can-be-cast logic would still apply). Also, this answer is framed for a two-player game; the context here doesn't specify how priority passes among more than two players, so in a multiplayer game the order in which players receive priority after the active player could differ, though the underlying point — instants can be cast outside the main phase while sorceries cannot — would still hold.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Players receive priority in the draw step after a card has been drawn.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Frogtosser Banneret]. Will it affect the cost of [Knowledge Exploitation]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Knowledge Exploitation is a Rogue spell and Frogtosser Banneret reduces its generic mana cost by {1}, including when cast for an alternative cost like prowl.
entries.answer:
Yes. Knowledge Exploitation is a Rogue spell (Kindred Sorcery — Rogue), so Frogtosser Banneret's ability ('Goblin spells and Rogue spells you cast cost {1} less to cast') applies to it, reducing its total cost by {1} generic mana no matter how it's cast.

Frogtosser Banneret's cost reduction is a static ability that modifies the total cost of the spell as it's being cast, per rule [601.2f] ("The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost... plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions"). Per [Frogtosser Banneret ruling #1], this reduction applies 'regardless of whether you chose to pay additional or alternative costs,' and that ruling explicitly uses prowl as its example.

So the effect is:
- If Ashley casts Knowledge Exploitation for its normal mana cost of {5}{U}{U}, Frogtosser Banneret reduces the generic portion by {1}, making the total cost {4}{U}{U}.
- If Ashley instead pays the prowl alternative cost of {3}{U} (per [118.9] and [118.9c], alternative costs replace the mana cost but the spell's mana cost value is unchanged for other purposes), Frogtosser Banneret still reduces the generic portion by {1}, per [118.7] and [118.7a] (cost reductions by generic mana only affect the generic component), making the total prowl cost {2}{U}.

Either way, only the generic mana component is reduced; the colored {U} symbols are unaffected, consistent with [118.7a] and [118.7b].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Knowledge Exploitation is a Rogue.

entries.question: Amir casts [Archon of Cruelty], and before it resolves Norah casts [Surge of Salvation]. What happens when the Archon resolves?
entries.reason: Both say the Archon enters the battlefield but its triggered ETB ability has no legal target because Surge of Salvation gives Norah hexproof, so the ability doesn't do anything and Amir doesn't draw or gain life.
entries.answer:
Archon of Cruelty first finishes resolving as a spell: since it's a creature spell with no targets, under rule [608.3a] it becomes a permanent and enters the battlefield under Amir's control. That entry causes its triggered ability ("Whenever this creature enters or attacks, target opponent sacrifices a creature or planeswalker of their choice, discards a card, and loses 3 life. You draw a card and gain 3 life.") to trigger, and Amir must choose a target opponent for it.

Because Norah cast Surge of Salvation before Archon of Cruelty resolved, and that spell already resolved (it's an instant, so it resolves before Archon of Cruelty does, since the stack resolves last-in-first-out), Norah and the permanents she controls have hexproof until end of turn (per Surge of Salvation's text). Hexproof means Norah can't be the target of spells or abilities that her opponents control. In a two-player game, this leaves Amir with no legal target for Archon of Cruelty's "target opponent" clause, so the ability can't be put on the stack (or, if you assume it was already on the stack when Norah gained hexproof, it would find no legal target to resolve against and do nothing) — either way, no sacrifice, no discard, no life loss for Norah, and Amir also doesn't draw a card or gain 3 life, since that part of the ability is bundled into the same targeted instruction that can't be carried out.

In a multiplayer game, if there are other opponents besides Norah, Amir simply targets one of them instead — hexproof only stops Norah herself from being targeted by Amir's spells/abilities; it doesn't stop Amir from targeting a different opponent, and it doesn't protect Norah's opponents-only status in general. Archon of Cruelty itself still enters the battlefield and is Amir's regardless of any of this, since Surge of Salvation only grants hexproof and damage prevention — it doesn't restrict who can control an entering permanent or how it enters. Note also that Surge of Salvation's damage-prevention clause (preventing damage from black/red sources to creatures Norah controls) is irrelevant here, because Archon of Cruelty's ability causes direct life loss, not damage.

One timing assumption: I'm assuming Surge of Salvation fully resolved (so Norah already has hexproof) before Archon of Cruelty's own resolution/trigger is dealt with, which is guaranteed by the stack (Surge of Salvation was cast in response and resolves first). If instead the trigger had already been put on the stack with Norah chosen as the target before Surge of Salvation resolved, the ruling for Surge of Salvation ([Surge of Salvation ruling #0]) confirms hexproof applies based on permanents/players affected as it resolves — but hexproof would still prevent the already-targeted ability from resolving against Norah once she has hexproof, since a spell/ability with an illegal target when it tries to resolve is countered by the game rules for that portion.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Archon of Cruelty's ability triggers but is not placed onto the stack, since there are no legal targets for it. Amir will not draw a card or gain life.

entries.question: Adelynn controls [Clockwork Beast] which has one +1/+0 counter on it. They want to activate its ability with X = 8. Can they?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: X=8 may be announced and paid, but only up to 6 +1/+0 counters can be placed due to the creature's seven-counter cap.
entries.answer:
Yes, Adelynn can activate Clockwork Beast's ability announcing X = 8, but the resulting effect will still be capped by the creature's own text so only up to 6 of the eight are actually usable. The activation cost is {X}, {T}; per rule [107.3a], the controller (Adelynn) chooses and announces the value of X as part of activating the ability, and nothing about the cap on the +1/+0 counters restricts what X can be declared as — the cap is part of the ability's effect, not its cost. So as long as Adelynn can pay {8} generic mana and tap Clockwork Beast (rule [118.3] requires having the resources to pay a cost in full, and [602.1]/[602.1a] describe the cost as everything before the colon), the activation is legal. When the ability resolves, its text says 'Put up to X +1/+0 counters on this creature. This ability can't cause the total number of +1/+0 counters on this creature to be greater than seven.' Since Clockwork Beast currently has one +1/+0 counter, only 6 more can be added before hitting the cap of seven, so Adelynn may put anywhere from 0 up to 6 counters on it despite X being 8 — the extra 2 simply have no effect, consistent with [Clockwork Beast ruling #1] ('If Clockwork Beast has seven or fewer +1/+0 counters on it when its last ability resolves, it can wind up a maximum of seven such counters on it') and [Clockwork Beast ruling #2], which confirms Adelynn can choose to put fewer than X counters on it. Also note the ability can only be activated during Adelynn's upkeep, per its printed activation restriction.

entries.answer_gold: Yes, but when it resolves Adelynn can't choose to put the full 8 +1/+0 counters on it; only up to 6.

entries.question: Naomi has 7 life and controls two [Death's Shadow]s. Angelo uses [Ajani Unyielding] to exile one of the Death's Shadows. What happens next?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: the exiled Death's Shadow causes Naomi to gain 6 life and then state-based actions cause the remaining Death's Shadow to have 0 toughness and be put into the graveyard before priority is received.
entries.answer:
Naomi gains 6 life, bringing her total to 13. Ajani Unyielding's -2 ability reads "Exile target creature. Its controller gains life equal to its power," and per Ajani Unyielding ruling #1, that life total is based on the creature's power as it last existed on the battlefield. Death's Shadow's -X/-X ability (where X = its controller's life total) only applies while Death's Shadow is on the battlefield (Death's Shadow ruling #0); in every other zone it's just 13/13. So the moment before it was exiled, the targeted Death's Shadow was on the battlefield with Naomi at 7 life, making it a 6/6 (13/13 with -7/-7). That last-existing battlefield power of 6 is what Naomi gains as life, going from 7 to 13. The exiled Death's Shadow itself becomes a new object in exile (rule 400.7/406.7) and is simply a 13/13 card there, since its ability no longer applies outside the battlefield.

This also has a knock-on effect on Naomi's remaining Death's Shadow, which is still on the battlefield: with Naomi now at 13 life, that Death's Shadow's own -X/-X ability gives it -13/-13, making it a 13/13 with -13/-13 = 0/0. A 0-toughness creature is checked and dealt with by state-based actions (rule 704.1 defines state-based actions as automatic game actions checked whenever their conditions are met); the specific sub-rule stating that a 0-toughness creature is put into its owner's graveyard isn't included in the rules text provided to me, but 704.1 confirms this kind of check happens automatically and immediately once the life total changes, before any player gets priority. So functionally, expect Naomi's remaining Death's Shadow to die as a state-based action right after her life total updates, though I can't cite the exact toughness-based clause from the given context.

Assuming timing: this all happens as Ajani Unyielding's -2 ability resolves (the exile and life gain happen simultaneously as part of that one resolution), immediately followed by a state-based action check. If instead Naomi's life total changed by some other effect before Ajani Unyielding's ability resolved, the life gained would still be 6, since it's fixed by the exiled Death's Shadow's last battlefield power, not by any later life total.

entries.answer_gold: Death's Shadow is a 6/6 when it gets exiled, so Naomi gains 6 life. Before Angelo receives priority again, state-based actions are checked, and the game sees that the remaining Death's Shadow now has 0 toughness, and it will be put into Naomi's graveyard.

entries.question: Aniyah currently controls Nico's commander. Can Aniyah cast [Fierce Guardianship] for its alternative cost?

Fierce Guardianship's alternative cost only asks whether Aniyah controls a commander, and rule 903.3d says that when an effect refers to "controlling a commander," it means controlling a permanent on the battlefield that is a commander — it does not require that the commander be Aniyah's own. Since Aniyah currently controls the permanent that is Nico's commander (per rule 110.2b, the permanent's controller is the player who currently has control of it, which is Aniyah in this case), Aniyah satisfies Fierce Guardianship's condition "If you control a commander." Fierce Guardianship (card text) therefore lets Aniyah cast it without paying its mana cost of {2}{U}, using the alternative-cost rules in 118.9c (the alternative cost replaces the mana cost but doesn't change what the spell's mana cost is considered to be for other purposes). entries.question: Nia controls [Hollowhenge Huntmaster]. Anders casts [Flesh Duplicate]. Can they have it enter the battlefield as a copy of Hollowhenge Huntmaster?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Flesh Duplicate can enter as a copy of Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster because the copy effect doesn't target.
entries.answer:
Yes. Flesh Duplicate's ability lets its controller choose to have it enter as a copy of "any creature on the battlefield," with no restriction on who controls that creature, so Anders can choose to copy Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster even though Nia, not Anders, controls the original.

When this happens, per rule [707.2] and [707.2a], Flesh Duplicate's copiable values (name, color indicator, card type, subtypes, rules text, power/toughness) become those printed on Hollowhenge Huntmaster as it currently exists (the transformed, 'night' face). So the resulting permanent, now controlled by Anders (the copy's controller is whoever controls the copy, not the original), will be:
- Named Hollowhenge Huntmaster
- A green (via its color indicator, rule [204.1]) Werewolf creature, 6/6
- Have "Hexproof"
- Have "Other permanents you control have hexproof" — this now applies to Anders's other permanents, since the copy is controlled by Anders
- Have "At the beginning of combat on your turn, put two +1/+1 counters on each creature you control" — again referring to Anders's creatures
- Have Nightbound (the day/night trigger is a global game state, not player-specific, so this ability functions normally for whoever controls it)

Additionally, Flesh Duplicate's own text is a copy effect with a built-in exception (rule [707.9a]): "except it has vanishing 3 if that creature doesn't have vanishing." Since Hollowhenge Huntmaster does not have vanishing, this exception applies, and the copy also gains vanishing 3 as part of its copiable values, entering with three time counters on it.

One caveat on timing: as with any copy, any choices normally made on entering the battlefield (there are none extra here beyond the copy choice itself) are made fresh by Anders, not copied from Nia's permanent (rule [707.6] illustrates this principle, though Hollowhenge Huntmaster has no 'as this enters' choice to make).

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Hexproof prevents Hollowhenge Huntmaster from being the target of an opponent's spell or ability, but Flesh Duplicate doesn't target anything.

entries.question: Ada casts [Shaman of the Pack]. In response to its trigger, Nickolas kills it with [Foolish Fate]. How much life does Nickolas lose?

entries.answer:
Nickolas loses 0 life from Shaman of the Pack's triggered ability (assuming Ada controls no other Elves), because Shaman of the Pack is destroyed before its own triggered ability resolves, and the ability's life-loss total is counted at the time it resolves.

Here's the sequence: Shaman of the Pack enters the battlefield, and its triggered ability ("target opponent loses life equal to the number of Elves you control") is put on the stack targeting Nickolas as the target opponent (since this is presumably a two-player game between Ada and Nickolas). In response to that trigger, Nickolas casts Foolish Fate targeting Shaman of the Pack and it resolves, destroying Shaman of the Pack before the triggered ability gets a chance to resolve.

When the Shaman of the Pack triggered ability finally resolves, the game checks how many Elves Ada currently controls. Per [Shaman of the Pack ruling #0], you count the number of Elves you control 'as Shaman of the Pack's ability resolves, including Shaman of the Pack if it's still on the battlefield' — the clear implication being that if Shaman of the Pack is no longer on the battlefield (as is the case here, since it's now in the graveyard), it is not counted. This is a fresh state-based count taken at resolution, not a 'last known information' snapshot from when the ability triggered — [113.7a] governs when a source's own information (such as its power/toughness for a damage-dealing ability) is checked, but here the relevant count is simply 'Elves you control' on the current battlefield, and Shaman of the Pack's own ruling tells us directly how to evaluate it in this scenario.

Since the question doesn't mention Ada controlling any other Elves, the count is 0, so Nickolas loses 0 life. If Ada does control other Elf creatures, Nickolas would instead lose life equal to that number.

Separately, Foolish Fate's Infusion ability ('If you gained life this turn, that creature's controller loses 3 life') would make Shaman of the Pack's controller — Ada, not Nickolas — lose 3 life if Nickolas had gained life this turn; nothing in the question indicates that happened, and in any case it would not cause Nickolas himself to lose life.

entries.answer_gold: 0. When Shaman of the Pack's trigger resolves, Ada controls no Elves.
