entries.question: Amina attacks with [Retaliation]. Nico declares no blocks and then casts [Curtain of Light] targeting Retaliation. Does Retaliation trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Retaliation’s ability does not trigger (no trigger occurs).
entries.answer:
No — this exact scenario is impossible, because Retaliation is an Enchantment, not a creature, so it can never be an "attacking creature" in the first place. Rule [506.3e] states that only a creature can attack; Retaliation's card text merely grants creatures you control the triggered ability "Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature, this creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn." Retaliation itself never attacks and is never blocked or unblocked. Consequently, Curtain of Light ("Target unblocked attacking creature becomes blocked") has no legal target if you try to target Retaliation, since Retaliation isn't an unblocked attacking creature — see [Curtain of Light ruling #1], which confirms the spell only has legal targets among unblocked attacking creatures during the combat phase. If a player actually attempted to cast Curtain of Light targeting Retaliation, that would be an illegal action: under [733.1], the entire action is reversed, any payments are canceled, and "no abilities trigger and no effects apply as a result of an undone action." So Retaliation's granted ability does not trigger, because the whole attempted play is undone as illegal rather than resolving. If instead you meant that a creature you control (which has Retaliation's granted ability due to Retaliation being on the battlefield) is the attacker being targeted, then Curtain of Light making it blocked would indeed cause that creature's "becomes blocked by a creature" trigger to fire, per [509.3c] and [509.3d], since it was unblocked and then became blocked. But as literally stated — attacking with, and targeting, Retaliation the enchantment — that cannot happen.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Retaliation became blocked, but not by any creatures.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Rest in Peace] and targets Nataly's [Dauthi Voidwalker] with [Lightning Bolt]. What happens to each card?
entries.reason: The candidate denies that Dauthi Voidwalker's replacement ability can apply to Lightning Bolt (and omits the controller's choice), while the reference says both replacement effects apply to the Bolt so its controller chooses whether it is exiled with a void counter.
entries.answer:
Both Lightning Bolt and Dauthi Voidwalker end up in exile, not in any graveyard — but for different reasons tied to Rest in Peace, not to Dauthi Voidwalker's own ability.

What happens to Dauthi Voidwalker: Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Dauthi Voidwalker (a 3/2), which is lethal damage. Under rule [704.5g], a creature with lethal damage marked on it "has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed" as a state-based action, and this destruction event is normally what sends it to the graveyard, satisfying the definition of "dies" in [700.4] (put into a graveyard from the battlefield). However, Rest in Peace's ability — "If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead" — is a replacement effect ([614.1]) that intercepts this event and sends Dauthi Voidwalker to exile instead of to Nataly's graveyard.

Importantly, Dauthi Voidwalker's own ability ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it") does NOT apply to itself here: Dauthi Voidwalker is owned/controlled by Nataly, and it would be going to Nataly's own graveyard, not "an opponent's" graveyard from Nataly's perspective (its controller). So the only applicable replacement effect is Ariel's Rest in Peace, and no APNAP choice ([101.4], [616.1f]) is even needed since just one effect applies — Dauthi Voidwalker is simply exiled with no void counter, and no "dies" trigger occurs because it never reaches a graveyard.

What happens to Lightning Bolt: after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving, it would normally be put into Ariel's graveyard as a used instant. Rest in Peace's text explicitly covers "a card or token" being put into a graveyard "from anywhere," which includes spells going to the graveyard after resolving — this is confirmed by Rest in Peace's own ruling that even a spell destroying Rest in Peace itself still gets exiled afterward instead of hitting the graveyard [Rest in Peace ruling #1]. So Lightning Bolt is exiled instead of going to Ariel's graveyard.

Note on card text overriding general rules: Rest in Peace's printed replacement effect overrides the normal graveyard-bound outcome that rules [704.5g] and [700.4] would otherwise produce, and it takes priority over Dauthi Voidwalker's ability simply because Dauthi Voidwalker's ability doesn't apply to this particular event at all (it only affects opponents' cards from its controller's point of view). This analysis holds the same whether the game has two players or more, since Dauthi Voidwalker's ability is defined relative to its own controller regardless of table size, and only one replacement effect (Rest in Peace) is actually competing for this event.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Ariel chooses whether Lightning Bolt goes to exile with or without a counter.

There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Lightning Bolt going to the graveyard with it going to exile, so its controller gets to choose which to apply.

Then state-based actions are checked and Dauthi Voidwalker is put into exile.

entries.question: Ainsley and Noor are starting a two-player game. Ainsley decides to keep their hand of 7 cards. Noor decides to mulligan. Can Ainsley now decide to mulligan?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: once Ainsley keeps their opening hand they cannot later choose to mulligan, even if the other player does.
entries.answer:
No. Once Ainsley declared that they would keep their hand of 7 cards, that hand became their opening hand, and rule 103.5 says a player who chooses not to take a mulligan may not take any further mulligans, regardless of what other players decide afterward. Noor's later decision to mulligan does not reopen that choice for Ainsley.

The mulligan process works like this: the starting player declares first whether they will mulligan, then each other player in turn order does the same, and only after all players have declared does anyone actually shuffle back and redraw (103.5). Declaring 'keep' locks in that player's opening hand immediately — it's a one-way decision. Since this is a two-player game, there's no multiplayer wrinkle here (the multiplayer/Brawl rule in 800.6 and 103.5c only changes how many cards get put on the bottom for later mulligans, not whether a player who already kept can change their mind).

So in this scenario, Ainsley is locked into their 7-card opening hand, while Noor proceeds to shuffle their hand back in, draw a new 7-card hand, and (since this would be Noor's first mulligan) put back 0 cards, per 103.5.
entries.answer_gold: No.

entries.question: Anahi casts [Aura Mutation] targeting Nehemiah's [Leyline of the Void]. Will Aura Mutation go to Anahi's graveyard or exile?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Aura Mutation destroys Leyline of the Void during resolution so the Leyline's replacement effect isn't present when Aura Mutation is put into the graveyard, so it goes to Anahi's graveyard.
entries.answer:
Aura Mutation goes to Anahi's graveyard, not to exile. Because Aura Mutation itself destroys Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void as part of resolving its own text, the Leyline of the Void is gone from the battlefield before Aura Mutation reaches the step where it would be put into a graveyard - so its replacement effect ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") is no longer in effect when Aura Mutation actually leaves the stack.

Here's the sequencing: when a spell resolves, its stated instructions (here, "Destroy target enchantment. Create X 1/1 green Saproling creature tokens...") are carried out per rule [608.2c], and only after all such instructional steps are completed does the spell reach the final steps described in [608.2n] and [608.2m], at which point, as the final part of its resolution, the instant is put into its owner's graveyard as stated in [304.2] and [404.1]. So the order is: Aura Mutation destroys Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void and creates its Saproling tokens first, and only afterward does Aura Mutation itself get put into a graveyard.

By the time that last step happens, Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void has already been destroyed and put into Nehemiah's own graveyard (its own controller's graveyard, not an opponent's, so its own exile clause never even applied to itself). Since Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void is no longer on the battlefield, its static replacement ability ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") is no longer active and cannot intercept Aura Mutation going to Anahi's graveyard, since a permanent's replacement effect generally only applies while that permanent is on the battlefield to generate it. So Aura Mutation ends up in Anahi's graveyard as a normal instant.

This assumes Aura Mutation successfully resolves (its target, Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void, remains legal at resolution per [608.2b]) - if for some reason the Leyline of the Void had already left the battlefield or become an illegal target before Aura Mutation resolved, Aura Mutation would be removed from the stack and still go to Anahi's graveyard under [608.2b] and [404.1], with the same ultimate result (exile of Leyline of the Void never happening and Aura Mutation still landing in Anahi's graveyard, unaffected either way).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Graveyard. Leyline of the Void is destroyed before Aura Mutation goes to the graveyard, since going to the graveyard is the last part of a spell resolving.

entries.question: Ari controls [Omnath, Locus of Creation] and [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines]. They play [Tainted Peak]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both explain that Elesh Norn causes Omnath's landfall to trigger twice, which when resolved gives 4 life first and then {R}{G}{U}{W} (with no third trigger), so the candidate reaches the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
Playing Tainted Peak causes Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability to trigger twice instead of once, and the two resulting triggers resolve one after the other, giving Ari 4 life and then filling their mana pool with {R}{G}{W}{U}.

Here's why: Tainted Peak, a land Ari controls, enters the battlefield. Normally this would cause exactly one instance of Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability ("Whenever a land you control enters...") to trigger. However, Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines has the static ability "If a permanent entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." Since Tainted Peak entering is what causes Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability to trigger, and Omnath, Locus of Creation is a permanent Ari controls, Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines' ability makes that landfall ability trigger a second time as well. (Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines' other ability, which shuts off opponents' entering-triggers, is irrelevant here since Ari controls both permanents.)

Both resulting triggered abilities are separate objects that go on the stack — per the ruling on Omnath, Locus of Creation, landfall always uses the stack and can be responded to, so it is not a mana ability even on later resolutions in the same turn [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #4]. Since Ari controls both triggered abilities, Ari chooses the order to put them on the stack [603.3b] (this ordering step is the APNAP-order procedure referenced in [603.3b] and [101.4], but since only Ari has triggers here, Ari simply picks the order).

Whichever one resolves first counts as the first time Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability has resolved this turn, so Ari gains 4 life. The one that resolves second counts as the second time, so Ari adds {R}{G}{W}{U} to their mana pool [Omnath, Locus of Creation text]. Because only one land entered, there is no third resolution, so no damage is dealt this turn [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #3]. Note Tainted Peak itself only taps for {C}, or for {B} or {R} if Ari controls a Swamp — it is not itself producing the {R}{G}{W}{U}; that mana comes purely from Omnath, Locus of Creation's second landfall resolution.

This assumes no one responds to either trigger on the stack; if an opponent responds (e.g., removing Omnath, Locus of Creation or Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines) between the two triggers resolving, the second trigger could fail to do anything or the doubling could be undone before it applies, per how zone-change/ability-based effects check state at resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability triggers twice. The first instance of the ability will cause Ari to gain 4 life and the second instance will add {R}{G}{U}{W} to their mana pool. Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines will cause the ability to trigger twice since it triggers as the result of a permanent entering the battlefield. Omnath, Locus of Creation's triggered ability has an effect depending on how many times its resolved this turn, so the second instance that resolves will have the second effect.

entries.question: Amiya controls [Fetid Gargantua] with two +1/+1 counters on it. Nico controls [Soul-Scar Mage] and casts [Scorching Lava] targeting Fetid Gargantua. After Scorching Lava resolves, can Fetid Gargantua adapt again?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Soul-Scar Mage turns the damage into -1/-1 counters which are removed against Fetid Gargantua's +1/+1 counters by state-based actions leaving it with no +1/+1 counters, so Adapt can be activated again and will put counters on.
entries.answer:
Yes. Soul-Scar Mage's replacement effect turns Scorching Lava's 2 damage to Fetid Gargantua into 2 -1/-1 counters instead of damage (Soul-Scar Mage's printed ability, and Soul-Scar Mage ruling #2 confirms this is a replacement, not damage prevention). Fetid Gargantua already had two +1/+1 counters on it, so after Scorching Lava resolves it has two +1/+1 counters and two -1/-1 counters simultaneously. As a state-based action, since a permanent can't have both +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters, N of each are removed, where N is the smaller number present [704.5q, 122.3]. Here N=2, so all four counters (both +1/+1 and both -1/-1) are removed, leaving Fetid Gargantua with zero +1/+1 counters. Since Fetid Gargantua's Adapt ability only puts counters on it 'if this permanent has no +1/+1 counters on it' [701.46a], and Fetid Gargantua's own ruling confirms 'If a creature somehow loses all of its +1/+1 counters, it can adapt again and get more +1/+1 counters' [Fetid Gargantua ruling #1], Amiya can activate {2}{B}: Adapt 2 on Fetid Gargantua again and this time it will actually put two more +1/+1 counters on it (also triggering its draw-two-cards ability). Note: Amiya could always activate the Adapt ability even before this happened [Fetid Gargantua ruling #0], but it wouldn't have put counters on while Fetid Gargantua still had a +1/+1 counter — after the counters cancel out, activating it will now succeed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. If a permanent has both -1/-1 and +1/+1 counters on it, they are removed as a state-based action. Adapt checks the number of +1/+1 counters on Fetid Gargantua as it resolves, it doesn't matter if it's been activated in the past.

entries.question: Ari controls [Emeria Shepherd]. They play [Sacred Peaks], and target [Garenbrig Carver] in their graveyard. In response, Noelle activates [Alchemist's Refuge]. When that ability resolves, they casts [Blood Moon]. When Emeria Shepherd's ability resolves, where is Garenbrig Carver?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference — Blood Moon makes Sacred Peaks not a Plains at resolution, so Emeria Shepherd can only return Garenbrig Carver to Ari's hand.
entries.answer:
Garenbrig Carver ends up in Ari's hand, not on the battlefield — Emeria Shepherd's ability only gets to use its "return to hand" mode, because by the time the triggered ability resolves, Sacred Peaks is no longer a Plains.

Here's the sequence: Ari plays Sacred Peaks, which triggers Emeria Shepherd's landfall ability ("Whenever a land you control enters, you may return target nonland permanent card from your graveyard to your hand. If that land is a Plains, you may return that nonland permanent card to the battlefield instead."), targeting Garenbrig Carver in the graveyard. That triggered ability goes on the stack. In response, Noelle activates Alchemist's Refuge's ability ("{G}{U}, {T}: You may cast spells this turn as though they had flash"), which resolves first, giving Noelle flash permission. Noelle then casts Blood Moon, which goes on top of the stack above Emeria Shepherd's still-pending trigger.

Blood Moon resolves first (last-in-first-out stack resolution). Its text, "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," is a card-text effect that overrides Sacred Peaks' normal characteristics — Sacred Peaks (a nonbasic Land — Mountain Plains) becomes simply a Mountain and stops being a Plains, since Blood Moon's static effect sets its types outright.

Only after that does Emeria Shepherd's triggered ability resolve. The "if that land is a Plains" clause is a condition inside the effect that is checked using the object's current characteristics at resolution, not a special look-back-in-time trigger condition — rule [603.10] frames "looking back in time" as a limited exception to the normal rule that objects are evaluated as they exist at the relevant point in the game (here, at resolution), and Emeria Shepherd's land-type check isn't one of those listed look-back exceptions. Since Sacred Peaks is a Mountain (not a Plains) at that moment because of Blood Moon's effect, the "return to the battlefield instead" branch is unavailable, and Ari may only return Garenbrig Carver to their hand.

Garenbrig Carver itself never leaves the graveyard during this sequence except via Emeria Shepherd's resolution, so it remains a legal target for the whole time [603.6], [603.6c]. Card text: Emeria Shepherd's printed ability and Blood Moon's printed ability both override how the general zone/characteristic rules would otherwise apply, and I'm applying them as written.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Blood Moon fully resolves (including any state-based actions afterward) before Emeria Shepherd's trigger resolves, which is guaranteed by normal stack ordering since Blood Moon was cast on top of the already-triggered ability. If instead Blood Moon had resolved before Sacred Peaks entered the battlefield (impossible here since the land drop is what triggered everything), the outcome would be the same — Sacred Peaks would never have been a Plains at all.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Ari's hand.

Blood Moon changes Sacred Peaks's subtypes to "Mountain", and Sacred Peaks loses all other subtypes. During the resolution of the ability, Sacred Peaks is no longer a Plains and therefore Garenbrig Carver will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [General Ferrous Rokiric]. What happens when they cast [Illusion]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude General Ferrous Rokiric's ability does not trigger because Illusion is monocolored on the stack, so no Golem is created.
entries.answer:
Casting Illusion does not trigger General Ferrous Rokiric's ability, because Illusion is a monocolored (blue) card, not a multicolored one — so General Ferrous Rokiric's Golem-making trigger simply doesn't fire, and Illusion just resolves and enters the battlefield as normal.

General Ferrous Rokiric's relevant ability reads: "Whenever you cast a multicolored spell, create a 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token." The trigger condition is specifically "a multicolored spell," meaning a spell with two or more colors. The card data for Illusion lists it as a single color (its color identity is U, i.e., blue only) — it has no second color, so it is monocolored, not multicolored. Casting it therefore does not meet the condition needed to trigger General Ferrous Rokiric's token-creation ability, and Ainsley does not get a 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token from this cast.

As a side note, General Ferrous Rokiric's other ability, Hexproof from monocolored, only matters when something is trying to target General Ferrous Rokiric with a monocolored source; it has no bearing on whether casting the monocolored Illusion triggers the Golem-making ability, since that ability isn't a targeted effect being cast at General Ferrous Rokiric at all — it's just an unrelated spell being cast by its controller. So the only consequence of casting Illusion here is that Illusion itself resolves and enters the battlefield normally; no Golem token is created because the 'multicolored spell' condition was never met.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: General Ferrous Rokiric won't trigger. While Illusion is a multicolored card elsewhere, on the stack it's a monocolored card.

entries.question:
Aydan casts [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded], and Nico answers by casting [Spell Queller], exiling Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with its triggered ability.
When Spell Queller leaves the battlefield, can Aydan choose to cast [Birthright Boon] or do they have to cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference conclude that Spell Queller’s leave‑the‑battlefield ability creates a new casting of the card, so Aydan may choose to cast either Kellan, the Fae‑Blooded or its Adventure, Birthright Boon.
entries.answer:
Yes — when Spell Queller's leaves-the-battlefield ability lets Aydan cast the exiled card, Aydan gets to choose again whether to cast it as the creature spell Kellan, the Fae-Blooded or as the Adventure sorcery spell Birthright Boon.

Here's why: Aydan originally cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (the creature face, not the Adventure), and Nico's Spell Queller exiled that spell with its 'enters' ability. When Spell Queller later leaves the battlefield, its second triggered ability lets Aydan 'cast that card' without paying its mana cost. Per Spell Queller ruling #2, this new casting 'has no relation to the spell that player originally cast,' and any choices made for the original spell aren't carried over. That means Aydan isn't locked into re-casting the same face that was exiled — the act of casting the card is treated as a brand-new casting.

Because it's a fresh casting of the card, the normal rule for adventurer cards applies: rule [715.3d] says that 'as a player plays an adventurer card, the player chooses whether they play the card normally or as an Adventure' — this choice is made as part of the casting process itself. Since Spell Queller's ability triggers a new casting (Spell Queller ruling #2), Aydan makes this choice fresh and may pick either Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (creature) or Birthright Boon (Adventure sorcery).

Note on timing: Spell Queller ruling #3 confirms that 'timing permissions based on the card's type are ignored' when casting this way, so the fact that Birthright Boon is normally sorcery-speed doesn't stop Aydan from casting it at whatever point Spell Queller leaves the battlefield (though other restrictions, if any existed, would still apply). Also, since the original spell was Kellan, the Fae-Blooded (not Birthright Boon), Kellan ruling #4 — which says an adventurer card only grants permission to cast the permanent later if it was exiled by resolving as the Adventure — is not relevant here; the permission to cast at all is coming from Spell Queller's own ability, not from Kellan's Adventure mechanic.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aydan can choose to cast either Kellan, the Fae-Blooded or Birthright Boon when Spell Queller leaves the battlefield.

entries.question: Can Nicolas cast [Memory Lapse] targeting Aubrianna's [Underworld Charger] that is escaping from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both say escape is an alternative cost that puts Underworld Charger on the stack as a spell and that Memory Lapse can target and counter it (with the candidate's extra replacement-effect detail consistent with the reference).
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Aubrianna activates Underworld Charger's escape ability and it becomes a spell on the stack, it is a legal target for Memory Lapse. Escape (rule 702.138a) works as an alternative cost under the normal casting rules (601.2b), so once Underworld Charger is cast this way it exists on the stack as a creature spell like any other. Memory Lapse's text says "Counter target spell," and per rule 109.2b, a description using the word "spell" refers to an object on the stack — the escaping Underworld Charger spell qualifies, and spells are legal targets under rule 115.2's exception for objects that can't exist on the battlefield. So Nicolas may cast Memory Lapse targeting it.

If Memory Lapse resolves and counters the Underworld Charger spell, Memory Lapse's own replacement effect determines what happens next: instead of going to Aubrianna's graveyard, the countered Underworld Charger card is put on top of Aubrianna's library (Memory Lapse card text). Note that this differs from the Flashback interaction described in the Memory Lapse rulings — Flashback has a built-in replacement that would send the card to exile instead of the graveyard when it leaves the stack, overriding Memory Lapse's own replacement (per the Memory Lapse ruling about flashback). Escape, however, has no such 'exile instead of graveyard' clause (unlike Flashback, rule 702.34a, or Jump-start, rule 702.133a); escape only changes how the card is cast, not what happens to it afterward. So there's no competing replacement effect here, and Memory Lapse's 'put it on top of its owner's library' effect applies cleanly, sending Underworld Charger to the top of Aubrianna's library rather than her graveyard.

This analysis assumes the standard two-player framing implied by 'owner's library' and 'that player's graveyard' in Memory Lapse's text; the rules provided don't include multiplayer-specific wording for Memory Lapse, but nothing here depends on how many players are in the game — the targeting and replacement mechanics work the same regardless of player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Escape is an alternative cost ([702.138a]), which means that once paid the escaped spell is on the stack, and can be interacted with as normal. Countering a spell means to remove that spell from the stack before it resolves. Underworld Charger is a legal target for Memory Lapse.

entries.question: Ariyah has [Guardian Naga] in their graveyard. Can they flash back Guardian Naga's Adventure with [Flashback]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Guardian Naga in the graveyard is only a creature card (not an instant or sorcery) and therefore cannot be targeted by Flashback, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
No. In Ariyah's graveyard, Guardian Naga has only its normal characteristics — it is a creature card, not an instant or sorcery card. Rule [715.4] states that in every zone except the stack (and even on the stack when not cast as the Adventure), an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics; the Adventure side's characteristics (Banishing Coils, an instant) only apply while the spell is being cast/is on the stack specifically as the Adventure. The spell Flashback requires you to target 'target instant or sorcery card in your graveyard,' and Guardian Naga does not meet that requirement while sitting in the graveyard, since it's a creature card there, not an instant or sorcery card. It does not matter that Guardian Naga 'has an Adventure' in the sense of rule [715.2a]/[Guardian Naga // Banishing Coils ruling #7] — that phrasing only matters for effects that specifically ask whether a card 'has an Adventure,' not for effects like Flashback that check the card's actual current type. So Guardian Naga is not a legal target for the Flashback spell, and Ariyah cannot give it flashback or cast it as Banishing Coils this way. (This assumes Guardian Naga is sitting in the graveyard as itself, not currently on the stack as an Adventure spell — if it were somehow on the stack as the Banishing Coils Adventure spell, the Flashback spell still couldn't target it there since Flashback only targets cards in a graveyard.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. An Adventure defines alternative characteristics the card can have when cast as an Adventure. Adventurer cards only have their normal characteristics in every zone other than the stack, so it's not a legal target for Flashback.

entries.question: Ace controls [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker] and activates its ability, turning it into a creature. They then play a second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker. What happens when the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that when the second Sarkhan enters, the legend rule is applied as a state-based action and Ace must choose one Sarkhan to put into their graveyard.
entries.answer:
As soon as the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker enters the battlefield, the legend rule triggers as a state-based action, and Ace must choose one of the two Sarkhans to keep — the other is put into its owner's graveyard.

When a planeswalker spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control [306.2], and it enters with loyalty counters equal to its printed loyalty (4, from Sarkhan's intrinsic replacement ability) [306.5b]. Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is a legendary planeswalker card [306.4], and its own text notes that when it uses its +1 ability it becomes a legendary 4/4 red Dragon creature (it keeps the legendary supertype, per its printed text and [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker ruling #1], which confirms it retains its loyalty counters while a creature). Because Ace now controls two legendary permanents both named "Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker" — the original, currently a creature with its existing loyalty counters, and the newly-entered planeswalker — rule [704.5j] (the "legend rule") applies: it only cares about matching names, controller, and the legendary supertype, not about current card type. This is checked as a state-based action [704.1], which will be checked before any player receives priority, so it happens essentially immediately after the second Sarkhan resolves.

Under the legend rule, Ace chooses which one to keep; the other is put into Ace's graveyard [704.5j], [Legend Rule]. If Ace keeps the newly-entered planeswalker, the original Sarkhan (now a creature with its accumulated loyalty counters) is put into the graveyard. If Ace instead keeps the original Sarkhan (which is currently a creature, not a planeswalker, but still legendary), the freshly-resolved second Sarkhan planeswalker is put into the graveyard before it can be activated. Note this scenario is not the "copy" case described in [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker ruling #2] since Ace cast an actual second copy of the card rather than creating a copy via an effect, but the same legend-rule outcome results either way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: As soon as the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked and Ace will need to choose one Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker to put into their graveyard. Regardless of what card type they are, both Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker are legendary permanents with the same name, and therefore the 'legend rule' applies.

entries.answer:
