Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Loxodon Wayfarer is considered an attacking creature until the end of the combat phase, and is therefore still a legal target for Reconnaissance's activated ability.

entries.question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—saying the activation is illegal because the exile-from-graveyard cost can't be paid with an empty graveyard, whereas the reference says the activation is legal.
entries.answer:
No, Arjun cannot activate Molten-Tail Masticore's first activated ability. That ability costs "{4}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: This creature deals 4 damage to any target," and exiling a creature card from the graveyard is part of the activation cost. Under rule 118.3, a player can't pay a cost without having the necessary resources to pay it fully — since Arjun's graveyard has no cards at all, there is no creature card available to exile, so this cost cannot be paid, and the ability can't legally be activated (rule 602.5 confirms a player can't even begin to activate an ability that's prohibited/impossible to pay for). Thermopod's own abilities (its {S} haste ability and its 'Sacrifice a creature: Add {R}' mana ability) don't change this — they could help produce mana or fill the graveyard with a non-creature card via sacrifice, but sacrificing Thermopod itself would put a creature card in the graveyard, which isn't what's happening here since Arjun currently has zero cards in the graveyard when the question is posed. As stated, with an empty graveyard, the additional cost simply cannot be met.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Arjun first puts the ability onto the stack, after which it won't matter if Molten-Tail Masticore is on the battlefield anymore. Arjun then has a chance to activate mana abilities, at which point they can sacrifice Molten-Tail Masticore. Then Arjun pays the cost of the spell, exiling Molten-Tail Masticore from their graveyard.

entries.question: Can Ashley pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast [Beseech the Queen] or is Ashley limited to only paying {B}{B}{B} to do so?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Ashley may choose to pay {6} (via the {2} options for each {2/B}) and can pay that {6} with six black mana, resulting in a legal {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} payment.
entries.answer:
Ashley is not limited to {B}{B}{B} -- she can legally pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} for Beseech the Queen. Beseech the Queen's cost is {2/B}{2/B}{2/B}, where each {2/B} is a monocolored hybrid symbol that can be paid with either one black mana or two mana of any type (including two black mana, since generic-mana costs can always be paid with mana of any color). As Ashley proposes casting the spell, she chooses for each of the three {2/B} symbols how to pay it (rule 118.13a: 'If the mana cost of a spell ... contains a mana symbol that can be paid in multiple ways, the choice of how to pay for that symbol is made as its controller proposes that spell'). If she chooses the '2 generic mana' option for all three symbols, she owes {2}{2}{2}, i.e. 6 generic mana total, and she may pay that entirely with six black mana, since generic mana can be paid with mana of any color. This exactly matches Beseech the Queen ruling #3, which explicitly lists {B}{B}{B}, {2}{B}{B}, {4}{B}, or {6} as valid ways to pay -- and paying that {6} (or any of the generic portions) with black mana produces the all-black {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} payment. Note that regardless of how she pays, Beseech the Queen's mana value remains 6 and it is still black (Beseech the Queen rulings #1-#2), since alternative ways of paying a hybrid cost don't change the spell's mana cost or color identity (rules 118.9c/118.8d apply the same underlying principle to alternative/additional costs, and rule 601.2f confirms the total cost is locked in and paid without changing the printed mana cost). This scenario assumes a standard two-player or multiplayer casting sequence; the payment mechanics here don't differ based on player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: After the first step of casting a spell, which is announcing it and moving it to the stack, Ashley makes choices regarding modes, alternative costs, additional costs, etc. This step includes deciding whether they will be paying {B} or {2} for each hybrid symbol ({2/B}) in Beseech the Queen's mana cost. They may always choose to cast it for {6} instead of {B}{B}{B} (or {2}{B}{B} or {4}{B}). Later on during the casting of the spell, the colorless parts of the mana cost may be paid with any color, including black.

entries.question: Arielle has [Blessed Hippogriff] in their graveyard. Arielle casts [Mission Briefing], can they choose to cast the adventure of Blessed Hippogriff?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling — Blessed Hippogriff is a creature card in the graveyard and thus cannot be chosen by Mission Briefing as an instant or sorcery because its Adventure characteristics aren't present there.
entries.answer:
No. In the graveyard, Blessed Hippogriff has only its normal characteristics (a creature card), not the alternative Adventure characteristics of Tyr's Blessing. Rule 715.4 states that in every zone except the stack (and while on the stack not as an Adventure), an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics. Mission Briefing requires Arielle to choose "an instant or sorcery card in your graveyard," and since Blessed Hippogriff is a creature card while sitting in the graveyard, it does not qualify as an instant or sorcery card there — even though its Adventure half, Tyr's Blessing, is an Instant. Therefore Arielle cannot select Blessed Hippogriff with Mission Briefing at all, whether to cast it as the creature or as the Tyr's Blessing Adventure. If Arielle instead had a spell in the graveyard that actually is an instant or sorcery card by its normal characteristics, Mission Briefing would let her cast that spell this turn, and if that card happened to be an exiled Adventure creature (per 715.3d) rather than a graveyard card, different rules would apply — but that's not the scenario here since the card is in the graveyard as a creature card.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Adventurer cards have an alternative set of characteristics, however any time an Adventurer card is anywhere other than the stack it only has the characteristics of the creature portion. Mission Briefing requires Arielle to choose an instant or sorcery card in their graveyard, and they cannot choose Blessed Hippogriff.

entries.question: Neriah controls [Cliffhaven Sell-Sword]. Ari casts [Oubliette] targeting it. Will Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phase back in at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling as the reference: Oubliette's "until this leaves the battlefield" phasing prevents the creature from phasing in at the untap step and it only phases in when Oubliette leaves.
entries.answer:
No. Cliffhaven Sell-Sword will not phase back in during Neriah's untap step. Oubliette's triggered ability phases Cliffhaven Sell-Sword out "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield," which is the special kind of one-shot phasing effect described in rule 610.4a: a second one-shot effect is created that will cause Cliffhaven Sell-Sword to phase in only when Oubliette leaves the battlefield. Rule 610.4a explicitly states that a permanent phased out this way doesn't phase in as a result of the turn-based action during a player's untap step (rule 502.1/703.4a), which is the normal way phased-out permanents would phase in (rule 702.26a). This is confirmed by [Oubliette ruling #7], which says the phased-out creature phases in immediately after Oubliette leaves the battlefield, not during its controller's untap step. So Cliffhaven Sell-Sword remains phased out indefinitely (treated as though it doesn't exist, per Oubliette's reminder text and rule 702.26c/610.4) through as many of Neriah's untap steps as pass, until something removes Oubliette from the battlefield. When that happens, Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phases in tapped, per Oubliette's own text ("Tap that creature as it phases in this way"), which overrides the normal phasing rule that a permanent phases in with the same tapped/untapped status it had when it phased out. This is a two-player-framed scenario (Neriah vs. Ari); note that in a multiplayer game, if the controller of a phased-out permanent leaves the game, rule 702.26n provides a different phase-in timing tied to that departed player's next turn, which doesn't apply here since both players are assumed to remain in the game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Effects that phase a permanent out until a certain event prevent that permanent from phasing back in normally.

entries.question: Nico controls [Lazav, the Multifarious], which is currently a copy of [Lazav, Dimir Mastermind]. Abram discards [Kasimir the Lone Wolf] due to hand size at the end of their turn. Lazav, the Multifarious's ability triggers. After it resolves, what is Lazav, the Multifarious named?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude the permanent's name becomes "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind" when the copy ability resolves.
entries.answer:
After the trigger resolves, the permanent that was called "Lazav, the Multifarious" is now named "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind."

Here's why: Lazav, the Multifarious is currently a copy of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind (with the exceptions that its name is "Lazav, the Multifarious," it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has Lazav, the Multifarious's own {X} activated ability). Because it copied the full printed text of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it also copied that card's triggered ability: "Whenever a creature card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, you may have [this creature] become a copy of that card, except its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has hexproof and this ability." Per rule 201.5b, the self-referential part of that ability ("you may have Lazav become a copy...") now reads as "Lazav, the Multifarious" since that's the object's current name, but the explicit instruction "except its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind" is not a self-reference — it's a direct instruction about what the new name will be, so it is unaffected by the renaming rule.

When Abram discards Kasimir the Lone Wolf (a creature card) to their graveyard due to hand size, this is a creature card being put into an opponent's graveyard (from Nico's perspective) from anywhere, so the inherited triggered ability fires (707.11, 707.9b for the modified copy effect). If Nico chooses to have it resolve, Lazav, the Multifarious becomes a copy of Kasimir the Lone Wolf (a 5/3 Legendary Creature — Human Warrior, mana value 6), except: its name is explicitly set to "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind" (a name-setting continuous effect per rule 612.8, which means it loses any other name it had and has only this specified name), it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has hexproof and the triggered ability itself (again with 201.5b converting the ability's internal self-reference to whatever name the permanent has at that point, i.e. "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind"). This is analogous to the Lazav, Dimir Mastermind ruling explaining that Lazav becomes a copy of the graveyard creature card using its last-known information (ruling #0), and that this copying does not trigger 'enters' abilities of the copied card (ruling #2). It also matches Lazav, the Multifarious's own ruling that it copies exactly what's printed on the target card except for the specifically modified characteristics (Lazav, the Multifarious ruling #1).

So, assuming Nico elects for the ability to actually copy (the trigger says "you may"), the permanent ends up named "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind," now a 5/3 Legendary Creature — Human Warrior Shapeshifter with hexproof and the "whenever a creature card is put into an opponent's graveyard..." triggered ability. If Nico instead declines the optional effect, the permanent keeps its current name and copy state as a copy of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's card (still named "Lazav, the Multifarious").

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind". Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's ability changes the card's name to "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind", regardless of what it was originally named.

entries.question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
entries.reason: The reference says either half may be cast, while the candidate insists only the instant half (Road) can be cast, so they reach different conclusions.
entries.answer:
Alivia can only cast Road, the instant half of Road // Ruin - not Ruin, the sorcery/aftermath half. Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability reads 'you may cast target instant card from your graveyard without paying its mana cost,' so it can only target and cast a card using its instant characteristics. While Road // Ruin sits in the graveyard (not on the stack), it has the combined characteristics of both halves - it is simultaneously an instant card and a sorcery card, per the card's own ruling (Road // Ruin ruling #3: 'While not on the stack, the characteristics of a split card are the combination of its two halves... it is both an instant card and a sorcery card'). That combined status makes it a legal target for Torrential Gearhulk's ability. However, per rule 601.3e, when an effect lets you cast a spell using only a subset of its characteristics (here, 'instant card'), only the alternative/qualifying characteristics are used to determine what can legally be cast - the rule's own Melek, Izzet Paragon example shows that an effect restricted to casting instants can only cast the instant-type option of a card with mixed characteristics, not the other side. Applying that logic here, Torrential Gearhulk's ability lets Alivia cast only the Road face (the instant), not the Ruin face (a sorcery). This also lines up with Road // Ruin ruling #0, which confirms that when you cast a split card you put only the half you're casting onto the stack, with the other half's characteristics ignored - so Alivia would be casting Road alone, as an instant spell, without paying its mana cost. Separately, Ruin could never be cast this way regardless, since Ruin has aftermath and can normally only be cast from the graveyard as its own sorcery spell (Road // Ruin ruling #5 notes that if another effect lets you cast a split card with aftermath from a zone other than the graveyard, you can't cast the aftermath half at all) - but here the deciding factor is simply that Torrential Gearhulk's ability only ever authorizes casting the instant portion. Finally, per Torrential Gearhulk ruling #0, this casting happens immediately as part of the ability's resolution - Alivia cannot hold Road to cast it later in the turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Either side. Torrential Gearhulk has a targeting restriction that requires Alivia to select an instant in their graveyard. Split cards have the type of both sides simultaneously. Therefore Road // Ruin is both an instant and a sorcery card and satisfies the targeting restriction on Torrential Gearhulk. When Alivia goes to cast Road // Ruin, nothing cares about which half is cast, so either is legal.

entries.question: Alvaro controls [Draugr Thought-Thief] and [Lotusguard Disciple]. Nico controls [Sands of Time] and [Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]. If Alvaro casts [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats], can they choose to only have the cost reduced by {1}?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Alvaro cannot choose to only apply a {1} reduction — Zagras's cost reduction equals the party size and is applied fully, yielding {2}{B}{R} in this case.
entries.answer:
No. Alvaro cannot choose to apply only a {1} reduction — Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's cost reduction is a fixed, mandatory effect based on the actual number of creatures in Alvaro's party at the time the total cost is determined, not an optional or scalable reduction. 

Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats reads 'This spell costs {1} less to cast for each creature in your party.' A party consists of up to one each of a Cleric, Rogue, Warrior, and Wizard. Alvaro controls Draugr Thought-Thief (a Zombie Rogue) and Lotusguard Disciple (a Bird Cleric), which together form a party of 2 (one Rogue, one Cleric). Per rule 601.2f, when a spell is cast the total cost is determined by taking the mana cost, adding any additional costs/increases, and then applying all cost reductions — 'If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order,' but this only lets a player choose the *order* in which stacking reduction effects are applied, not whether to apply a given reduction fully or partially. Zagras's own reduction effect is not optional and is not itself variable by player choice; per [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #3] and [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats ruling #4], the amount is fixed by the party count, and no player may even change that count after casting begins but before the cost is paid — meaning the reduction amount can't be manipulated by choice at all, let alone underused.

Since Zagras's mana cost is {4}{B}{R}, and cost reduction effects that reduce 'the cost' by a generic amount only affect the generic mana component (rule 118.7a), the {2} reduction (for 2 party creatures) applies entirely to the {4}, leaving a total cost of {2}{B}{R}. Once determined, this total cost becomes 'locked in' per rule 601.2f and can't be changed afterward. Alvaro must pay {2}{B}{R}; they cannot elect to pay {3}{B}{R} by only accepting a {1} reduction.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's cost is reduced by the number of creatures in Alvaro's party, which is determined by the game, and is calculated to be the highest possible amount.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Oko, Thief of Crowns], [Gilded Goose], and a Food token. Adriel uses Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability to make the Food token into a 3/3 Elk. Can Adriel then sacrifice it to Gilded Goose?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Oko's +1 removes the token's artifact/Food status so it cannot be sacrificed to pay Gilded Goose's "sacrifice a Food" cost.
entries.answer:
No. Once Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability resolves on the Food token, that permanent loses all its abilities and becomes just a green Elk creature with base power/toughness 3/3 — it is no longer an artifact and therefore no longer a Food. Since Gilded Goose's mana ability requires Adriel to "Sacrifice a Food," and the transformed permanent is now only a creature (an Elk), it can't be used to pay that cost.

Oko's +1 ability text reads: "Target artifact or creature loses all abilities and becomes a green Elk creature with base power and toughness 3/3." Per the official ruling on Oko, Thief of Crowns, this ability "overwrites all colors and creature types the affected creature has. It's just a green Elk. The creature keeps any supertypes (such as legendary) it has, but loses any other card types it has (such as artifact)." So the former Food token loses the artifact card type entirely (Oko, Thief of Crowns ruling #5). Because "Food" is a subtype that only exists on an artifact (a Food token is defined as a colorless Food artifact token per the Food Token rule and rule 111.10b), a permanent that is no longer an artifact cannot still be a Food. General rule 205.1b confirms that when an effect changes an object's types this way (here, Oko's own text controls, overriding how types would normally persist), only supertypes carry over unless the effect says otherwise — and Oko's ruling explicitly says artifact is lost.

Gilded Goose's third ability costs "{T}, Sacrifice a Food: Add one mana of any color," which requires sacrificing a permanent that is a Food. Since the Elk is no longer a Food (or an artifact at all), Adriel cannot sacrifice it to that ability. Adriel could still sacrifice the 3/3 Elk to some other effect that just needs "sacrifice a creature," since it is a creature and sacrificing simply means moving it from the battlefield to the graveyard (rule 701.21a), but not specifically to Gilded Goose's Food-sacrifice ability.

This analysis assumes the +1 ability has already fully resolved before any attempt to activate Gilded Goose's ability; if Adriel tried to activate Gilded Goose's ability first (targeting/sacrificing the Food before Oko's ability resolves), that would work fine since the token is still a Food at that point — but once Oko's ability has resolved, the option is gone.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability is a type-changing effect which will overwrite any previous types and subtypes the object had. When Gilded Goose asks Adriel to sacrifice a Food, it is saying that Adriel needs to sacrifice a permanent with the subtype "Food".

entries.question: Natasha controls a [Lifeline] and 2 [Scarwood Goblins]. Adriel casts [Plague Wind]. Does Lifeline trigger and return the creatures to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Lifeline triggers for each Scarwood Goblins but its intervening "if another creature is on the battlefield" isn't satisfied (no other creature survives), so neither trigger returns a creature.
entries.answer:
No creature comes back. Lifeline triggers twice (once for each Scarwood Goblins that dies), but because both Scarwood Goblins are destroyed simultaneously by Plague Wind and are the only creatures Natasha controls, Lifeline's intervening-if clause — "if another creature is on the battlefield" — is not satisfied, so neither trigger will do anything at the beginning of the next end step.

Plague Wind reads "Destroy all creatures you don't control. They can't be regenerated," so it destroys both of Natasha's Scarwood Goblins (Adriel doesn't control them) at the same time via a single resolution. Being destroyed and put into the graveyard from the battlefield means each Scarwood Goblins "dies" (rule 700.4). Lifeline's ability reads "Whenever a creature dies, if another creature is on the battlefield, return the first card to the battlefield under its owner's control at the beginning of the next end step." Since one event (Plague Wind's resolution) causes two dies-events, Lifeline triggers once for each Scarwood Goblins that dies (rule 603.2c).

However, Lifeline's ability has an intervening-if clause ("if another creature is on the battlefield"), which must be true both when the ability would trigger/be put on the stack and again when it resolves. Because both Scarwood Goblins die at the same time and (per the scenario) they are the only creatures on the battlefield, there is no "other creature" on the battlefield at that moment for either trigger to point to, and this matches Lifeline's own ruling: if all creatures on the battlefield go to the graveyard at once, none of them are returned at end of turn, precisely because of this intervening-if requirement. So both Lifeline triggers fail to do anything, and no Scarwood Goblins returns to the battlefield.

If instead Adriel or another player had a third creature that survived (e.g., a creature Adriel controls, which Plague Wind doesn't destroy), then at the time each Lifeline trigger checks and resolves there would be "another creature" on the battlefield, and Lifeline would work normally, returning the two Scarwood Goblins one at a time at the beginning of the next end step (per Lifeline's ruling that multiple returning creatures come back one at a time, not simultaneously).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the game state immediately before the event in question occurred when determining whether they trigger. There was another creature on the battlefield at that time, so Lifeline will trigger for both creatures that died. However, Lifeline has an intervening "if" clause that checks for that condition again as the trigger begins to resolve. There is not another creature on the battlefield at that time, so the ability is removed from the stack. Neither Scarwood Goblins returns to the battlefield.

entries.question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude the original Stream of Thought is countered by Chalice of the Void while Alfred still creates two replicate copies that resolve normally, so the core ruling is identical.
entries.answer:
Stream of Thought still gets countered by Chalice of the Void, but Alfred's replicate payments still produce two copies of Stream of Thought that go on to resolve normally.

Here's why. Stream of Thought's replicate cost of {2}{U}{U} is an *additional* cost paid on top of the spell's mana cost (rule [702.56a]), and rule [601.2f] treats "mana cost" and "additional costs" as separate components of the total cost. Because mana value is based on the mana cost printed on the spell, not on additional costs like replicate that were paid, Stream of Thought's mana value remains 1 no matter how many times Alfred pays replicate. Nico's Chalice of the Void has 1 charge counter, so its triggered ability ("Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters on this artifact, counter that spell") triggers and counters Stream of Thought when it's cast.

At the same time, casting Stream of Thought with replicate paid twice also triggers its replicate ability: "When you cast this spell, if a replicate cost was paid for it, copy it for each time its replicate cost was paid" ([702.56a]). Per [Stream of Thought ruling #3], you copy Stream of Thought for each replicate payment *even if the spell is countered* — Chalice countering the original does not stop the copies from being made. So two copies of Stream of Thought are put on the stack (Alfred may choose new targets for each, per [702.56a]/[707.10]).

Those two copies are not affected by Chalice of the Void at all, because a copy of a spell isn't cast (rule [707.10b]: "a copy of a spell isn't cast") — Chalice only triggers on a player *casting* a spell, and copies bypass that entirely. Each copy resolves normally: the target player mills four cards, and Alfred may shuffle up to four cards from his graveyard into his library for each copy.

One wrinkle: normally, per [Stream of Thought ruling #1], replicate copies resolve *before* the original spell, so their shuffle effect can't put the physical Stream of Thought card into the library (it's still on the stack). Here, though, the original was countered (moving the card to the graveyard) by Chalice's trigger. If Chalice's trigger resolves before the replicate trigger, the Stream of Thought card is already in the graveyard by the time the copies resolve, so a copy's shuffle effect actually could shuffle it into the library. If the replicate trigger resolves first instead, the copies are created while the original spell is still on the stack (not yet countered), matching the normal ruling where the card can't be shuffled in by the copies. Which trigger resolves first depends on turn-order (APNAP) rules for simultaneous triggers, which aren't part of the rules given here, so I can't say for certain which order applies in this specific game state — but either way, the core outcome (Stream of Thought countered, two copies made and resolving normally) doesn't change.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The original Stream of Thought is countered, the two copies resolve as normal. Replicate and Chalice of the Void both trigger when the spell is cast. Since the Chalice of the Void trigger is controlled by the player last in turn order, it will resolve first, countering Stream of Thought. Then Stream of Thought's trigger resolves and creates two copies of Stream of Thought. The copies are not cast, so they don't trigger Chalice of the Void.

entries.question: Adrienne attacks with [Sporeweb Weaver], and Nicolas blocks it with [Serpent Assassin]. Can Nicolas use [Tishana's Tidebinder] to counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line: Tishana's Tidebinder can be cast in response and its ETB trigger can target and counter Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability on the stack, so hexproof on the creature is irrelevant.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nicolas can cast Tishana's Tidebinder (using its flash ability) after Sporeweb Weaver's damage-triggered ability is on the stack, and Tishana's Tidebinder's own enters-the-battlefield trigger can then target and counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability.

Here's the timing: when Adrienne's Sporeweb Weaver (blocked by Nicolas's Serpent Assassin) and Serpent Assassin deal combat damage, that damage is dealt simultaneously to both creatures as a single turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, and no player gets priority between assignment and the dealing of damage [510.2]. Sporeweb Weaver is dealt damage in that event, and its triggered ability ("Whenever this creature is dealt damage, you gain 1 life and create a 1/1 green Saproling creature token") triggers at that moment but has to wait to actually be put on the stack [120.4d]. Per Sporeweb Weaver's own ruling, it triggers only once no matter how much damage or how many sources dealt it, and it triggers even if the damage kills it [Sporeweb Weaver ruling #1][Sporeweb Weaver ruling #2].

Once that trigger is placed on the stack, players get priority [117.1]. Because Tishana's Tidebinder has flash, Nicolas may cast it at that point, in response to Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability sitting on the stack. Tishana's Tidebinder's card text reads: "When this creature enters, you may destroy target nonblack creature" — wait, that's Serpent Assassin; Tishana's Tidebinder's actual text is "When this creature enters, counter up to one target activated or triggered ability." Since Tishana's Tidebinder's ability targets an activated or triggered ability, that ability must already exist — i.e., it must already be on the stack — so Nicolas must cast Tishana's Tidebinder (and let its trigger resolve) while Sporeweb Weaver's damage trigger is on the stack, not beforehand [603.1]. If Nicolas does this and targets Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability, that ability is countered when Tishana's Tidebinder's trigger resolves, and Adrienne gets no life gain or Saproling token from that instance.

Note that because Sporeweb Weaver's ability is a triggered ability (an object, once on the stack) rather than a static or replacement effect, Tishana's Tidebinder cannot prevent the trigger from existing in the first place — it can only counter it after it has actually triggered and gone on the stack. Also, per Tishana's Tidebinder's own text, since the source of the countered ability here (Sporeweb Weaver) is a creature, if the ability is countered this way Sporeweb Weaver would lose all abilities for as long as Tishana's Tidebinder remains on the battlefield — but Sporeweb Weaver's damage-trigger ability has already resolved to trigger and gone to the stack for this instance, so that only affects future triggers/abilities, not the already-created (and now countered) trigger object.

This is a two-player scenario as described, but note the framework used (turn-based action, priority) generalizes with an APNAP ordering component in multiplayer per rule 703.4k; the core answer doesn't change with more players, only the order in which multiple defending/attacking players announce damage assignments would matter first.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Tishana's Tidebinder's ability targets Sporeweb Weaver's ability, not Sporeweb Weaver itself, so hexproof doesn't matter.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Insurrection cannot be cast and therefore Tempted resolves, which contradicts the reference that Insurrection resolves first giving Autumn control of the tokens and making Tempted's targets illegal.
entries.answer:
Autumn's attempt to cast Insurrection is illegal, so it never actually gets cast, and Tempted by the Oriq stays on the stack to resolve normally targeting the Soldier tokens.

Here's why: Insurrection is a sorcery, and sorceries can normally only be cast when a player could cast a sorcery — with an object (Tempted by the Oriq) already on the stack, Autumn does not otherwise have permission to cast it. Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born's Cosmic Awareness ability reads, "As long as an opponent has cast a spell this turn, you may cast spells as though they had flash." The only spell cast this turn so far is Tempted by the Oriq, and Autumn herself cast it — it was not cast by an opponent (Breanna or Case). Because the ability's condition requires an *opponent* to have cast a spell, and that hasn't happened, Cosmic Awareness does not grant Autumn flash permission at this moment. Captain Mar-Vell's printed text is what defines this condition, and it overrides nothing here since no general rule contradicts it — it simply isn't satisfied.

Since Autumn is not legally allowed to cast Insurrection at that time, rule [601.2a] applies: a player must be legally allowed to cast a spell to begin the casting process, and if the requirements can't be met, the casting is illegal and "the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed." So the illegal casting of Insurrection is unwound completely — it goes back to Autumn's hand as if she never attempted to cast it, no mana is paid, and no priority passes for it.

Tempted by the Oriq remains the only spell on the stack, controlled by Autumn. Once players return to that point and pass priority in succession, it will resolve per [608.1]/[117.4], checking at that time under [608.2b] whether Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens are still legal targets (still controlled by those players, mana value 3 or less, etc.) before Autumn gains control of them.

One clarifying note on the multiplayer aspect: this scenario has three players (Autumn, Breanna, Case), so it's a multiplayer game. Nothing here changes because of that under the standard single-stack model — rule [405.2] describes one shared stack where objects are added to the top regardless of how many players there are. If your table is instead using a variant like Grand Melee with multiple simultaneous stacks [807.5b], the specific stack a spell is put on matters (e.g., it would need to match the stack of anything it targets), but that variant isn't indicated here, so this answer assumes the normal single-stack multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Insurrection resolves and Autumn gains control of all the Soldier tokens. Then Tempted by the Oriq begins to resolve, but its targets are now illegal, so it does not resolve and is removed from the stack.

entries.question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude each Aminatou's Augury creates an independent permission tied to the cards it exiled, so Amelia may cast the instant from each resolution.
entries.answer:
Yes. Amelia can cast one instant from each Aminatou's Augury resolution, so both instants can be cast (though each only once).

Each casting of Aminatou's Augury is a separate spell that resolves separately, exiling its own top eight cards and creating its own permission to cast spells "from among the exiled cards" for that resolution. The clause "for each nonland card type, you may cast a spell of that type from among the exiled cards" is a linked ability tied only to the cards exiled by that specific resolution of Aminatou's Augury, not to some global pool shared across all castings of the card [607.1]. This is the same principle behind why exiled cards from multiple similar effects must be tracked in separate piles, since each pile has its own rules for what can be done with it [406.5].

So: the first Aminatou's Augury exiled an artifact card and an instant card, granting Amelia permission to cast one artifact spell and one instant spell (without paying its mana cost) from that specific pile before end of turn. The second Aminatou's Augury exiled a different instant card, granting a separate permission to cast one instant spell from that second pile. These are independent permissions from independent resolutions, so Amelia may cast the instant from the first pile AND the instant from the second pile - two different instant spells total.

The only restriction is that once a card is cast this way it leaves exile and can't be cast again [Aminatou's Augury ruling #6], but that just means each individual instant card can only be cast once, not that only one instant total can be cast across both Augurys.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate effect that applies to cards it exiled. Casting an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury doesn't preclude Amelia from casting an instant off the second one.

entries.question: Agustin casts [Seasoned Pyromancer] and has two other cards in hand, one of which is a land card. Nico controls [Leyline of the Void]. How many tokens are created?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude only one 1/1 token is created because the nonland card is still considered discarded (even though Leyline exiles it), so Seasoned Pyromancer's ability sees one nonland discard.
entries.answer:
One 1/1 red Elemental token is created. Seasoned Pyromancer's triggered ability says: "When this creature enters, discard two cards, then draw two cards. For each nonland card discarded this way, create a 1/1 red Elemental creature token." Agustin has two other cards in hand, a land card and (implicitly) a nonland card, and both are discarded to satisfy the "discard two cards" instruction. Only the nonland card triggers token creation, so normally this would create exactly one token.

Nico's Leyline of the Void reads, "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." Since Agustin is Nico's opponent, both of the discarded cards (the land and the nonland card) would be put into Agustin's graveyard as part of the discard, and Leyline of the Void's replacement effect changes that destination to exile instead. This does not change the fact that the cards were discarded, however - a replacement effect only changes *how* an event affects the object (here, redirecting the resulting zone), not whether the underlying event (discarding) took place. This is the same principle described in rule 616.1a, where replacement effects 'modify the way an event affects an object or player' rather than negating the event itself. Because Seasoned Pyromancer's ability cares about cards 'discarded this way,' not about where they end up, the nonland card still counts as discarded even though Leyline of the Void sends it to exile rather than the graveyard.

So the discard-and-draw resolves normally (both cards go to exile instead of the graveyard because of Leyline of the Void), Agustin draws two new cards, and exactly one 1/1 red Elemental token is created for the one nonland card discarded.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One token is created. The cards discarded from hand can still be seen by Seasoned Pyromancer's effect even though going to the graveyard was replaced by going to exile.

entries.question: Aranza controls a [Welding Jar] enchanted by Nico's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Aranza's upkeep, Nico casts [Word of Seizing] to take control of the Welding Jar. What happens as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both state that Aranza is dealt 2 damage because she cannot sacrifice the Welding Jar after Nico gains control of it, so the "unless" clause cannot be paid.
entries.answer:
This Aura (Curse Artifact) deals 2 damage to Aranza. Nico keeps control of the Welding Jar (with haste) until end of turn, but that fact doesn't let Aranza off the hook, and Nico's control of the Welding Jar doesn't obligate Nico to do anything either.

Here's why: Word of Seizing was cast in response to the triggered ability, so it resolves first (it's on top of the stack). When it resolves, Nico untaps the Welding Jar and gains control of it until end of turn, and it gains haste [Word of Seizing]. Curse Artifact's own text ("Enchant artifact," with no "you control" restriction) means it simply stays attached to the Welding Jar through this control change — the Aura doesn't fall off or stop functioning just because the enchanted artifact's controller changed [Curse Artifact].

Now Curse Artifact's triggered ability resolves. Its trigger condition identified 'that player' as "enchanted artifact's controller" — Aranza — at the moment the ability triggered (the beginning of her upkeep). Just as rule [608.2k] establishes that when an ability's effect refers back to a specific object already identified by the trigger condition, it keeps affecting that same object even if its characteristics change, the same 'that player' reference set up in the trigger condition stays fixed to Aranza for purposes of the effect, regardless of who controls the Welding Jar by the time the ability resolves. The ability itself is controlled by Nico throughout (since Nico controls Curse Artifact, the source of the triggered ability) per [603.3a] and [113.8], but that's a separate question from who 'that player' is in the effect text.

So the effect reads: "this Aura deals 2 damage to Aranza unless Aranza sacrifices the Welding Jar." Because Nico now controls the Welding Jar (due to Word of Seizing), Aranza does not control it and therefore cannot sacrifice it — sacrificing a permanent requires being its controller. Since Aranza has no way to satisfy the "unless" clause, Curse Artifact's ability simply deals 2 damage to Aranza as it resolves. It doesn't matter whether Nico later sacrifices the Welding Jar (e.g., with its own ability) — the clause specifically requires 'that player' (Aranza) to be the one sacrificing it, not just anyone.

Timing note: this assumes the normal stack order — Word of Seizing, cast in response, resolves completely before the Curse Artifact trigger resolves. If instead Word of Seizing had somehow resolved after the trigger (not possible here since it was cast in response and stacks are last-in-first-out), Aranza would still have controlled the Welding Jar at resolution and could have chosen to sacrifice it instead of taking damage.

This is all based on specific named players (Aranza, Nico), not "each opponent" or turn-order language, so the analysis is the same whether this is a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aranza is dealt 2 damage. Sacrificing the Welding Jar is a cost. If the cost isn't paid, the default action of dealing 2 damage to Aranza happens. Aranza cannot sacrifice a permanent that they don't control.

entries.question: Alina controls a [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle] and 5 [Mountain]s. They plays a 6th Mountain and target Nico with Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger. In response, Nico activates [Memorial to War], targeting the Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle. Will they be dealt 3 damage?
entries.reason: Both say the triggered ability resolves despite Valakut being destroyed—its condition is rechecked and still true (Alina still controls five other Mountains), so Nico is dealt 3 damage.
entries.answer:
Yes — Nico will be dealt 3 damage. Memorial to War's activated ability ("{4}{R}, {T}, Sacrifice this land: Destroy target land") is on top of the stack, so it resolves first and destroys Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle before Valakut's triggered ability resolves. However, that doesn't stop Valakut's ability. Once an ability is triggered and put on the stack it exists independently of its source; destruction of the source afterward doesn't affect the ability, and the ability can still perform its action (dealing damage) using the source's last known information [113.7a]. Rule 608.2h confirms that if the source is no longer in the zone it's expected to be in, the effect uses its last-known information to still carry out the action.

Valakut's triggered ability has an intervening "if" clause, which is rechecked both when it triggers and again when it resolves [608.2a; Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #3]. That clause only cares about Alina's Mountain count ("if you control at least five other Mountains"), not about whether Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle itself is still on the battlefield. Destroying Valakut doesn't remove any Mountains from Alina's board — Valakut is a land but not a Mountain — so Alina still controls the sixth Mountain plus the original five, meaning the condition ("at least five other Mountains") is still true when the ability resolves. Since the condition holds and Nico is still a legal target (he's a player, and players remain legal targets absent something like hexproof or leaving the game), Valakut's ability resolves normally and deals 3 damage to Nico, with Valakut itself (now in the graveyard) serving as the source via last-known information.

This assumes Memorial to War's ability was activated and put on the stack after Valakut's trigger was already on the stack, so it resolves first — which matches the order described in the question (Nico responds to the trigger). If instead Memorial to War somehow resolved before the trigger was placed on the stack, the trigger still checks Alina's Mountain count at the (unaffected) trigger moment, so the outcome would be the same either way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Removing the source of an ability on the stack does not affect that ability.

entries.question: Arely equips [Barbed Batterfist] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — Champion of the Flame becomes a 4/2 and does not die when Barbed Batterfist is attached.
entries.answer:
No, Champion of the Flame does not die. Champion of the Flame is a 1/1 creature with the static ability "This creature gets +2/+2 for each Aura and Equipment attached to it." Once Barbed Batterfist is attached, that ability grants Champion of the Flame +2/+2 (for the one Equipment attached), taking it to a base 3/3. Barbed Batterfist's own ability, "Equipped creature gets +1/-1," then adds +1/-1 on top of that. Adding these together (both are power/toughness-modifying continuous effects in the same layer, so the order doesn't matter since addition is commutative): 1+2+1 = 4 power, and 1+2-1 = 2 toughness. Champion of the Flame ends up as a 4/2 creature. Since its toughness (2) is greater than 0, the state-based action in [704.5f] that would put a creature with toughness 0 or less into its owner's graveyard does not apply, so Champion of the Flame survives. Note this assumes Champion of the Flame had no damage already marked on it before Barbed Batterfist was equipped; if it already had damage marked equal to or greater than 2, the [Champion of the Flame ruling #0] explains that shifting power/toughness from an Aura or Equipment leaving or moving can turn previously nonlethal damage into lethal, but that's a different scenario than the one described here where Barbed Batterfist is simply being newly attached.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, Champion of the Flame will be a 4/2 and not die. All continuous effects are applied instantly before state based actions are checked.

entries.question: Aviana controls a [Meng Huo's Horde] and a [Deathrite Shaman]. Nico controls a [Propaganda]. Can Aviana use Deathrite Shaman's ability to pay for the Meng Huo's Horde to attack?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude No — Deathrite Shaman's ability isn't a mana ability so it can't be activated during the declare-attackers window to pay Propaganda's additional cost, so Aviana can't use it to pay for Meng Huo's Horde.
entries.answer:
No — not during the attack-declaration step itself. Deathrite Shaman's mana-producing ability ("{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color.") requires a target (the land card in a graveyard), and per rule 605.1a an activated ability only qualifies as a mana ability if it doesn't require a target. Rule 605.5a is explicit: "An ability with a target is not a mana ability, even if it could put mana into a player's mana pool when it resolves." The same is true of Deathrite Shaman's other two abilities, which also target cards in graveyards. So none of Deathrite Shaman's abilities are mana abilities — they're ordinary activated abilities that must be put on the stack and follow the normal activation procedure in rule 602.2b, which requires Aviana to have priority.

When Aviana declares Meng Huo's Horde as an attacker against Nico, Nico's Propaganda imposes an additional cost of {2} on that declaration (Propaganda ruling #3: "Paying this cost is not an instant or any other kind of ability, it is an additional cost on the declaration of the attacker"). Rule 508.1i says that during the turn-based action of declaring attackers, "If any of the costs require mana, the active player then has a chance to activate mana abilities" — but that window is specifically for mana abilities, not for ordinary activated abilities like Deathrite Shaman's. Since Deathrite Shaman's ability isn't a mana ability, Aviana can't activate it during that special window to conjure the {2} needed for the Propaganda cost.

Aviana could still make this work indirectly: activate Deathrite Shaman's ability earlier, at any point they have priority before the declare attackers step (for example, in the beginning of combat step), producing mana that sits in their mana pool, and then use that already-in-pool mana to pay the Propaganda {2} cost when attackers are declared. The rules given here don't address whether/when mana pools empty between steps, so I can't confirm from the provided rules whether that mana would still be available by the time attackers are declared — that's a gap in what's been provided, not something I can resolve with these rules alone.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Propaganda imposes a cost on Meng Huo's Horde attacking, which must be paid as a part of declaring it as an attacker. Deathrite Shaman's ability is not a mana ability, so the last time it could be activated before attackers are declared is during the beginning of combat step. At the end of that step, the mana would empty from Aviana's mana pool.

entries.question: Amos casts [Rise from the Grave] targeting [Rhizome Lurcher] in their graveyard. Assuming there are no other cards in any graveyards, how many +1/+1 counters will Rhizome Lurcher enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both conclude Rhizome Lurcher enters with one +1/+1 counter because its replacement effect counts itself in the graveyard when determining how it will enter.
entries.answer:
Rhizome Lurcher will enter the battlefield with 1 +1/+1 counter. Rhizome Lurcher's undergrowth ability reads "This creature enters with a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard" [614.1c]. Normally you'd check the graveyard's contents as the permanent enters, but per the card's own ruling, when Rhizome Lurcher is returned from a graveyard to the battlefield (as Rise from the Grave does here), its undergrowth ability counts itself even though it is no longer physically in the graveyard by the time it's on the battlefield [Rhizome Lurcher ruling #0]. Since the question specifies there are no other cards in any graveyards, the only creature card being counted is Rhizome Lurcher itself, giving it exactly 1 +1/+1 counter as it enters under Amos's control via Rise from the Grave's effect (which also makes it a black Zombie in addition to its other types, though that doesn't affect the counter count). This replacement effect is applied as the permanent enters the battlefield, per the general rule that such 'enters with' effects are replacement effects checked against the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield [614.12].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Rhizome Lurcher has a replacement effect that modifies how it will enter the battlefield. The game needs to know how Rhizome Lurcher will enter the battlefield, and must do that before it enters the battlefield. At that point it will be in the graveyard and will count itself.

entries.question: Ava controls [Undead Minotaur] enchanted with [Shade's Form]. Nico casts [Hour of Revelation] to destroy both Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Will Undead Minotaur return to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Shade's Form's "when enchanted creature dies" trigger fires even though both it and Undead Minotaur are destroyed simultaneously, and that the trigger returns Undead Minotaur to the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Yes — Undead Minotaur will return to the battlefield under Ava's control. When Nico's Hour of Revelation resolves and destroys all nonland permanents, Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form are destroyed simultaneously. Shade's Form's ability reads "When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control." This is a leaves-the-battlefield trigger keyed to the enchanted creature (Undead Minotaur) dying, and per rule [603.6e], such an ability can find the new object that the enchanted permanent became in the zone it moved to — here, the Undead Minotaur card sitting in the graveyard. The fact that Shade's Form itself is also destroyed at the same moment doesn't stop its dies-trigger from firing, because the trigger is checking the enchanted creature's death, and abilities of this type look at the game state as the event happened rather than requiring the Aura to still be on the battlefield afterward; rule [603.6e] explicitly covers this scenario for Auras whose ability triggers on the enchanted permanent leaving the battlefield. Once triggered, the ability goes on the stack and, when it resolves, it looks for the Undead Minotaur card in the graveyard [400.7]; since nothing else has moved that card out of the graveyard in the meantime, the ability succeeds and returns Undead Minotaur to the battlefield under Ava's control (Shade's Form's controller). Note this assumes no other effect exiles or otherwise moves the Undead Minotaur card out of the graveyard before Shade's Form's triggered ability resolves — if that happened, the ability would fail to find the object and do nothing, per the general zone-change-trigger rule in [603.6e]. This analysis applies regardless of whether the game has two players or more, since nothing about turn order or defending-player choices is relevant here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Shade's Form has a triggered ability that occurs when the enchanted permanent dies. For most triggers the game checks to see if they occur right after every event. However for "dies" triggers the game checks what the game state looked like right before they triggered to see if they trigger. In this case, checking right before Hour of Revelation resolved results in Shade's Form triggering and returning Undead Minotaur to the battlefield.

entries.question: Amara controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nehemiah casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Wayward Angel is a black, ability-less 3/3, while the reference concludes it is a black, ability-less 6/6 — the two reach different final power/toughness rulings due to conflicting layer/ability treatment.
entries.answer:
After Humility resolves, Wayward Angel becomes a black, ability-less 3/3 creature — Angel Horror named "Wayward Angel" with mana cost {4}{W}{W}.

Here's why, working through Magic's layer system (rule 613.1, 613.2c):

1. Wayward Angel's threshold clause ("As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, this creature gets +3/+3, is black, has trample, and has '...sacrifice a creature'") is a static ability, not a characteristic-defining ability, because it only sets characteristics *conditionally* on graveyard count — rule [604.3a] explicitly excludes abilities that "set the values of such characteristics only if certain conditions are met" from being CDAs. That matters because a real CDA can't be stripped by a 'loses all abilities' effect, but a normal granted ability can be [113.12].

2. Because more than seven cards are in Amara's graveyard, threshold is active, so before Humility resolves Wayward Angel's color-setting effect (layer 5) already makes it black — per the Wayward Angel ruling, it is black and not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #0].

3. Humility's static ability "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" is a layer 6 (abilities) and layer 7b (set P/T) effect. Layer 5 (color) is calculated before layer 6 (abilities) in the fixed layer order, so the color already locked in during layer 5 is not retroactively undone when the threshold ability is stripped in layer 6 — this mirrors exactly how the Humility/Opalescence interaction works, where an earlier layer's result (e.g., the layer 4 type-change) survives even though the source permanent loses its abilities in layer 6 [Humility ruling #0][Humility ruling #2][613.2c]. So Wayward Angel remains black.

4. In layer 6, however, Humility (with a later timestamp than Wayward Angel, since Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield when Humility was cast) strips away Wayward Angel's flying, vigilance, and the entire threshold ability itself (trample, the upkeep sacrifice ability, and the ability that would have produced +3/+3). Once the threshold ability is gone, none of its not-yet-applied effects (the +3/+3 boost, which is a layer 7c effect) can occur, since the source ability no longer exists by the time layer 7 is reached. Wayward Angel ends layer 6 with no abilities at all.

5. In layer 7b, Humility's own ability (Humility is not itself a creature here, so it keeps its own ability) sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1, overwriting the printed 4/4 [208.4b].

6. In layer 7c, Muraganda Petroglyphs checks whether Wayward Angel "has no abilities." Since step 4 stripped every ability Wayward Angel had, it now qualifies, and Muraganda Petroglyphs' own ability (which belongs to Muraganda Petroglyphs, not to Wayward Angel, so it doesn't itself grant Wayward Angel an ability — see the Runeclaw Bear/'is red' example in [113.12]) applies +2/+2. Final power/toughness: 1/1 base + 2/+2 = 3/3.

So Wayward Angel is: name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, card type Creature — Angel Horror, color black, no abilities (no flying, vigilance, trample, threshold, or the sacrifice trigger), and power/toughness 3/3.

This conclusion doesn't depend on how many players are in the game — nothing here involves opponent choice, turn order, or other multiplayer-specific rules, so the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game.

One timing note: this assumes Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield with threshold active before Humility was cast (so Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp for layer 6/7 ordering purposes). If Humility had instead entered the battlefield first and Wayward Angel entered afterward, the timestamp order for the layer-6 'loses all abilities' vs. Wayward Angel's own printed abilities could differ, but since Humility's effect is a continuous 'lose all abilities' effect that keeps re-applying to whatever creature is on the battlefield, Wayward Angel would still end up losing its abilities either way — the black color from layer 5 is the one detail sensitive to relative timing, and only applies if threshold's color-setting effect was 'in effect' before layer 6 strips the ability that produces it, which is guaranteed by the fixed layer order regardless of timestamps.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Wayward Angel is a Black, 6/6 creature with no abilities. The rest of its characteristics remain the same as printed on the card. 
Wayward Angel's threshold ability changes both its color, abilities, and P/T. Therefore, it applies in layers 5, 6, and 7 with the appropriate parts applying in their appropriate layers, and the layers are applied in order. Similarly, Humility's effect is applied in layers 6 and 7, as appropriate. 
Applying layers in order:
- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. The effects are then applied in timestamp order with Wayward Angel's ability applying first, since it has an earlier timestamp. So in layer 6, Wayward Angel first gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.", and then loses all abilities to Humility.
- In layer 7, P/T setting effects are applied first, so that Humility first turns Wayward Angel into a 1/1. Then effects modifying P/T are applied, of which there are two: Wayward Angel's own ability that, even though removed, continues to apply and gives it +3/+3, and Muraganda Petroglyphs's ability giving Wayward Angel +2/+2 since it now has no abilities. Wayward Angel's P/T is finally 6/6.

entries.question: Nayeli controls [Trinisphere]. Ainsley casts [Noxious Revival], paying 2 life for the Phyrexian mana. What is the total cost of the Noxious Revival?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the cost is {2} plus 2 life, whereas the correct ruling is {3} plus 2 life, so the final costs do not match.
entries.answer:
The total cost Ainsley must pay is 2 life (for the {G/P} symbol, which Ainsley chose to pay via life) plus {2} of generic mana added by Trinisphere — i.e., the equivalent of a {2}{G/P} cost, paid as {2} generic mana plus 2 life.

Here's why: Noxious Revival's mana cost is just {G/P}, a single Phyrexian mana symbol. For purposes of determining a spell's total cost, a Phyrexian mana symbol is treated as one unit of the mana component of the cost regardless of how it's ultimately paid (this is the same principle behind rule [202.3g] and [Noxious Revival ruling #1], which count a Phyrexian symbol as 1 toward mana value no matter the payment method). Since Trinisphere's effect triggers on 'each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast' ([Trinisphere ruling #0] confirms you check the mana component of the cost against three mana), and {G/P} amounts to only 1 mana, Trinisphere increases the cost to three mana total. Just as Trinisphere's own text illustrates that a {1}{B} spell becomes {2}{B} (adding generic mana to reach three, while leaving the colored symbol untouched), a {G/P} spell becomes {2}{G/P} — Trinisphere adds {2} generic mana, and the original {G/P} symbol is unaffected in kind.

Under rule [601.2b], the player announces whether to pay 2 life or a colored mana for each Phyrexian symbol before the total cost is finally locked in under [601.2f]; Ainsley announced paying 2 life for the {G/P}. That choice doesn't change how Trinisphere evaluates the mana component of the cost (it's still counted as contributing 1 'mana' to the pre-Trinisphere cost) — it only determines how that symbol is actually paid. So the resulting total cost, once locked in per [601.2f] and [Total Cost], is: 2 life (paid instead of {G} for the Phyrexian symbol) + {2} generic mana (Trinisphere's increase, payable with any color of mana or colorless mana, per Trinisphere's own reminder text and [107.4f]/[106.9] on Phyrexian symbols being colored, one-color-only, not generic).

Note: the spell's mana value remains 1, unaffected by Trinisphere's cost increase or by how the Phyrexian symbol is paid ([Trinisphere ruling #0], [202.3g]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: {3} and 2 life. While casting Noxious Revival, Ainsley chooses whether to pay life or mana for each Phyrexian mana symbol in the cost. Trinisphere is applied afterwards and increases the cost up to the minimum of 3 mana.

entries.question: Amare casts [Insatiable Hemophage] targeting [Canal Monitor] to mutate unto it. Can Nico cast [Withering Boon] to counter Insatiable Hemophage?
entries.reason: Both conclude that a spell cast for its mutate cost is still a creature spell on the stack and thus a legal target for Withering Boon, so it can be countered.
entries.answer:
Yes. Even though Amare cast Insatiable Hemophage for its mutate cost, it is still a creature spell while it's on the stack — mutate is a spell ability that gives the creature spell a target (per rule [702.140e/702.140b] framework), not a different spell type. Rule [608.3d] explicitly refers to it as a "mutating creature spell," confirming it remains a creature spell for as long as it's on the stack. Withering Boon says "Counter target creature spell," so Insatiable Hemophage is a fully legal target for it.

Nico casts Withering Boon (paying {1}{B} plus the additional cost of 3 life, per its printed text) targeting Insatiable Hemophage while it sits on the stack, before it resolves. When Withering Boon resolves, it counters Insatiable Hemophage: the spell is removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard. Because the spell never resolves, it never reaches the mutate resolution steps in [702.140b] and [702.140c] — it never merges with Canal Monitor, and its "Whenever this creature mutates" trigger never happens, since that ability only triggers on an actual mutation event, which requires the spell to resolve and merge successfully.

Note on timing: this assumes Nico casts Withering Boon while Insatiable Hemophage is still on the stack (the normal window, since counter spells must target spells, per [115.2], which only exist on the stack). If Insatiable Hemophage had already resolved and merged with Canal Monitor per [702.140c], it would be too late — Withering Boon could no longer target it, since it would no longer be a spell at all, but part of a merged permanent.

entries.answer_gold: Yes, Nico can use Withering Boon to counter Insatiable Hemophage if it was cast for the mutate cost. A spell that was cast for a mutate cost is still a creature spell and, therefore, can be countered by Withering Boon. ([702.140a])

entries.question: Amirah controls Azors Gateway with 4 different CMC cards exiled by it. They targets it with [Karn's Touch]. After that resolves, they activates [Azor's Gateway], and transforms it into [Sanctum of the Sun]. What are the characteristics of the new object after it has transformed?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Sanctum of the Sun becomes a 0/0 artifact creature (ma nv alue 0) after transforming, while the reference states it is a 2/2, so they reach different conclusions about its power/toughness.
entries.answer:
After Azor's Gateway // Sanctum of the Sun transforms, the resulting object is still the same permanent as before (rule [712.18]: transforming does not create a new object), so the continuous effect from Karn's Touch keeps applying to it.

Concretely, the permanent is now:
- The back face, Sanctum of the Sun (a Legendary Land), which untapped and transformed as part of resolving its own ability ("gain 5 life, untap Azor's Gateway, and transform it").
- Still an artifact creature, because Karn's Touch's effect ("Target noncreature artifact becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value until end of turn") was already applied while it was Azor's Gateway, and per rule [712.18] and rule [112.4] that continuous effect keeps applying to the permanent even after it transforms. So Sanctum of the Sun is a Legendary Artifact Land Creature until end of turn.
- Its power and toughness are still defined as "equal to its mana value." Since Sanctum of the Sun has no printed mana cost, its mana value is 0, so as the permanent's mana value changes with the new face, the effect recalculates and the creature is 0/0.
- It retains all its abilities, as Karn's Touch explicitly notes ("It retains its abilities"), so it still has Sanctum of the Sun's ability, "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total," plus whatever base characteristics the land face has (it's colorless, since neither face gives it a color and Karn's Touch does not change color).

Note: the provided rules do not include the state-based action for creatures with 0 toughness, so I can't confirm from the given rules whether a 0/0 creature would then be put into the graveyard — that would require a rule not present in this context.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 Legendary artifact creature land with the ability "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total". The requirement that Azor's Gateway be an artifact is part of the targeting restriction of the spell, after the spell resolves, it creates a continuous effect on the permanent that was targeted (in this case Azor's Gateway) that lasts until end of turn. When a double-faced card transforms it doesn't become a new object, and any effects that applied to it before the transformation will continue to apply afterwards.

entries.question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
entries.reason: The candidate says Paralyze can attach to Onakke Ogre when it returns, whereas the reference states Onakke Ogre isn't on the battlefield when the attachment choice is made, so the candidate reaches a different conclusion.
entries.answer:
At the beginning of that end step, Nicholas (Paralyze's controller) chooses what Paralyze enchants, and the only legal choices are Onakke Ogre or Ascended Lawmage — Paralyze cannot attach to Cemetery Gate.

Here's why. Sudden Disappearance exiled all nonland permanents Nicholas controlled — that includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze, since Paralyze was a permanent Nicholas controlled (even though it enchanted his own creature). All the exiled cards return to the battlefield simultaneously at the beginning of the next end step, under each card's owner's control. Sudden Disappearance's return effect does not say what Paralyze will be attached to when it comes back, so rule [303.4f] governs: when an Aura enters the battlefield under a player's control by a means other than resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn't specify what it enchants, that player (Nicholas, since Paralyze returns under its owner's control) chooses what it enchants, and must choose a legal object according to Paralyze's enchant ability ('Enchant creature') and any other applicable effects.

Because Onakke Ogre is returning to the battlefield at the same moment via the same effect, it is available as a choice — Nicholas may simply have Paralyze come back attached to his own Onakke Ogre. Alternatively, Paralyze's enchant ability only says 'creature,' with no controller restriction, so any other creature on the battlefield is also eligible. Ascended Lawmage has hexproof, but hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities an opponent controls — the choice a player makes under [303.4f] as an Aura enters the battlefield is not a targeting event, so hexproof does not prevent Nicholas from choosing to enchant Ascended Lawmage with Paralyze.

Cemetery Gate, however, has protection from black printed on it, and Paralyze is a black Aura ({B} cost). Protection's 'can't be enchanted by' component is an 'applicable effect' under [303.4f] that makes Cemetery Gate an illegal object for Paralyze to enchant, so Nicholas cannot choose it.

If Nicholas were to somehow fail to attach Paralyze to any legal creature (there is no reason he would, since two legal choices exist), the state-based action in [704.5m] would send the unattached Aura straight to its owner's graveyard.

This answer assumes there is no other creature relevant to the game state besides these three; if any other creature is present, it would also be a legal target subject to the same protection/hexproof analysis.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just Ascended Lawmage. Cemetery Gate has protection from black, so it can't be enchanted by anything black. Onakke Ogre isn't on the battlefield when Nicholas chooses what to enchant. Hexproof doesn't prevent an Aura from becoming attached to the Ascended Lawmage.

entries.question: Amaris controls [Eruth, Tormented Prophet] and, during their draw step, they attempt to dredge [Golgari Grave-Troll]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the two replacement effects compete for the same draw, the affected player (Amaris) chooses one to apply, and once chosen that replacement fully replaces the draw so the other effect does not apply.
entries.answer:
Because both Golgari Grave-Troll's dredge ability and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's replacement effect are trying to replace the same draw event for the same player, Amaris (the affected player) must choose only one of them to apply — they cannot combine both effects on a single draw. If Amaris chooses to dredge Golgari Grave-Troll, the draw is replaced entirely by dredge: Amaris mills six cards and returns Golgari Grave-Troll from the graveyard to hand instead of drawing, and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's exile effect never gets a chance to apply to that draw, since the draw event has already been fully replaced. If Amaris instead lets Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect apply, then instead of drawing, Amaris exiles the top two cards of their library and may play those cards this turn, and the dredge ability of Golgari Grave-Troll is not used (it stays in the graveyard, and Amaris draws no card the normal way).

Details: When two or more replacement effects could apply to the same event affecting a player, rule 616.1g says the affected player (Amaris) chooses which one applies. Only that chosen effect modifies the draw (121.6b, 121.7). Golgari Grave-Troll's own ruling confirms a single card draw can't be replaced by multiple dredge-type effects, reinforcing that only one replacement effect governs each individual draw. Dredge itself (702.52a) requires 'if you would draw a card, you may instead mill N cards and return this card from your graveyard to your hand' — Amaris needs at least 6 cards in their library to dredge for Golgari Grave-Troll, per 702.52b and the Golgari Grave-Troll ruling that you can't attempt to dredge without enough cards in your library. If Amaris has fewer than 6 cards in their library, the dredge option isn't available at all, and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect would be the only one that could apply to the draw (and per Eruth's own ruling, it can still apply even with fewer than two cards in the library, simply exiling however many cards exist without causing a loss from drawing off an empty library).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Amaris is replacing their normal draw-step draw and is deciding, at the moment that draw would happen, which single replacement effect to apply. If instead Amaris had already chosen and applied one effect (say, already resolved Eruth, Tormented Prophet's exile) before even considering dredge, then dredge simply would not apply to that already-replaced draw, since a draw can only be replaced once.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Amaris can dredge Golgari Grave-Troll instead of drawing. There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Amaris's draw. Since they are the affected player, they choose whether to exile the card with Eruth, Tormented Prophet or dredge with Golgari Grave-Troll. Once one of the replacement effects has been applied, the "draw" event no longer exists, and the other replacement effect does not apply.

entries.question: Nicole controls [Oraxid]. Can Austin cast [First Volley] targeting Oraxid with [Evermind] spliced onto it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Austin cannot target Oraxid because splicing Evermind does not change First Volley's color, so Oraxid's protection from red still makes it an illegal target.
entries.answer:
No. Austin cannot legally target Oraxid with First Volley even after splicing Evermind onto it, because splicing does not change First Volley's color, and Oraxid's protection from red keyword makes it an illegal target for a red spell's targeting requirement.

Splice is a text-changing effect: per [702.47c], "the spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards. ... The spell doesn't gain any other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, supertypes, card types, subtypes, etc.) of the spliced cards." First Volley is the main spell (a red instant), and Evermind is only revealed and spliced on for its rules text ("Draw a card"); Evermind's own color (blue) never transfers to the spell on the stack. So the resulting spell — First Volley with Evermind's text added — is still red, exactly as illustrated by the reverse example in [702.47c], where a spell keeps the color of whichever card is the host, not the spliced card.

Because the spell remains red, and Oraxid has protection from red, Oraxid cannot be chosen as First Volley's required target ("target creature"), since protection from a color prevents that permanent from being targeted by sources of that color. When announcing targets during casting, per [601.2c] the player must choose a legal target for each instance of "target" the spell requires; if Oraxid is the only creature Austin wants to target and it's illegal, Austin cannot complete casting the spell targeting Oraxid — he would need a different, legal target, or he can't cast it at all if no legal target exists.

Note that splicing Evermind on doesn't help here at all with respect to Oraxid's protection — Evermind's own effect ("draw a card") has no target, and it doesn't change the color of First Volley's damage-dealing text, which still originates from a red spell.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Evermind has a color indicator making it blue, which is not granted by splice since it's not part of the card's text.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Gisa and Geralf] and has cast a spell with it this turn. They casts [Acrobatic Maneuver], targeting the Gisa and Geralf. After it resolves, can they cast another card from their graveyard?
