entries.reason: Both answers conclude that exiling and returning Gisa and Geralf creates a new object that grants a fresh once-per-turn permission to cast a Zombie creature card from the graveyard, so Aubrey can cast another.
entries.answer:
Yes. Because Acrobatic Maneuver exiles Gisa and Geralf and then returns it to the battlefield, the returning permanent is a new object (a new Gisa and Geralf) under Aubrey's control [400.7g]. Gisa and Geralf's ruling states that if you cast one Zombie creature spell from your graveyard and then have a new Gisa and Geralf come under your control that same turn, you may cast another Zombie creature spell from your graveyard that turn [Gisa and Geralf ruling #3]. So even though Aubrey already used the 'once during each of your turns' permission from the original Gisa and Geralf, the new Gisa and Geralf that enters via Acrobatic Maneuver's exile-and-return effect grants a fresh use of that permission.

Note the caveat: the ability only lets Aubrey cast a Zombie creature spell from their graveyard, not just any card — 'another card from their graveyard' is only permitted if it's a Zombie creature spell that Gisa and Geralf's ability enables. If Aubrey wants to cast a non-Zombie card or a Zombie spell that isn't a creature spell, this ability won't allow it, though Acrobatic Maneuver's own 'draw a card' effect gives them a new card in hand regardless.

Timing assumption: this assumes Acrobatic Maneuver has already fully resolved (Gisa and Geralf is back on the battlefield as a new object) before Aubrey tries to cast the second Zombie spell. If instead they tried to cast it in response to Acrobatic Maneuver before it resolves, the original Gisa and Geralf's permission would still be used up and the new object wouldn't yet exist, so no second cast would be available until after resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Gisa and Geralf's effect allows Aubrey to cast one spell with that effect. If the Gisa and Geralf leaves the battlefield and then returns, it is a completely new object, generating a new effect. That effect counts no cards cast with it yet this turn.

entries.question: In a game of commander, Natasha has shuffled their commander into their library. Adan casts [Praetor's Grasp] targeting Natasha and finds Natasha's commander. Can Natasha choose to put it into the command zone?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Natasha may choose to move her commander from exile to the command zone as an optional state-based action despite it being face-down under Praetor's Grasp.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Praetor's Grasp resolves and Natasha's commander is exiled face down, the next time state-based actions are checked, Natasha (as the card's owner) may choose to put that commander card into the command zone instead of leaving it in exile. This is because rule 903.9a establishes that as a state-based action: if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. Rule 704.6d confirms this is one of the additional state-based actions checked in a Commander game.

The commander designation is an attribute of the card itself, not of the object it represents, so it doesn't matter that the card is face down or that it's sitting in an opponent's (Adan's) exile zone under Praetor's Grasp's effect - rule 903.3d confirms the card retains its commander designation through all zone changes, including exile. Since Natasha is the card's owner (ownership doesn't change just because Adan exiled it via Praetor's Grasp), Natasha is the one who gets to make this choice, not Adan.

If Natasha does move the commander card to the command zone, it leaves the exile zone entirely, which means Praetor's Grasp's exiled card is gone - Adan will no longer be able to play it, since Praetor's Grasp only lets Adan play the card 'for as long as it remains exiled.' Note that this state-based action is optional; if Natasha declines, the commander card simply stays in exile under Praetor's Grasp's effect and Adan retains the ability to play it (following all normal timing and cost rules per the Praetor's Grasp ruling).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Despite being face-down, it's still Natasha's commander, and they can choose to have it move to the command zone as a state-based action.

entries.question: Nico controls [Lion's Eye Diamond]. Addison casts [Wipe Away] targeting the Lion's Eye Diamond. Can Nico activate it in response?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Lion's Eye Diamond's ability is a mana ability and split second doesn't prevent activating mana abilities, so Nico can activate it in response.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can activate Lion's Eye Diamond's mana ability in response to Addison's Wipe Away, even though Wipe Away has split second.

Lion's Eye Diamond's ability ("Discard your hand, Sacrifice this artifact: Add three mana of any one color.") is a mana ability — it produces mana, doesn't require a target, and isn't a loyalty ability [605.1]. Split second normally stops players from casting spells or activating non-mana abilities while a split-second spell like Wipe Away is on the stack, but it explicitly carves out an exception: "Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack" [702.61b]. Since Lion's Eye Diamond's ability qualifies as a mana ability, that exception applies here.

Separately, mana abilities can generally be activated any time a player has priority, including in the middle of another spell resolving or being on the stack [605.3a], and Nico does have priority to respond to Addison's cast of Wipe Away under the normal priority/response rules [117.1b], [Respond], [117.7]. When Nico activates Lion's Eye Diamond, the ability doesn't go on the stack — it resolves immediately (paying its cost of discarding Nico's hand and sacrificing the artifact), and Nico gets priority back afterward [605.3b], [405.6c].

This is a two-player scenario as framed in your question (Nico and Addison), so no multiplayer-specific wrinkle applies; the rules cited here don't differ based on player count anyway, since split second and mana-ability activation timing work the same regardless of how many players are at the table.

One practical note: because Lion's Eye Diamond will be sacrificed as part of paying that mana ability's cost, it will no longer be on the battlefield by the time Wipe Away tries to resolve. The provided rules don't include the specific 'no legal target' resolution rule, so I won't state what happens to Wipe Away beyond noting Lion's Eye Diamond will already be gone.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Lion's Eye Diamond's ability is a mana ability. Split second does not prevent mana abilities from being activated. "Activate only as an instant" simply means that Nico must have priority, not that Nico could actually cast an instant at that time.

entries.question: Avah controls [Dakmor Scorpion] and [Winding Constrictor]. Nelson casts [Cannibalize] targeting them both. When it resolves, they choose to exile Winding Constrictor and to put +1/+1 counters on Dakmor Scorpion. How many +1/+1 counters are placed on Dakmor Scorpion?
entries.reason: Both conclude Winding Constrictor is exiled before the counters are placed, so it can't apply its replacement effect and Dakmor Scorpion gets only the two +1/+1 counters.
entries.answer:
Only 2 +1/+1 counters are placed on Dakmor Scorpion. Cannibalize's text reads "Exile one of those creatures and put two +1/+1 counters on the other," which describes two sequential effects: first the exile, then the counter placement. Because the exile of Winding Constrictor happens first, Winding Constrictor is no longer on the battlefield by the time the two +1/+1 counters are put on Dakmor Scorpion. Winding Constrictor's replacement effect ("If one or more counters would be put on an artifact or creature you control, that many plus one of each of those kinds of counters are put on that permanent instead") only applies while Winding Constrictor is on the battlefield to see and modify the event. Since it has already been exiled when the counter-placement effect happens, it cannot apply its 'plus one' modification (as described in Winding Constrictor's own rulings, which only address cases where Winding Constrictor remains in play). So Dakmor Scorpion simply receives the base two +1/+1 counters specified by Cannibalize, not three.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2. Spells resolve in the order printed on the card. Winding Constrictor is exiled before placing the counters on Dakmor Scorpion.

entries.question: Alex controls [Rhythm of the Wild], [Grumgully, the Generous], [Renata, Called to the Hunt], and [Hardened Scales]. Alex then casts [Grizzled Outrider]. If they chooses to put a counter on Grizzled Outrider for Rhythm of the Wild, how many +1/+1 counters will it enter with in total?
entries.reason: The candidate claims 6 counters, but the correct result is 4 because Hardened Scales only applies once to the enter-with-counters replacement (it doesn't add a counter for each separate enter-with effect).
entries.answer:
Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield with 6 +1/+1 counters on it (assuming Alex chooses the +1/+1 counter option from Rhythm of the Wild's riot rather than haste).

Here's why: Grizzled Outrider (a nontoken, non-Human creature) is affected by three separate "enters the battlefield with an additional/chosen +1/+1 counter" replacement effects that modify how it enters the battlefield: Rhythm of the Wild's riot (Alex chooses the +1/+1 counter option), Grumgully, the Generous's "each other non-Human creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter," and Renata, Called to the Hunt's "each other creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter." None of these conflict with each other (they don't try to modify the exact same instance of the event in mutually exclusive ways), so per rule 614.12b and 616.1f, Alex (as the affected object's controller) chooses the order in which to apply them, and all three end up applying, one after another, until none are left.

Hardened Scales reads "If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead." Under rule 614.16, this kind of replacement effect applies not just to a spell or ability's own counter-placement, but also to a counter placement caused by another replacement effect. Since each of the three enter-with-a-counter effects (Rhythm of the Wild, Grumgully, and Renata) independently causes a "1 or more +1/+1 counters would be put on this creature" event, Hardened Scales applies separately to each of those three events, per Hardened Scales ruling #0 ("if a creature you control would enter the battlefield with a number of +1/+1 counters on it, it enters with that many plus one instead") and ruling #1 (the controller chooses the order in which multiple counter-modifying effects apply).

So the math is:
- Rhythm of the Wild's riot counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2
- Grumgully, the Generous's additional counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2
- Renata, Called to the Hunt's additional counter: 1 counter → boosted by Hardened Scales to 2

Total: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 +1/+1 counters on Grizzled Outrider as it enters the battlefield.

(If Alex had instead chosen haste from Rhythm of the Wild's riot for that instance, only Grumgully's and Renata's counters would apply, each boosted to 2 by Hardened Scales, for a total of 4 counters.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Four. Every card on the battlefield has a replacement effect that modifies how Grizzled Outrider will enter the battlefield. When applying replacement effects, each effect has a chance to apply once and only once, so even though Alex can choose which order to apply the effects in, Hardened Scales will only get one chance to modify how many counters Grizzled Outrider enters the battlefield with, and will only ever add one additional counter.

entries.question: Ann has a [Sphere of Resistance], a Plains and a Swamp. Can Ann cast [Prismatic Ending] targeting [Drake Familiar]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Prismatic Ending can target Drake Familiar, Ann can choose X=0 and Sphere of Resistance makes the cost {1}{W}, and paying Plains+Swamp (two colors) meets Converge to exile the mana-value-2 Drake Familiar.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ann can cast Prismatic Ending and choose Drake Familiar as its target, and if she pays correctly she can also actually exile Drake Familiar.

Drake Familiar is a nonland permanent on the battlefield, so it's a legal target for Prismatic Ending's targeting requirement regardless of its mana value (rule 115.2); the mana‑value/colors‑spent check from Prismatic Ending's Converge ability only determines whether the exile effect actually happens, not whether the target is legal.

Prismatic Ending's cost is {X}{W}. Ann controls Sphere of Resistance, whose text ('Spells cost {1} more to cast') is a cost increase applied when the total cost is determined (rule 601.2f) — this adds {1} generic to whatever X and W already require. Ann only has two lands, a Plains and a Swamp, so she has at most 2 mana available.

If Ann chooses X = 0, the base cost is {W}. Sphere of Resistance's increase makes the total cost {1}{W} — that is, 1 generic mana plus one white mana specifically (Sphere's effect only adds a generic requirement; it doesn't touch or replace the {W} symbol). Ann pays this with her Swamp (for the generic {1}) and her Plains (for the {W}), spending exactly her two lands' worth of mana.

Drake Familiar has mana value 2 (its cost is {1}{U}). Prismatic Ending's Converge ability exiles the target only if its mana value is less than or equal to the number of *colors* of mana spent to cast Prismatic Ending (Prismatic Ending card text; see also Prismatic Ending ruling #0). Because Ann spent one black mana (from the Swamp) and one white mana (from the Plains), she spent two colors of mana, which is enough (2 ≤ 2) to exile Drake Familiar, mana value 2.

So: Ann can legally target Drake Familiar with Prismatic Ending, and by choosing X=0 and paying with her Swamp and Plains (total cost {1}{W} after Sphere of Resistance's tax), she spends two colors and successfully exiles Drake Familiar. If she instead chose a higher X or paid the generic portion with a different mana source that reduced the number of distinct colors spent below 2, the target would remain legal but the exile would fail to happen since Drake Familiar's mana value (2) would exceed the colors spent. This answer assumes a normal two-player or general game state with no other cost or color-affecting effects in play; nothing here depends on player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes Ann can cast Prismatic Ending targeting Drake Familiar. Ann can target Drake Familiar regardless of whether the final spell will exile it or not, as any card is targetable with Prismatic Ending, and it's only exiled if the conditions are met. Then Ann chooses the value of X, in this case they can select 0, then add Sphere of Resistance's tax resulting in a required mana payment of two. If Ann chooses to use two different colors of mana, when the spell resolves it will see that two colors were spent and exile the target if it's mana value is two or less.

entries.question: Abram attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Skewer the Critics] from Nico's library. Can Abram pay Skewer the Critics's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Robber of the Rich lets Abram spend colorless mana as though it were red, so he can pay Skewer the Critics's {R} spectacle cost with {C}.
entries.answer:
Yes. Skewer the Critics's spectacle cost is {R} (a single red mana symbol, not generic), but Robber of the Rich's triggered ability lets Abram "spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell" when casting the exiled card. Under rule 118.14/609.4b, this means any mana Abram taps for cost — including {C} colorless mana — can be spent as though it were red mana for the purpose of paying that {R} spectacle cost. So Abram may tap a source that produces {C} and apply it toward the {R} in Skewer the Critics's spectacle cost, effectively paying the whole spectacle cost with colorless-producing sources.

A few things to note: Skewer the Critics's card text ("Spectacle {R}") sets the alternative cost as one red mana symbol per rule 702.137a, and per rule 118.9c the alternative cost doesn't change the spell's mana cost, only what Abram actually pays. Robber of the Rich's own text overrides the normal restriction that {R} can only be paid with red mana, since its granted permission ("spend mana as though it were mana of any color") specifically applies to casting that exiled card, per rule 609.4b — it doesn't change the cost itself, just how it may be paid. Also remember Nico must have lost life this turn for spectacle to be legally payable at all (per Skewer the Critics's rulings), and per ruling #2 this can still only be cast at sorcery speed (Abram's main phase, empty stack), since spectacle and Robber of the Rich's ability don't change timing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Abram to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Haakon, Stromgald Scourge] and has [Foulmire Knight] in their graveyard. Can Aspen cast the Adventure portion of Foulmire Knight from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both conclude Aspen cannot cast the Adventure (Profane Insight) from the graveyard with Haakon because the Adventure on the stack isn't a Knight and Haakon only permits casting Knight spells.
entries.answer:
No. Aspen can cast Foulmire Knight (the creature) from the graveyard using Haakon, Stromgald Scourge's ability, but not Profane Insight (the Adventure side).

Haakon, Stromgald Scourge's ability reads "you may cast Knight spells from your graveyard." This is a restriction on which spells the ability lets you cast: only spells that are Knights. Foulmire Knight // Profane Insight is an adventurer card. Under rule [715.3a] and [715.3b], when a player chooses to cast the Adventure half, only its alternative characteristics are evaluated to see if it can be cast, and while on the stack as an Adventure the spell has only those alternative characteristics. Profane Insight's alternative characteristics are "Instant — Adventure" — it is not a Knight. Because Haakon's ability only grants permission to cast Knight spells, and Profane Insight does not have the creature type Knight when cast as an Adventure, Haakon's ability does not authorize casting it.

This mirrors the logic in rule [601.3e]'s Melek, Izzet Paragon / Garruk's Horde examples: an effect that lets you cast spells of a certain quality (creature spells, instant/sorcery spells, Knight spells, etc.) only lets you cast the version of the adventurer card matching that quality — you can cast Foulmire Knight's creature side (a Knight) with Haakon's ability, but you cannot cast Profane Insight (not a Knight) with it, even though the physical card is the same one sitting in the graveyard. Note also [715.3d]: casting a card as an Adventure isn't itself forbidden by other effects, but the *permission* granted must actually cover the Adventure's alternative characteristics, which Haakon's Knight-only permission does not.

So from the graveyard, Aspen may only cast Foulmire Knight (the 1/1 deathtouch Zombie Knight creature spell) via Haakon's ability; Profane Insight cannot be cast that way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. When determining if it's legal to begin casting a spell by moving it to the stack with Haakon, Stromgald Scourge, the game takes into account any alternative characteristics it would have on the stack. Haakon, Stromgald Scourge does not permit Aspen to move an Adventure to the stack, since it's not a Knight.

entries.question: Ayaan controls [Essence of the Wild] and casts [Evil Twin]. Can they have the Evil Twin enter the battlefield as a copy of Nico's [Quakestrider Ceratops]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Essence of the Wild's replacement effect will overwrite or apply after Evil Twin's own copy effect so the Twin cannot enter as Quakestrider Ceratops and instead becomes a copy of Essence of the Wild.
entries.answer:
No. Even though Ayaan could initially choose to apply Evil Twin's own replacement effect and pick Quakestrider Ceratops, Essence of the Wild's static ability ("Creatures you control enter as a copy of this creature") is also a replacement effect modifying how Evil Twin enters the battlefield, and it will still be applicable afterward, overwriting that choice. As Essence of the Wild's own ruling states, no matter what order the two copy effects are applied, the creature will end up as a copy of Essence of the Wild when it enters [Essence of the Wild ruling #6].

Here's why: Evil Twin's inherent ability and Essence of the Wild's static ability are both replacement effects that would cause Evil Twin to become a copy of something as it enters the battlefield. Since Ayaan controls the affected object (Evil Twin), Ayaan chooses which replacement effect to apply first, per rule [616.1c], which specifically covers the case where multiple replacement effects would cause an object to become a copy of something else as it enters the battlefield. After the first chosen effect is applied, rule [616.1f] requires the process to repeat, checking which replacement effects are still applicable to the entering event. Essence of the Wild's ability applies to any creature Ayaan controls entering the battlefield — that condition is still true regardless of which copy effect was applied first, so it applies again (or, if applied first, it simply overrides Evil Twin's own copy choice outright). Because an object becomes a copy of another object precisely as it enters the battlefield rather than afterward [707.5], this all happens before Evil Twin is actually on the battlefield, so there's no window where it 'locks in' as a copy of Quakestrider Ceratops before Essence of the Wild's effect can apply.

So regardless of the order Ayaan chooses, Evil Twin will enter the battlefield as a copy of Essence of the Wild (a 6/6 Avatar), not as a copy of Nico's Quakestrider Ceratops. Note that Evil Twin's own added ability ("{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature") is an exception added on top of whichever copy effect actually ends up defining Evil Twin's copiable values, but since Essence of the Wild's effect is what applies last, Evil Twin will be a copy of Essence of the Wild with that extra destroy ability attached, not a Quakestrider Ceratops.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Essence of the Wild and Evil Twin both have replacement effects that want to modify how Evil Twin enters the battlefield. Ayaan, as the affected player, may apply them in whatever order they wishes. Unfortunately neither order will result in Evil Twin entering as a copy of Quakestrider Ceratops. If they applies Evil Twin first, that ability will set Evil Twin's copiable values to those of Quakestrider Ceratops. Then Essence of the Wild will set them to its own copiable values. If they applies Essence of the Wild first, that will set Evil Twin's copiable values to Essence of the Wild. This will overwrite Evil Twin's ability, so it will no longer apply.

entries.question: Alex controls [Obosh, the Preypiercer] and casts their last card, [Flame Spill], targeting a 1/1 creature that Nevaeh controls. How much damage will Nevaeh take?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling (1 damage assigned to the creature and 3 to Nevaeh, then doubled by Obosh to 2 and 6) and correctly concludes Nevaeh takes 6.
entries.answer:
Nevaeh will take 6 damage from Flame Spill.

Reasoning: Flame Spill has mana value 3 (odd), and Alex controls Obosh, the Preypiercer, whose ability doubles damage from any source Alex controls with an odd mana value. Flame Spill is such a source, so its damage gets doubled — and per [Obosh, the Preypiercer ruling #2], the doubled damage is still considered to be dealt by Flame Spill itself, not by Obosh, the Preypiercer.

Flame Spill's text reads: 'Flame Spill deals 4 damage to target creature. Excess damage is dealt to that creature's controller instead.' Per [120.4a] and [Flame Spill ruling #0], the excess-damage split is calculated first using the unmodified damage amount (4) and the target creature's lethal damage threshold, ignoring any replacement effects (like Obosh's doubling) that will modify the damage afterward. The 1/1 creature Nevaeh controls has a toughness of 1 with no damage marked, so its lethal damage is 1. That means, before any doubling, 1 damage is assigned to the creature and the excess, 3 damage, is assigned to Nevaeh.

Per [Flame Spill ruling #1], these two damage instances (to the creature and to Nevaeh) are dealt simultaneously, and each 'may be modified by replacement or prevention effects.' Since Flame Spill (the source) has an odd mana value and is controlled by Alex, Obosh, the Preypiercer's replacement effect applies separately to each of these two damage events (this is not the same replacement effect being invoked twice on the same event — see [614.5] — but two distinct damage events, each getting one application of the doubling).

So the 1 damage to the 1/1 creature becomes 2 damage (still lethal, so the creature is destroyed as a state-based action), and the 3 damage to Nevaeh becomes 6 damage. Nevaeh takes a total of 6 damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Six. First Alex will allocate one damage to the token and three to Nevaeh. Obosh, the Preypiercer's replacement effect will then double the three damage being dealt to Nevaeh to six.

entries.question: Alessandro activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Noor with it. Noor doesn't block it and then casts [Through the Breach], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Melira's later-applied continuous effect removes infect from Inkmoth Nexus, so it deals 1 normal damage and Noor does not get a poison counter.
entries.answer:
At the moment combat damage is dealt, Inkmoth Nexus will have lost infect because of Melira, Sylvok Outcast, so it deals its 1 damage to Noor as ordinary life loss instead of giving Noor a poison counter.

Here's why. Inkmoth Nexus's activated ability ("{1}: This land becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn") was used before combat, giving it infect with an earlier timestamp. Noor then casts Through the Breach as an instant (its text: "You may put a creature card from your hand onto the battlefield. That creature gains haste. Sacrifice that creature at the beginning of the next end step.") to put Melira, Sylvok Outcast onto the battlefield. Melira's static ability "Creatures your opponents control lose infect" is a continuous effect that starts applying the moment she enters the battlefield — which is after Inkmoth Nexus already had infect. Per the logic explained in [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #3] (which discusses the same timestamp interaction in reverse, where a creature gains infect after Melira enters and the more-recently-applied effect wins), whichever infect-affecting effect has the later timestamp wins. Here, Melira's effect is the more recent one, so it overrides the earlier infect-granting effect and Inkmoth Nexus loses infect for the rest of the turn. [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #2] confirms this same principle for a creature that has infect when Melira enters: it loses infect.

Because Inkmoth Nexus no longer has infect by the time the combat damage step's damage event is calculated and dealt (rule [120.4b]: damage is dealt as modified by replacement/prevention effects and the relevant characteristics at that time), the reminder text on Inkmoth Nexus ("It deals damage to creatures in the form of -1/-1 counters and to players in the form of poison counters") no longer applies. Instead, Inkmoth Nexus simply deals 1 combat damage to Noor as ordinary damage, reducing Noor's life total by 1 — Noor does not get a poison counter. As a backstop, Melira's own text "You can't get poison counters" would also have stopped Noor from getting a poison counter even if infect had somehow still applied, but since infect is removed entirely, that clause isn't even needed here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Noor casts Through the Breach during the declare blockers step (after declining to block, as instants can be cast then), so Melira, Sylvok Outcast is already on the battlefield with her static ability active before the combat damage step begins. If instead Through the Breach were somehow cast after combat damage had already been dealt (which isn't possible here since no block was declared and damage hasn't yet occurred), the outcome would be unchanged — but if the game state had already locked in a poison-counter damage event before Melira arrived, that event would have already resolved as poison damage. Since the question places Through the Breach's casting before the damage step, the loss-of-infect applies in time.

This is a two-player scenario (Alessandro vs. Noor); the rules provided are framed for two players, so this answer doesn't need multiplayer-specific adjustments.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Inkmoth Nexus's ability gives it infect, and Melira, Sylvok Outcast's effect makes it lose infect. The effects are applied in timestamp order, so Inkmoth Nexus does not have infect. Noor will lose 1 life when damage is dealt.

(There is no dependency here because neither effect changes the text or the existence of the other, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to.)

entries.question: Alex controls [Extus, Oriq Overlord] and uses [Illithid Harvester] to try to turn it face down. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: double-faced permanents like Extus can't be turned face down, so Illithid Harvester's attempt does nothing (though it may still target).
entries.answer:
Nothing happens to Extus, Oriq Overlord — it stays face up on the battlefield with its normal characteristics (a 2/4 Human Warlock with double strike and Magecraft), and it does not become a 2/2 Horror creature. Extus, Oriq Overlord // Awaken the Blood Avatar is a double-faced (modal DFC) card, and rule [712.16] states that double-faced permanents can't be turned face down — if a spell or ability tries to turn a double-faced permanent face down, nothing happens and the attempt doesn't change any of its characteristics or their copiable values. This is confirmed directly for Illithid Harvester by its own ruling: [Illithid Harvester // Plant Tadpoles ruling #2] explicitly says Illithid Harvester's triggered ability can't turn double-faced cards face down. Illithid Harvester's Ceremorphosis ability can still legally target Extus, Oriq Overlord if it is a tapped nontoken creature (targeting isn't restricted), and the ability resolves normally, but the part of the effect trying to turn Extus face down simply fails for that target — Extus remains an ordinary face-up permanent, untouched.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing happens. Double-faced permanents can't be turned face down.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Jibbirik Omnivore], a token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore produced by [Stolen Identity], a 1/1 Saproling token created by [Morbid Bloom], [Moonscarred Werewolf], and a token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf produced by [Twinflame]. Nash casts [Ratchet Bomb] and activates its second ability. As Ratchet Bomb's ability resolves, what is destroyed?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling and reasoning: only the Saproling token and the Twinflame token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf (mana value 0) are destroyed, while Jibbirik (and its Stolen Identity copy) and the actual Moonscarred Werewolf (mana value 2) are not.
entries.answer:
Assuming Ratchet Bomb has zero charge counters on it when its second ability resolves (the question only describes Nash casting Ratchet Bomb and then activating the sacrifice ability — no activations of the "put a charge counter" ability are mentioned), the ability destroys every nonland permanent whose mana value is 0. That means it destroys the 1/1 Saproling token created by Morbid Bloom and the token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf produced by Twinflame. It does NOT destroy Jibbirik Omnivore, the token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore produced by Stolen Identity, or Moonscarred Werewolf itself, because all three have mana value 2.

Here's why each permanent has the mana value it does:

- Jibbirik Omnivore has printed mana cost {1}{G}, so its mana value is 2 [202.3a].
- The token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore made by Stolen Identity copies the copiable values of the original Jibbirik Omnivore, including its mana cost {1}{G} [707.2, 111.13], so it too has mana value 2.
- The 1/1 Saproling token created by Morbid Bloom is defined entirely by the ability that made it, and that ability does not give the token a mana cost. A token with no defined mana cost has no mana cost at all, and an object with no mana cost has mana value 0 (unless it's a back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or a melded permanent, which this is not) [111.3, 202.3a]. So this Saproling token has mana value 0.
- Moonscarred Werewolf is the back face of the nonmodal double-faced card Scorned Villager // Moonscarred Werewolf. While a permanent is showing its back face, its mana value is still calculated using the front face's mana cost — here, Scorned Villager's cost {1}{G} — giving it mana value 2, not 0 [712.8e, 202.3b].
- The token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf produced by Twinflame is a copy of the *back face* of a nonmodal double-faced permanent. Rule 202.3b and 712.8e both specifically state that a permanent copying the back face of a nonmodal double-faced object has mana value 0, even though the back face itself (Moonscarred Werewolf) has mana value 2. So this Twinflame token has mana value 0, unlike the original Moonscarred Werewolf it copied.

Ratchet Bomb itself is not on the battlefield when its ability resolves (it was sacrificed as part of the activation cost), so it is not affected by its own ability regardless of mana value.

If Nash had actually used the {T}: put a charge counter ability one or more times before sacrificing Ratchet Bomb (which the question doesn't state), the number of charge counters would instead need to match mana value 2, and the destroyed set would instead be Jibbirik Omnivore, the Stolen Identity token copy of Jibbirik Omnivore, and Moonscarred Werewolf — with the two mana-value-0 tokens surviving. Since the question describes no counter-adding activations, the 0-counter reading above is the one that applies.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Saproling token and the token copy of Moonscarred Werewolf. Copy effects copy mana cost, so the token Jibbirik Omnivore doesn't have a mana value of 0. Tokens that are created by an effect that sets their characteristics only have those characteristics. The Saproling token has no mana cost, so its mana value is 0. The mana value of transformed transforming double-faced cards is determined by their front face, so the Moonscarred Werewolf isn't destroyed. Copies of double-faced cards have a mana value of 0.

entries.question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Minas Tirith enters untapped (arguing Living Plane makes it a legendary creature as it enters), which contradicts the reference ruling that it enters tapped.
entries.answer:
Minas Tirith enters the battlefield untapped in this scenario. Minas Tirith's ability reads "Minas Tirith enters tapped unless you control a legendary creature." This is a replacement effect that modifies how Minas Tirith enters the battlefield [614.1c]. To determine whether that condition is met, rule [614.12] says you check the characteristics of the entering permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it. Living Plane's static ability, "All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands," is already active on the battlefield before Minas Tirith is played, and per [611.3c] a continuous effect that modifies characteristics of a permanent does so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield, not after a delay. So as Minas Tirith enters, it's already a 1/1 creature - and since Minas Tirith is a Legendary Land, it's a legendary creature the instant it hits the battlefield. That satisfies its own "unless you control a legendary creature" clause, so the enters-tapped replacement doesn't apply, and Minas Tirith enters untapped.

This is different from the situation described in [Minas Tirith ruling #0], where the land requires a legendary creature to already be on the battlefield beforehand, and simultaneous entry of a separate legendary creature doesn't count (that land would enter tapped). Here there's no second permanent entering at the same time - Living Plane is already an established, pre-existing continuous effect on the battlefield, so it's not a case of two objects entering simultaneously; it's a pre-existing effect that shapes what Minas Tirith looks like the instant it becomes a permanent, which is exactly the situation rule [614.12] is written to handle. I'm assuming Living Plane was already on the battlefield before Minas Tirith was played (as the question states, "Ayla controls Living Plane and plays Minas Tirith"); if instead Living Plane were being put onto the battlefield at the exact same time as Minas Tirith, that would be a simultaneous-entry case and, per the logic of ruling #0, Minas Tirith would enter tapped instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Tapped. When applying an enters-the-battlefield replacement effect, the game considers the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, so it sees that it would be a creature, but it doesn't consider the permanent to actually be on the battlefield yet. Effectively, a legendary creature is entering the battlefield.

entries.question: Andy controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Andy then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Badlands becomes a Plains tapping for {W}, whereas the correct ruling is that it becomes a Mountain and can tap only for {R}.
entries.answer:
Badlands ends up as a Plains and can be tapped only for {W}.

Here's why: Badlands is a nonbasic land whose printed subtype is Swamp Mountain, and it normally has "{T}: Add {B} or {R}" from those two basic land types (Badlands ruling #0). Both Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and Conversion's "All Mountains are Plains" are continuous effects that set a land's subtype (layer 4 type-setting effects). Because Badlands is nonbasic (it never had the basic supertype, and setting its subtype doesn't add or remove supertypes per [305.7]), Magus of the Moon's effect keeps applying to it even after its type changes -- and because Conversion's effect only cares about whatever is currently a Mountain, which set of lands counts as "Mountains" is itself determined by Magus of the Moon's effect. That makes Conversion's effect dependent on Magus of the Moon's effect, so Magus of the Moon's type-setting is applied first, and Conversion's is applied afterward using the result.

Step 1 -- Magus of the Moon: Badlands is nonbasic, so its subtype is set to Mountain. Per [305.7], it loses its old subtypes (Swamp and Mountain) along with the abilities generated by them, and gains the land type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}" (Magus of the Moon ruling #2; see also ruling #4, which confirms Magus of the Moon's type-changing effect keeps applying even under complications).

Step 2 -- Conversion: Badlands is now literally a Mountain, so Conversion's "All Mountains are Plains" applies to it. Again per [305.7], its subtype is set to Plains, it loses the Mountain type and the {T}: Add {R} ability that came with it, and it gains the Plains type and the intrinsic "{T}: Add {W}" ability (see [305.6] and Conversion ruling #1, which confirms Conversion's effect is a continuous, immediately-applied type change).

Badlands remains a nonbasic land throughout (Conversion doesn't add the basic supertype -- see [113.12] on characteristic-setting effects not granting or removing supertypes), so this reasoning is stable: it stays eligible for Magus of the Moon's "nonbasic lands" clause the whole time, but its actual current type after both effects settle is Plains. Badlands ruling #2 confirms that a land-type-changing effect on a dual land removes the old land types completely, which is what happens twice here.

This is a two-player-neutral interaction (nothing about player count changes how continuous effects layer), so the same result holds whether Andy is in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Note: the specific rule governing how to order two effects that are 'dependent' on each other (i.e., which one is applied first when the timestamp order alone wouldn't give a consistent answer) wasn't included in the rules text I was given, so my ordering above is inferred from how [305.7] describes basic-type-setting effects interacting, plus the card rulings for Magus of the Moon, Conversion, and Badlands, which together describe exactly this chain of type changes.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Only {R}. Both Magus of the Moon and Conversion only apply in layer 4. The effects are applied in timestamp order, resulting in Conversion applying first to make Badlands a Plains, then Magus of the Moon applies making it a Mountain.

entries.question: Amy controls a [Trigon of Corruption] enchanted by Neil's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Amy's upkeep, they cast [Aura Graft] to attach the Curse Artifact to [Sungrass Egg]. Which artifact does Amy have the choice to sacrifice as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: The reference says the artifact referenced is the one Curse Artifact was attached to when the ability triggered (Trigon of Corruption), while the candidate says it updates to whatever it's attached to when the ability resolves (Sungrass Egg), so they reach opposite conclusions.
entries.answer:
Amy has the choice to sacrifice Sungrass Egg when Curse Artifact's triggered ability resolves — not Trigon of Corruption. Curse Artifact's ability reads "unless they sacrifice that artifact," where "that artifact" refers back to "enchanted artifact." Per rule [303.4m], any reference to the "enchanted [object]" refers to whatever object the Aura is currently attached to, and this is a dynamic reference rather than something locked in when the ability triggered (this situation isn't one of the zone-change or unattached-trigger exceptions that would require looking back in time, per [603.10c] and [603.6e]). Because Aura Graft was cast in response to the trigger, it resolves first (spells and abilities resolve in last-in-first-out order), moving Curse Artifact from Trigon of Corruption to Sungrass Egg and giving it a new timestamp under [701.3c]. Once attached to Sungrass Egg, Curse Artifact's ability that "modifies" or references the enchanted permanent now applies to Sungrass Egg instead of Trigon of Corruption, consistent with the general principle in [604.4] that an Aura's effects move with it to whatever it's newly attached to. So when Curse Artifact's upkeep trigger finally resolves, "enchanted artifact" is read as Sungrass Egg, and Amy's choice is whether to sacrifice Sungrass Egg (not Trigon of Corruption) to avoid the 2 damage. Note: the player who takes the damage/must sacrifice ("that player") was fixed at the moment the ability triggered as the controller of the then-enchanted Trigon of Corruption — that was Amy, so Amy remains the player facing the choice; it's only the identity of the artifact referenced by "that artifact" that updates to Sungrass Egg by the time the ability resolves.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Trigon of Corruption. The "that artifact" that the trigger on the stack refers to is the one that Curse Artifact was attached to as the ability triggered.

entries.question: Nico controls [Blind Obedience]. Adonis's devotion to black is 0 and they cast [Erebos, God of the Dead]. Does it enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Erebos is not a creature as it enters (devotion is 0), so Blind Obedience's tapped-entry replacement doesn't apply and it enters untapped.
entries.answer:
Erebos, God of the Dead enters the battlefield untapped. Blind Obedience's ability "Artifacts and creatures your opponents control enter tapped" only affects permanents that are creatures (or artifacts) as they enter. Erebos, God of the Dead has the built-in text "As long as your devotion to black is less than five, Erebos isn't a creature." Per Erebos, God of the Dead ruling #6, when checking whether a replacement effect that affects creatures entering the battlefield (like Blind Obedience's) applies to a God, you check the controller's devotion to that color *before* the God is counted as being on the battlefield, and the mana symbols in the God's own mana cost do not count toward that check. Since Adonis's devotion to black is 0 before Erebos, God of the Dead is considered, and 0 is less than five, Erebos, God of the Dead is not a creature at the moment the replacement effect from Blind Obedience is being applied. Erebos, God of the Dead is also not an artifact. Therefore Blind Obedience's tapped-entry replacement effect does not apply to it, and it enters untapped (the default status per rule 110.5b, since no applicable replacement effect modifies it). This holds regardless of whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, since Blind Obedience's effect is about 'opponents' generally and the devotion check works the same way for any number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Untapped. To determine what replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters the battlefield, the game looks at the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield. On the battlefield Erebos, God of the Dead would not be a creature, so Blind Obedience's effect will not apply to it.

entries.question: Alex casts [Brainstorm] using the ability of [Jace, Telepath Unbound]. Nina casts [Memory Lapse] and counters Brainstorm. Where does Brainstorm go?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Brainstorm is exiled due to Jace's replacement effect winning, whereas the reference states Memory Lapse's self-replacement applies first and Brainstorm goes to Alex's library, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Brainstorm is exiled, not put on top of Alex's library. When Nina's Memory Lapse counters Brainstorm, it is removed from the stack as a countered spell [701.6a]. Normally a countered spell goes to its owner's graveyard [404.1], but two replacement effects are competing to change that destination here: Memory Lapse's own text ("put it on top of its owner's library instead of into that player's graveyard") and Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability, which put Brainstorm on the stack from Alex's graveyard and stipulates "If that spell would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead." The Memory Lapse rulings tell us exactly how this kind of clash resolves: Memory Lapse's self-replacement effect normally intercepts the graveyard-bound event first, but when the spell was set up to go to exile instead of the graveyard because of the way it was cast (the ruling specifically cites flashback, which uses the same 'would be put into your graveyard, exile it instead' wording that Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability uses), that exile replacement wins and the spell ends up in exile instead of the library [Memory Lapse ruling #0]. Since Jace, Telepath Unbound's -3 ability uses that identical pattern, Brainstorm's own countered-spell destination is overridden the same way: it goes to exile rather than to the top of Alex's library. Note that Nina, as the Memory Lapse's controller, doesn't get any say here beyond having countered the spell — the actual final zone is dictated by Jace, Telepath Unbound's replacement effect on Brainstorm itself. Also, per rule 733.1/701.6b there's no refund of the mana Alex spent casting Brainstorm regardless of where it ends up. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table, since it turns purely on replacement-effect interaction on a single spell rather than on turn order or opponent choices.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Alex's library.

Two replacement effects are trying to replace the same event. Since Memory Lapse's effect is a self-replacement effect, it applies first. Once it's applied, Brainstorm is moving to the library and Jace, Telepath Unbound's effect no longer applies.

entries.question: Nathalia controls [Welding Jar] and [Duskworker]. Ariel casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Duskworker with both. In response, Nathalia activates Welding Jar's ability targeting Duskworker. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling: Welding Jar's regeneration resolves first and replaces the destroy, removing the 2 damage and leaving Duskworker tapped and with no damage.
entries.answer:
Duskworker survives: Welding Jar's regeneration shield resolves first and is used up to save Duskworker from Prismari Command's "destroy" mode, and the 2 damage from the "deal damage" mode is also removed as part of that regeneration.

Step by step:

1. Ariel casts Prismari Command choosing the modes "Prismari Command deals 2 damage to any target" and "Destroy target artifact," and targets Duskworker with each instance of "target." This is legal: because Prismari Command uses the word "target" for two separate modes, the same object (Duskworker) can be chosen for each instance of "target" as long as it fits the targeting criteria [601.2c].

2. In response, Nathalia sacrifices Welding Jar (the cost) to activate "Sacrifice this artifact: Regenerate target artifact," targeting Duskworker, which is a legal target since Duskworker is an artifact creature (Welding Jar). This activated ability is put on top of the stack, above Prismari Command, and resolves first.

3. Welding Jar's ability resolves: Welding Jar itself is already gone (sacrificed as a cost) and Duskworker is regenerated — it receives a regeneration shield that will replace the next time it would be destroyed this turn, instead tapping it, removing it from combat, and removing all damage from it (Welding Jar).

4. Prismari Command then resolves. At this point the game checks whether Duskworker is still a legal target for each instance of "target": it's still on the battlefield and still an artifact, so both targets remain legal [608.2b]. Per the card's own ruling, as long as at least one target is legal the spell resolves and does as much as it can (Prismari Command ruling #1) — here both parts can still happen.

5. The "deals 2 damage" mode marks 2 damage on Duskworker. The "destroy target artifact" mode tries to destroy Duskworker, but because Duskworker now has the regeneration shield from step 3, that destruction is replaced: Duskworker is tapped, removed from combat (irrelevant here since it isn't in combat), and all damage is removed from it — including the 2 damage Prismari Command just dealt.

Net result: Duskworker remains on the battlefield, tapped, with no damage marked. Welding Jar is in its owner's graveyard (sacrificed as a cost), and Prismari Command goes to its owner's graveyard after resolving. Duskworker's own triggered ability ("Whenever this creature becomes blocked, regenerate it") never triggers here since there's no combat involved.

This assumes Nathalia's Welding Jar activation is put on the stack and fully resolves before Prismari Command resolves, which is required since it was activated in response (an activated ability resolves before the spell it responds to). If instead Nathalia had regenerated Duskworker only after Prismari Command had already resolved and destroyed it, the regeneration would do nothing, since Duskworker would no longer be on the battlefield.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Duskworker will end up tapped and have no damage marked on it. Welding Jar's ability will resolve first, regenerating Duskworker. When Prismari Command resolves, the game carries out the instructions in the order written. First, Prismari Command deals 2 damage to Duskworker. The replacement effect generated by the regeneration ability will not apply yet, as even though Duskworker has been dealt lethal damage, it would only be destroyed when state-based actions are checked, and state-based actions are checked when a player would get priority. Next Prismari Command tries to destroy Duskworker and the replacement effect applies, replacing the destruction event with Duskworker being tapped and having all damaged marked on it removed. Lastly Prismari Command finishes resolving and leaves the stack and state-based actions are checked. Since Duskworker no longer has any damage marked on it, it will not be die.

entries.question: Armando controls [Mana Reflection] and taps [Pyromancer's Goggles] to add {R}{R}. They spend one mana to cast [Into the Fray]. Later in the phase they spend the other mana to cast [Galvanic Discharge]. Which one(s) are copied?
entries.reason: Both conclude Mana Reflection doubles the Goggles' mana into two separate red mana, each with its own delayed trigger from Pyromancer's Goggles, so spending one copies Into the Fray and spending the other copies Galvanic Discharge.
entries.answer:
Both spells get copied: Armando gets one copy of Into the Fray and, later, one copy of Galvanic Discharge.

Here's why. Pyromancer's Goggles's ability is a mana ability ("{T}: Add {R}. When that mana is spent to cast a red instant or sorcery spell, copy that spell...") that is activated, not a mana ability that merely triggers off tapping a permanent. Mana Reflection's replacement effect ("If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead") therefore applies to it normally when Armando taps Pyromancer's Goggles: instead of producing a single {R}, the tap produces {R}{R} [106.12a][106.12b]. Note that Mana Reflection ruling #1 says a triggered mana ability that itself triggers 'whenever you tap' something is unaffected by Mana Reflection, but that exception doesn't apply here, because Pyromancer's Goggles's mana ability is the activated {T} ability being doubled, not a triggered ability of that kind [Mana Reflection ruling #1].

Because Mana Reflection is a replacement effect that increases the amount of mana produced, rule 106.6a says any additional effect or delayed-triggered-ability restriction created by the ability applies to all the mana produced, and a separate delayed triggered ability is created for each mana produced [106.6a]. So each of the two {R} mana Armando now has carries its own individual 'when this mana is spent on a red instant or sorcery, copy that spell' delayed trigger from Pyromancer's Goggles.

When Armando spends one of those {R} to cast Into the Fray (a red instant), that mana's delayed trigger fires and creates a copy of Into the Fray. Later in the same phase, when Armando spends the second {R} to cast Galvanic Discharge (also a red instant), that mana's own separate delayed trigger fires independently and creates a copy of Galvanic Discharge. Each spell is copied exactly once, tied to the specific mana spent on it, consistent with how Pyromancer's Goggles ruling #3 describes multiple copies arising when multiple Goggles-mana is spent (here, spent across two different spells rather than one).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Both are copied. Mana Reflection has a replacement effect that changes the amount of mana produced by Pyromancer's Goggles. A separate delayed trigger is created for each mana.

entries.question: Alden controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alden would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alden has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Clone enters with exactly one +1/+1 counter because Spark Double’s replacement effect can only apply once to the entering-the-battlefield event.
entries.answer:
Clone will enter the battlefield with only one +1/+1 counter, not four, no matter how many times Alden tries to re-copy Spark Double through the inherited ability. Here's why: Clone's own printed ability ("You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield") has no bonus-counter clause, so the first time Alden uses it to make Clone become a copy of Spark Double, no counter is added — Clone simply becomes Spark Double, copiable-values-wise, and as part of that copying it also picks up Spark Double's own replacement ability, "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature..." [707.9a]. Because Spark Double copies exactly what was printed on the original permanent [Spark Double ruling #0], copying it again always produces that identical ability. Since that newly-gained ability is itself a replacement effect that also modifies how Clone enters the battlefield, it can be applied to further shape the same entering-the-battlefield event, the way nested replacement effects can chain together on a single entering event [614.12b, 616.1g]. So Alden's second application — using the inherited Spark Double ability to designate Spark Double as the thing being copied again — does trigger the "except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter" exception, giving Clone one +1/+1 counter [Spark Double ruling #6]. But that is the *same* replacement effect (Spark Double's own copy ability, unchanged because Spark Double is just copying itself) that was just applied. Rule 614.5 says a replacement effect "doesn't invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event." Having already applied once, it cannot apply itself again to further modify Clone's entering-the-battlefield event, so the third and fourth attempts to "copy Spark Double again" through that same inherited ability don't add any further counters — they're not legal additional applications of that effect. Net result: exactly one bonus +1/+1 counter, from the single legitimate application of Spark Double's exception clause, regardless of how many times Alden nominally designates "copy Spark Double." This is a two-player-neutral rules interaction — nothing here depends on player count, since it's entirely about replacement-effect application on one object entering the battlefield.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Spark Double has a copy effect that includes an exception (entering with a +1/+1 counter). If another copy effect is applied afterwards, the exception from the first effect will not happen.

entries.question: Ahmed casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Nico. At their first opportunity, Ahmed sacrifices their [Abandoned Outpost]. How many cards will Ahmed be able to exile from Nico's library?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling: gravestorm counts permanents put into graveyard before the trigger resolves, so sacrificing Abandoned Outpost in time yields one copy and two exiled cards.
entries.answer:
Ahmed will be able to exile 2 cards from Nico's library. Bitter Ordeal reads "Search target player's library for a card and exile it. Then that player shuffles," and it has Gravestorm: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent put into a graveyard this turn." (Bitter Ordeal). When Ahmed casts Bitter Ordeal targeting Nico, the Gravestorm triggered ability triggers immediately as part of casting [603.2c], but that triggering only puts the ability on the stack — it "doesn't do anything at this point" [603.2c]. The actual counting of "permanents put into a graveyard this turn" happens when that triggered ability resolves, following the instructions in the order written using the game state at that time [608.2c]. Gravestorm is not one of the special "look back in time" zone-change triggers listed for determining whether an ability triggers [603.10a]; it's simply an ordinary ability that counts a turn-long running total at the moment it resolves. Because Ahmed sacrifices Abandoned Outpost (Abandoned Outpost's ability: "{T}, Sacrifice this land: Add one mana of any color") at their very first opportunity to act — i.e., while the Gravestorm trigger is still sitting on the stack above the Bitter Ordeal spell, before that trigger resolves — that sacrifice happens in time to be counted. So when the Gravestorm ability resolves, it sees one permanent (Abandoned Outpost) put into a graveyard this turn and creates one copy of Bitter Ordeal, still targeting Nico unless Ahmed chooses a new target. Ahmed therefore ends up with two instances of Bitter Ordeal's effect resolving against Nico's library: the original spell and the one copy, each searching Nico's library for a card, exiling it, and then having Nico shuffle. Assuming Nico's library has at least two cards, that means Ahmed exiles 2 cards total.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming "first opportunity" means the first time Ahmed receives priority after casting Bitter Ordeal — i.e., before the Gravestorm trigger has resolved. If instead the sacrifice happened only after the Gravestorm trigger had already resolved (too late to be counted), no copy would be created and Ahmed would only exile 1 card from Nico's library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2. Gravestorm cares about the number of permanents put into the graveyard before the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Autumn restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]'s last ability. They put a [Quilled Slagwurm] onto the battlefield as it resolves. Can it attack on their first turn?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the creature can attack on Autumn’s first turn, matching the reference’s ruling that Karn’s restart places it under the player’s control continuously since the turn began.
entries.answer:
Yes. Quilled Slagwurm can attack on Autumn's first turn. Karn Liberated's ultimate ability specifically overrides the normal 'summoning sickness' rule for permanents it puts onto the battlefield: according to [Karn Liberated ruling #5], permanents put onto the battlefield by Karn's -14 ability 'will have been under the starting controller's control continuously since the beginning of that player's first turn,' so creatures among them (including Quilled Slagwurm) can attack immediately, and this card text/ruling controls over any general rule that would otherwise require a creature to have been under its controller's control since their most recent turn began. Mechanically, the restart itself finishes resolving 'just before the first turn's untap step' [727.4], and per [Karn Liberated ruling #4] the cards left in exile with Karn are put onto the battlefield after the pregame procedure but before the new game's first turn, so Quilled Slagwurm is already on the battlefield when that first turn (and its untap step) begins — consistent with the ruling that treats it as having been under Autumn's control since the start of that turn. All the exiled cards remain involved in the new game per [727.2]. So there is no ambiguity in timing here: the card's own ability and its ruling explicitly grant it the ability to attack on the very first turn, overriding the general summoning-sickness expectation.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Karn's ability finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, so the creature has been controlled continuously since the turn began and can attack.

entries.question: Abel plays [Exotic Orchard]. What can it tap for if Nico controls only [Throne of Makindi] without any charge counters on it?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling that Exotic Orchard can produce any of the five colors (not colorless) because it looks at what Throne of Makindi's ability could produce if it resolved, ignoring costs.
entries.answer:
Exotic Orchard can be tapped to add one mana of any single color Abel chooses among white, blue, black, red, or green — it cannot produce {C} (colorless) even though Throne of Makindi can.

Exotic Orchard's ability is "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce" (Exotic Orchard card text). Under rule [106.7], the type of mana a permanent "could produce" includes anything an ability of that permanent would produce if it resolved, taking into account replacement effects, and you must ignore whether the ability's costs could actually be paid. Throne of Makindi has three abilities: "{T}: Add {C}", "{1}, {T}: Put a charge counter on this land" (not a mana ability), and "{T}, Remove a charge counter from this land: Add two mana of any one color. Spend this mana only to cast kicked spells" (Throne of Makindi card text). 

Because the last ability lets its controller choose any one color freely (it isn't tied to some other undefined choice the way Meteor Crater's color-matching ability is), Throne of Makindi "could produce" any of the five colors via that ability. The fact that it currently has no charge counter to remove is irrelevant — per [106.7] you ignore whether the cost (removing a counter) could be paid. This mirrors the logic in [Exotic Orchard ruling #4], where an opponent's Vivid Crag lets Exotic Orchard tap for any color regardless of whether Vivid Crag actually has a counter to remove or is even untapped.

However, Throne of Makindi's {T}: Add {C} ability only produces colorless mana, and colorless is not one of the five colors ([105.1], [Exotic Orchard ruling #2] specifically states Exotic Orchard can't be tapped for colorless mana even if the opponent's land could produce it). So that ability doesn't expand what Exotic Orchard can do.

Note also that the "spend this mana only to cast kicked spells" restriction is a spending restriction on Throne of Makindi's own mana, not a replacement effect on the type produced, so it doesn't carry over to Exotic Orchard's mana — mana Abel gets from Exotic Orchard is unrestricted.

Bottom line: with only Throne of Makindi (no charge counters) on Nico's side, Abel's Exotic Orchard can tap for one mana of any single color of Abel's choice — white, blue, black, red, or green.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color of mana. Exotic Orchard is limited by what an opponent's land's abilities could produce if they resolved, not if the opponent could pay the costs required.

entries.question: Abraham controls [Drought] and [Derelor]. How many Swamps would they have to sacrifice in order to cast a [Virulent Wound]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Drought counts only the printed {B} in Virulent Wound's mana cost so Abraham must sacrifice one Swamp (Derelor only increases mana to pay).
entries.answer:
Abraham has to sacrifice 1 Swamp to cast Virulent Wound (in addition to paying the mana cost, which totals {B}{B} once Derelor’s tax is applied).

Here's why. Virulent Wound's printed mana cost is {B} — it contains exactly one black mana symbol (rule 202.1 defines an object's mana cost as the symbols printed on it). Drought's ability reads: "Spells cost an additional 'Sacrifice a Swamp' to cast for each black mana symbol in their mana costs." That count is based on the spell's actual mana cost (the printed symbols), not on the final total cost after other cost-increasing effects are added. Since Virulent Wound's mana cost has only one {B}, Drought's additional cost is exactly one Swamp sacrifice.

Derelor's ability ("Black spells you cast cost {B} more to cast") is a separate cost increase. Per rule 601.2f, the total cost of a spell is the mana cost plus all additional costs and cost increases, minus reductions, all applied when the total cost is determined and then locked in. Derelor's {B} increase adds to the mana that must be paid, but it does not add a symbol to Virulent Wound's mana cost itself — additional/cost-increase effects are distinct from the mana cost proper (see rule 202.4, which notes additional costs from an object's text or an effect aren't part of the mana cost). Because Drought only counts symbols in the mana cost (not the fully modified total cost), Derelor's added {B} doesn't trigger a second Swamp sacrifice from Drought.

So, putting it together for the total cost of casting Virulent Wound: mana cost {B} (printed) + {B} (Derelor's increase) = {B}{B} to pay in mana, plus the additional cost of sacrificing 1 Swamp (from Drought, based on the single {B} in Virulent Wound's mana cost). If Abraham can't pay all of this — for example if they have no Swamps to sacrifice — rule 118.3c means they simply cannot cast the spell, since a cost can't be partially paid.

Note: this analysis holds regardless of player count, since none of the rules or card texts involved reference multiplayer-specific effects (they simply have you or your opponents, unaffected by the number of players).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 1. The mana cost of a spell doesn't change, regardless of what was paid for it.

entries.question: Abram controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Tropical Island], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Tropical Island a creature?
entries.reason: Both conclude Blood Moon removes Tropical Island's Forest type before Life and Limb can apply, so Life and Limb doesn't make it a creature.
entries.answer:
No. Tropical Island is not a creature in this scenario, because Blood Moon strips it of its Forest land type before Life and Limb's effect can check whether it's a Forest.

Here's why. Tropical Island is a land with the printed land types Forest and Island, but because it lacks the supertype "basic," it is a nonbasic land [305.8] (confirmed by [Tropical Island ruling #1], which notes it has basic land types but isn't itself a basic land). Blood Moon's static ability makes all nonbasic lands into Mountains. This is a type-setting effect: per [305.7], when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land "no longer has its old land type" and loses the land types it previously had (Forest and Island), gaining only the Mountain type (and its mana ability). Blood Moon's own ruling confirms this doesn't touch supertypes or names — Tropical Island stays nonbasic and keeps its name — but its land type does change to Mountain [Blood Moon ruling #3].

Life and Limb's ability reads "All Forests ... are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." This only affects objects that currently have the land type Forest [205.3i]; per [Life and Limb ruling #0], "Forest" here means the land type, not a creature type. Because these are both layer 4 (type-changing) continuous effects, and because Life and Limb's effect ("all Forests") checks for objects with the Forest land type while Blood Moon's effect determines what that land type is, Life and Limb's effect is dependent on Blood Moon's — applying Blood Moon changes which objects qualify as Forests. Dependent effects are applied after the effects they depend on, so Blood Moon's Mountain-setting is applied first: Tropical Island becomes just a (nonbasic) Mountain, no longer a Forest. When Life and Limb's effect is then checked, Tropical Island no longer has the Forest land type, so Life and Limb does not turn it into a creature.

So with Blood Moon, Life and Limb, and Tropical Island all on the battlefield in that entry order, Tropical Island ends up as a nonbasic land with only the Mountain land type, and it is not a creature.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Applying Blood Moon's effect first would prevent Life and Limb's effect from applying to Tropical Island and applying Life and Limb's effect first would not affect how Blood Moon's effect is applied or what it does, so Life and Limb's effect is dependent on Blood Moon's effect and waits to apply until afterwards. Since Blood Moon's effect makes Tropical Island no longer a Forest, Life and Limb doesn't apply to it at all.

entries.question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
entries.reason: The candidate says the +1/+1 counters remain on Skullbriar after it becomes a face-down manifested permanent, but the reference states the counters cease to exist once it enters the battlefield face down (even though Nixon can still deduce which is which).
entries.answer:
The three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave through the whole process, and that fact lets Nixon tell the two manifested creatures apart even though Ghastly Conscription tries to disguise them.

Walking through it: Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from the target graveyard face down, shuffles that face-down pile, then manifests each card (put onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature, per the card's own text). That's two zone changes for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave: graveyard → exile, and exile → battlefield. Skullbriar's own ability reads 'Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library.' Neither of those two moves is to a hand or a library, so under that ability the +1/+1 counters travel with the card each time, arriving on the battlefield already in place when it's manifested [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]. Ruling #6 confirms that when a card carrying Skullbriar's counter-retention text leaves the battlefield (or, as here, changes zones with that text active) the counters remain on it, and ruling #4 confirms it becomes a brand-new object each time but the counters themselves still stick around unless the card goes to a hand or library.

Once it lands on the battlefield as a manifested permanent, though, it's face down, and rule [708.2a] says a face-down permanent (absent other instructions) is 'a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost' — manifest doesn't grant it any different base characteristics. So the object no longer has Skullbriar's name or its counter ability once face down; it's just a nameless 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters already sitting on it, making it a 5/5 face-down creature. The Southern Elephant, by contrast, is manifested as a plain 2/2 face-down creature with no counters.

Because of that size difference, Nixon (and anyone watching) can immediately tell the two manifested creatures apart: the 5/5 (2/2 plus three +1/+1 counters) is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, and the 2/2 with no counters is Southern Elephant. Ghastly Conscription's shuffle is meant to hide which pile member is which [Ghastly Conscription ruling #0], but rule [708.6] requires a player to be able to easily differentiate their own face-down permanents at all times, and here the counters themselves are exactly such a distinguishing feature — so the shuffle doesn't actually conceal Skullbriar's identity from its own controller.

This assumes the graveyard-to-exile and exile-to-battlefield movements both occur as part of Ghastly Conscription's resolution with no player having priority to remove the counters in between (there's no chance to respond to a resolving spell's internal instructions), so the counters have no opportunity to be stripped off along the way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nixon will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Southern Elephant.

entries.question: Asa casts [Chatterstorm]. In response, Nico casts [Gather Specimens]. After everything resolves, Asa activates the second ability of [Homeward Path]. Who gains control of the token?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly states Nico owns the token due to Gather Specimens and thus keeps control, contradicting the correct ruling that the token is owned by its creator Asa and so Asa gains control via Homeward Path.
entries.answer:
Nico ends up controlling the token both before and after Homeward Path is activated — activating Homeward Path doesn't change anything here. Here's why: Chatterstorm creates a 1/1 green Squirrel creature token. Normally, per rule [111.2], the player who creates a token is its owner, and the token enters the battlefield under that player's control — that would be Asa. However, Nico's Gather Specimens is already resolved and its replacement effect is active for the rest of the turn: "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Since the Squirrel token would enter under Asa's control, and Asa is Nico's opponent, Gather Specimens replaces that and the token enters the battlefield under Nico's control instead. Because the token's actual owner is defined by whose control it entered under (as clarified by [Homeward Path ruling #1], "The owner of a token is the player under whose control the token was put onto the battlefield"), Nico is both the owner and the controller of the Squirrel token. When Asa later activates Homeward Path's second ability, "Each player gains control of all creatures they own," the Squirrel token is owned by Nico, so this ability causes Nico to gain control of it — which Nico already has. Asa's own creatures (if any) would return to Asa, but the Squirrel token stays with Nico throughout.
