This scenario is only defined for two players (Asa and Nico); no multiplayer-specific rule was given here, so if a third player's creatures were also on the battlefield, Homeward Path would still just return each player's own creatures to them per its plain text, but I don't have multiplayer-specific rules text to note any variation beyond that.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Asa does. Tokens are owned by the player that created them. Asa still created the token, regardless of under whose control it entered the battlefield.

entries.question: Aaliyah controls a [Squandered Resources] and a [Glacial Floodplain]. Nicolas controls [Blood Moon]. If Aaliyah sacrifices Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Blood Moon turns Glacial Floodplain into a Mountain that can only produce red mana, so Sacrificing it to Squandered Resources yields only {R}.
entries.answer:
Sacring Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources will yield {R} (red mana), not {W} or {U}. Nicolas's Blood Moon ("2}{R} Enchantment, 'Nonbasic lands are Mountains')') turns Glacial Floodplain — a nonbasic land (it has the basic land types Plains and and island but but but lking the it basicial't have the 'Basic' supertype) — into a Mountain. per the card's own rulings: it 'lose[s] any other land types and abilities' and gains 'the land type Mountain and gain the ability {T}: Add {R}.'' That overrides its printed text giving {W} or {{U} (Card text overrides the general rule that Squandered Resources checks only the printed ability). Squandered Resources' activated ability 'Sacrifice a land: Add one mana of any type the sacrificed land could produce' works by determining, at the moment the sacrifice cost is paid, what mana that land's abilities would produce if activated then, per rule [106.7] and the fact that Blood Moon's continuous effect from its static ability is not 'locked in' and applies at any given moment per [611.3a]. Since Blood Moon has already turned Glacial Floodplain into a Mountain with only '{T}: Add {R}' (its original Plains/Island typing and W/U mana ability are gone, per the Blood Moon ruling), the only mana type Glacial Floodplain could produce at the time it's sacrificed is {R}. Squandered Resources' ability therefore lets Aaliyah add one {R}. This is a two-player scenario as described (Aaliyah and Nicolas); nothing about multiplayer turn order or defending-player rules is relevant here, so the answer doesn't change in a larger game as long as Nicolas's Blood Moon is still affecting Aaliyah's lands (Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands in play, not just an opponent's, in any player count).

entries.answer_gold: Just {R}. Squandered Resources cares about what colors of mana it could produce on the battlefield.

entries.question: Neil controls [Willow Elf] enchanted with [Felidar Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Anger of the Gods]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate says the creature's controller can choose which replacement applies (allowing either survival or exile), while the reference concludes Felidar Umbra must apply first so Willow Elf survives, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Willow Elf (a 1/1) is dealt 3 damage by Anger of the Gods, which is lethal, so as a state-based action Willow Elf would be destroyed. At that moment two replacement effects are competing to modify what happens to Willow Elf: Felidar Umbra's umbra armor ability ("If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura") and Anger of the Gods' own replacement ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead"). Because both effects are trying to modify the same event affecting the same object, rule 616.1e/616.1f says Neil — as the controller of Willow Elf, the affected permanent — chooses which one to apply first, and once one is applied, the other is checked again and may no longer be applicable.

If Neil applies Felidar Umbra's umbra armor first: Willow Elf is never actually destroyed. Instead, all damage is removed from Willow Elf and Felidar Umbra itself is destroyed (put into Neil's graveyard) [702.89a, Felidar Umbra ruling #3, Felidar Umbra ruling #4]. Because Willow Elf never dies, Anger of the Gods' "exile instead of dying" clause has nothing left to modify and does nothing [Anger of the Gods ruling #0, 615.1... effectively 616.1f's rule that an already-resolved replacement leaves the other one moot]. Willow Elf survives on the battlefield, undamaged, with no Aura attached.

If Neil instead applies Anger of the Gods' replacement first: Willow Elf's would-be death (going to the graveyard) is replaced with exile instead [Anger of the Gods ruling #0]. Since Willow Elf was never destroyed in the graveyard-bound sense that umbra armor cares about, umbra armor's replacement no longer has anything to apply to, so Felidar Umbra is not saved by that ability. Willow Elf is exiled instead of dying. (What then happens to Felidar Umbra, now enchanting nothing, isn't covered by any rule given here, so I can't state its exact fate with a citation — only that Willow Elf itself ends up in exile under this branch.)

Either way, this is a single choice made by Willow Elf's controller (Neil); since only one player's permanent is involved, this works the same whether the game has two players or more than two — the APNAP ordering rule (101.4) only matters when multiple players must make such choices simultaneously, which isn't the case here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Felidar Umbra is destroyed and moves to the graveyard. Willow Elf remains on the battlefield. If it would die later in the turn, it'll be exiled instead. Felidar Umbra's effect replaces the "destroy" event while Anger of the Gods's effect replaces the "die" event, so Felidar Umbra has to be applied first.

entries.question: Asa controls [Library of Leng] and is discarding a card due to [Azra Oddsmaker]'s ability. Can they put the discarded card on top of their library? If so, what happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Library of Leng can replace Azra Oddsmaker's discard (which is part of the effect, not a cost), letting Asa put the card on top of their library while the ability still sees a card was discarded.
entries.answer:
Yes. Because discarding a card as part of Azra Oddsmaker's triggered ability ("At the beginning of combat on your turn, you may discard a card...") is part of resolving an effect and not a cost payment, Library of Leng's replacement ability can apply to it. Library of Leng's text says "If an effect causes you to discard a card, discard it, but you may put it on top of your library instead of into your graveyard," and per its ruling, this replaces the normal discard action (which sends the card to the graveyard) with one that puts the card on top of the library instead.

So Asa discards the card as required by Azra Oddsmaker, and instead of that card going to the graveyard, Asa may choose to put it on top of their library. The discard still counts as "discarding a card" for the purposes of Azra Oddsmaker's ability - Azra Oddsmaker only cares that a card was discarded, not where it ends up - so Asa still gets to choose a creature, and if that creature deals combat damage to a player this turn, Asa draws two cards.

Note: this only works because Azra Oddsmaker's discard is a cost-free effect within the ability, not a cost. Library of Leng's own ruling clarifies it cannot be used when a discard is paid as a cost (e.g., an activation cost written as "Discard a card:"), since costs aren't effects. Azra Oddsmaker's discard is not phrased as a cost, so Library of Leng applies here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Discarding a cost to the ability is a cost [118.12], but that doesn't stop it from being an effect as well. Library of Leng only changes where the card moves to, not that it was discarded, so the cost was paid and the remainder of Azra Oddsmaker's ability will resolve as normal.

entries.question: Noah controls [Compost]. Ainsley controls [Dune Beetle] and a token that was created as a copy of [Bogstomper]. Ainsley casts [Soulscour]. How many times does Compost trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate says Compost triggers once (for Dune Beetle), but the reference says it triggers zero times because Compost is in the graveyard after Soulscour's mass destruction and its ability can't function there, so the conclusions differ.
entries.answer:
Compost triggers exactly once. Compost's trigger condition is "Whenever a black card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere." When Ainsley's Soulscour resolves, it destroys all nonartifact permanents at once, which is a single event, but per rule [603.2c] a triggered ability "can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences" — so Compost checks each qualifying occurrence within that mass-destruction event separately. Ainsley controls two nonartifact permanents that die simultaneously: Dune Beetle and a token that was created as a copy of Bogstomper.

Dune Beetle is an actual black card, so its being put into Ainsley's graveyard is one qualifying occurrence, and Compost triggers for it.

The token copy of Bogstomper, however, is not a card at all — it's a token. The rules consistently distinguish "permanent" from "permanent card" (see the terminology used in [700.11], which specifically talks about "permanent cards" being put into a graveyard as distinct from permanents generally), reflecting that tokens are permanents but are not cards. Compost's trigger explicitly requires a black *card* to be put into the graveyard, not merely a black permanent. Since the Bogstomper token isn't a card, its death (it briefly hits the graveyard and then ceases to exist as a state-based action) doesn't satisfy Compost's trigger condition, so it does not generate a second trigger.

So out of the two black permanents Ainsley loses to Soulscour, only Dune Beetle actually causes Compost to trigger, giving Noah one opportunity to draw a card. This holds whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, since Compost only cares about cards going to "an opponent's" graveyard, and Ainsley is an opponent of Noah either way; the number of other players at the table doesn't change this count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
0. Soulscour destroys all permanents simultaneously. Compost's trigger checks immediately after the event in question to see if it should trigger. However by that time Compost is in the graveyard, and its ability doesn't function there.

(Compost doesn't fit the "leaves-the-battlefield" trigger exception because it's a "from anywhere" trigger.)

entries.question: Noor controls [Rhystic Study]. Alex casts [Mishra's Domination]. As Rhystic Study's trigger resolves, who makes their choice first? Does Noor choose whether or not to draw a card, and if yes, Alex may pay the mana to prevent it? Or does Alex choose to pay the mana first, and if they don't, Noor has the choice to draw a card?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Alex chooses whether to pay {1} first, and only afterward does Noor decide whether to draw, so the candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Alex chooses first. Rhystic Study's ability reads "you may draw a card unless that player pays {1}" — the paying is resolved before Noor's drawing choice. As the ability resolves, Alex first decides whether to pay {1}. Only after that does Noor decide whether to draw a card: if Alex pays, Noor's draw is prevented outright (there's no card to draw from), and if Alex declines to pay, Noor then gets the choice of whether to draw a card. [Rhystic Study ruling #1] states explicitly: "You don't have to decide whether or not to draw a card until after the player decides whether or not to pay." [Rhystic Study ruling #0] also confirms that Rhystic Study's trigger resolves before Mishra's Domination itself (Alex's spell) resolves, and it resolves even if that spell is later countered — but that's a separate timing point about the trigger versus the spell, not about the order of choices within the trigger's resolution. This is Rhystic Study's own printed text and ruling controlling the sequence, which is more specific than the general optional-ability rule [603.5] about triggered abilities with "may" effects going on the stack regardless of intent (the choice itself is still made at resolution, per that general rule, but the specific order of who chooses first is nailed down by the ruling).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Alex chooses first.

entries.question: Allison controls [Leyline of Anticipation]. In their draw step, they casts [Relentless Assault]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference — Relentless Assault can be cast during the draw step due to Leyline of Anticipation but creates no extra combat or main phase because it's not being cast in a main phase.
entries.answer:
Allison can legally cast Relentless Assault during their draw step because Leyline of Anticipation says "You may cast spells as though they had flash," and flash means "you may play this card any time you could cast an instant," i.e. any time you have priority [702.8a][304.5][609.4a]. Since a player has priority during the draw step, the casting of Relentless Assault is legal even though it's a sorcery.

However, when Relentless Assault resolves, its effects are only partially useful here. Relentless Assault untaps all creatures that attacked this turn — at this point, in the draw step, no creatures have attacked yet, so this does nothing. More importantly, the "additional combat phase followed by an additional main phase" only happens if Relentless Assault resolves during a main phase [Relentless Assault ruling #0]. Because Allison cast and resolved it during the draw step (not a main phase), that clause simply fails — no extra combat phase or extra main phase is created.

So the net effect of this play is essentially nothing beneficial: Relentless Assault resolves, untaps no creatures (since none attacked yet), and grants no additional combat/main phase, because the draw step is not a main phase.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There is no "this main phase" to add the combat step after, so no additional phase is created. The turn proceeds as normal.

entries.question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Albert can see the secret choice (misapplying rule 723.4 and treating the selection as visible), whereas the reference states the choice was made when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield and remains hidden, so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
Yes. Because Albert is controlling Brielle during Brielle's turn (per Worst Fears), rule [723.4] applies: any information about an object in the game that would be visible to the player being controlled (Brielle) is visible to both Brielle and the player controlling her (Albert). The identity of the opponent secretly chosen when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield is information about an object in the game (Stalking Leonin) that Brielle, as its controller, already knows. Since that information is visible to Brielle, it becomes visible to Albert as well while he controls her.

Note that this only covers information about game objects — if Stalking Leonin's chosen opponent had instead been recorded via some off-game method involving cards outside the game, rule [723.4] specifies that information about cards outside the game is visible only to the controlled player, not the controller. But the Stalking Leonin ruling [Stalking Leonin ruling #0] confirms the secret choice can be tracked by writing the name on paper kept with the card, which is information tied to the permanent (an in-game object), so it falls under the first sentence of [723.4] and is shared with Albert.

This also holds regardless of whether this is a two-player or multiplayer game, since [723.4] doesn't depend on player count — it's purely about what information the controlled player can see, which Albert then also sees.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Brielle. Albert can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

entries.question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—saying Primal Vigor won’t double the counter (1) while the reference correctly states replacement effects are applied as Rescuer Sphinx enters so Primal Vigor still doubles it to 2.
entries.answer:
Rescuer Sphinx will enter the battlefield with only 1 +1/+1 counter, not 2 -- Primal Vigor's doubling effect does not apply here.

Rescuer Sphinx's ability reads: "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Per [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0], the choice of what to return is made while Rescuer Sphinx is entering the battlefield, and "no player may take actions between the time you choose which permanent to return and the time Rescuer Sphinx is on the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter." This means the return of the chosen permanent to its owner's hand is resolved first, and only then does Rescuer Sphinx actually enter the battlefield with its counter.

Because Abdullah chose to return Primal Vigor itself, Primal Vigor is no longer on the battlefield by the time Rescuer Sphinx's counter is actually placed. Under rule [614.12], to determine which replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters, you check continuous effects from static abilities "that already exist and would apply to the permanent" -- and Primal Vigor's doubling ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature, twice that many...are put on that creature instead") is a continuous effect generated only while Primal Vigor is on the battlefield. Since Primal Vigor has already left the battlefield (been bounced to hand) before the counter is put on Rescuer Sphinx, its doubling effect is not present to apply, and Rescuer Sphinx simply enters with the single +1/+1 counter its own ability grants.

Note the timing assumption: this relies on the sequencing given explicitly in [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #0] that the return happens before Rescuer Sphinx is on the battlefield with the counter, all as part of one uninterrupted replacement-effect application (consistent with rule [614.1c] describing such effects as applying continuously as the permanent enters, not as separate events with priority in between). If Primal Vigor were instead left on the battlefield (i.e., some other permanent were bounced), Primal Vigor's own doubling text and [Primal Vigor ruling #2] confirm the counter would be doubled to 2.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Abdullah will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Primal Vigor will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.

entries.question: Arturo uses [Vengeful Ancestor] to goad [Craw Wurm]. After it's been goaded, Nico uses [Brokers Confluence], causing Craw Wurm to phase out. On Nico's turn, what are Nico's legal combat choices?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Craw Wurm stays goaded despite phasing, will be phased in for Nico's combat and must attack (and in a two‑player game must attack Arturo).
entries.answer:
Nico's Craw Wurm has already phased back in by the time combat begins on Nico's turn, and it is still goaded, so Nico is required to attack with it this combat — if only Arturo is available as an opponent, Craw Wurm must attack Arturo (since the "attack someone other than Arturo" clause is impossible to satisfy in a two‑player game and so drops away); attacking with Craw Wurm will also trigger Vengeful Ancestor's second ability, dealing 1 damage to Nico as Craw Wurm's controller.

Walking through why: Arturo's Vengeful Ancestor goaded Craw Wurm, and goad lasts 'until the next turn of the controller of that spell or ability' [701.15a; Vengeful Ancestor] — i.e., until Arturo's next turn, not Nico's. While goaded, Craw Wurm 'attacks each combat if able and attacks a player other than the controller of the permanent, spell, or ability that caused it to be goaded if able' [701.15b].

Nico then used Brokers Confluence to phase Craw Wurm out. Brokers Confluence's text is 'Target creature phases out... until its controller's next turn' — Craw Wurm's controller is Nico, so this is a one-shot phasing effect with a specified end point (Nico's next turn) under rule [610.4a]. Per [610.4a], a permanent phased out this way does *not* automatically phase back in via the normal untap-step phasing turn-based action [502.1]; instead, a second one-shot effect phases it in immediately once the specified event (the start of Nico's next turn) occurs. So by the time combat rolls around on that turn, Craw Wurm has phased in and is a normal permanent again [702.26c].

While it was phased out, Craw Wurm was treated as though it didn't exist and was removed from combat [702.26b; 506.4], but phasing doesn't change zones or control, and things like counters/stickers persist through phasing [702.26d]. The goaded designation is a status on the permanent itself (not a 'for as long as' continuous effect that would expire on losing sight of the object per 702.26f), so it survives the phase-out/phase-in round trip and is still in force, since the stated end point (Arturo's next turn) still hasn't arrived — this is Nico's turn.

So, assuming a two-player game with only Arturo and Nico: Craw Wurm must attack if able (it's untapped, controlled by the active player, and not otherwise restricted), and the 'must attack someone other than Arturo' half of the goad requirement is impossible to meet since Arturo is the only opponent — an impossible sub-requirement simply doesn't apply, so Craw Wurm's mandatory attack goes at Arturo. If this is instead a multiplayer game with a third player available, Nico would be required to attack that other player (or a planeswalker/battle they control) with Craw Wurm instead of Arturo, per the same rule [701.15b]. Either way, once Craw Wurm attacks as a goaded creature, Vengeful Ancestor's triggered ability deals 1 damage to Nico, Craw Wurm's controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Craw Wurm must attack, and since there aren't any other players in the game, it has to attack Arturo. Goaded creatures must attack, and must attack a player other than the one that goaded them if able. Phasing doesn't cause Craw Wurm to no longer be goaded, as the duration on the continuous effect hasn't ended when Craw Wurm phases back in.

entries.question: Arabella controls [Sylvok Explorer]. Nolan controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. If Arabella taps the Sylvok Explorer, what type(s) of mana can they produce?
entries.reason: Both conclude that because Gaea's Cradle would produce zero mana with no creatures, Sylvok Explorer has no mana type to copy and thus produces no mana.
entries.answer:
Tapping Sylvok Explorer here produces no mana at all. Sylvok Explorer's ability is "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land Nolan (the opponent) controls is Gaea's Cradle, whose ability is "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." Since Nolan controls no creatures, if Gaea's Cradle's ability were to resolve right now it would add zero mana. Under rule [106.7], the type of mana a permanent "could produce" is defined by what its own ability would produce if it resolved at this time (ignoring whether costs could be paid) — and the rule explicitly states that if that permanent wouldn't produce any mana under these conditions, there's no type of mana it could produce. Because Gaea's Cradle would produce zero mana with zero creatures, it currently has no defined type of mana it "could produce." That means Sylvok Explorer has no color to choose from when its ability resolves. Per rule [106.5], an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type instead produces no mana. So activating Sylvok Explorer in this exact board state (Arabella controls Sylvok Explorer; Nolan controls Gaea's Cradle and no creatures) taps Sylvok Explorer but adds no mana to Arabella's mana pool. Note this would change immediately if Nolan controlled even one creature — then Gaea's Cradle could produce {G}, and Sylvok Explorer could then be activated to add {G}.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. Gaea's Cradle couldn't produce any mana, so neither can Sylvok Explorer.

entries.question: Addisyn casts [Read the Runes] for X=2 and chooses to discard a card and sacrifice [All-Seeing Arbiter]. Will All-Seeing Arbiter trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude All-Seeing Arbiter is sacrificed before the discard required by Read the Runes and therefore its discard-triggered ability will not trigger.
entries.answer:
No. Because All-Seeing Arbiter has already been sacrificed by the time the discard happens, its "Whenever you discard a card" ability won't be on the battlefield to trigger, so it won't fire off this discard.

Read the Runes says: "Draw X cards. For each card drawn this way, discard a card unless you sacrifice a permanent." Per [Read the Runes ruling #1], the order of operations is fixed: you draw the cards first, then you sacrifice any permanents you want to sacrifice, and only afterward do you discard the required number of cards from your hand — there's no chance to do anything in between. So with X=2, Addisyn draws 2 cards, then sacrifices All-Seeing Arbiter (covering one of the two draws), and only after that does she discard the one remaining required card.

By the time that discard actually happens, All-Seeing Arbiter is already in the graveyard, not the battlefield. Its ability "Whenever you discard a card, target creature an opponent controls gets -X/-0..." is a normal triggered ability, not a leaves-the-battlefield ability, a sacrifice trigger, a graveyard-leaves trigger, or a public-zone-to-hand/library trigger — the only categories of trigger that "look back in time" under [603.10a]. Since it doesn't fall into any of those exceptions, the game checks the board state as it exists at the moment of the discard event (the normal rule in [603.10a]) to see whether the ability's source is around to trigger. All-Seeing Arbiter isn't on the battlefield anymore at that moment, so its discard-triggered ability simply doesn't exist to trigger ([603.2c] confirms triggered abilities trigger based on the game event matching the trigger condition of an ability that exists/applies at the relevant time).

Note: this assumes Addisyn sacrifices All-Seeing Arbiter for one of the two draws and only has to discard for the other draw, which matches the question's description ("discard a card and sacrifice All-Seeing Arbiter" for X=2). If instead the sacrifice happened after the discard in some other scenario, the ability could trigger, but Read the Runes' own ruling fixes the order as sacrifice-then-discard, so that alternate timing doesn't apply here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Addisyn will first choose whether they are sacrificing permanent, if they don't then they discard a card. Because it happens in this order, All-Seeing Arbiter will not be around to when Addisyn is discarding a card.

entries.question: Addison has six cards in their graveyard and casts [Epicenter] targeting Nataly. In response, Nataly casts [Blossoming Calm]. Before it resolves, Addison casts [Dampen Thought] targeting themself. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference — Epicenter fails to resolve because Nataly becomes an illegal target due to hexproof from Blossoming Calm, so no lands are sacrificed.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens to any land: Epicenter never resolves, because its target (Nataly) becomes illegal by the time it would resolve. Here's the full sequence.

Stack order (bottom to top): Epicenter (targeting Nataly, cast by Addison) → Blossoming Calm (cast by Nataly in response) → Dampen Thought (targeting Addison, cast by Addison in response to Blossoming Calm). Each new spell is put on top of the stack [405.2], and because it was cast in response to what was already there, it resolves first [117.7].

1. Dampen Thought resolves first. Its text says 'Target player mills four cards,' and Addison targeted themself, so Addison mills 4 cards. After the mill, as the final part of resolution, Dampen Thought (an instant) goes to Addison's graveyard [304.2, 608.2n]. Addison's graveyard now has 6 + 4 = 10 cards.

2. Blossoming Calm resolves next. Its text ('You gain hexproof until your next turn. You gain 2 life.') means Nataly (its caster/controller) gains hexproof until her next turn and gains 2 life. Hexproof means a permanent or player can't be the target of spells or abilities controlled by an opponent. Because Blossoming Calm has Rebound, instead of going to the graveyard it is exiled as it resolves, and Nataly may cast it again for free at the beginning of her next upkeep (per Blossoming Calm's printed Rebound text, which overrides the normal graveyard destination in rule 608.2n).

3. Epicenter, now on top of the stack, attempts to resolve. Before applying its effect, the game rechecks whether its target (Nataly) is still legal [608.2b]. Targets can become illegal if 'their characteristics may have changed' since being targeted — and Nataly's characteristics just changed: she now has hexproof against Addison (her opponent, and Epicenter's controller). Since Nataly is Epicenter's only target and she is now an illegal target for a spell controlled by an opponent, Epicenter does not resolve at all. It is removed from the stack and put into Addison's graveyard, with no effect [608.2b].

Because Epicenter never resolves, it doesn't matter that Addison's graveyard reached 7+ cards (triggering Epicenter's Threshold mode, 'each player sacrifices all lands they control instead') — that check only happens during resolution's effect-application steps, which never occur. So no one sacrifices any land, Nataly ends up with hexproof and 2 extra life, and Addison has milled 4 cards and has Epicenter and Dampen Thought in their graveyard.

(Timing note: this assumes Dampen Thought was cast in response to Blossoming Calm, i.e., after Blossoming Calm was already on the stack, as the question states with 'Before it resolves.' If instead the order of casting were reversed, the resolution order — and thus whether Nataly gains hexproof before Epicenter checks her legality — would be the same regardless, since Blossoming Calm is still below Dampen Thought on the stack and resolves before Epicenter either way.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Neither player will sacrifice any lands. The text on Epicenter is a self-replacement effect and changes what the spell is doing. However, before the replacement effect would be applied the game checks to see if all the targets for the spell are still legal. Nataly is no longer a legal target, therefore the spell won't resolve.

entries.question: Anson controls [Zirda, the Dawnwaker], [Sundial, Dawn Tyrant], and [Mobilized District]. How much does Anson have to pay to activate the second ability of Mobilized District?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes the cost must be {1}, but the correct ruling allows choosing the order of reductions so the cost can be either {1} or {0}.
entries.answer:
Anson pays {1} (one generic mana) to activate Mobilized District's second ability. Mobilized District's ability reads "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." Anson controls two legendary creatures – Zirda, the Dawnwaker and Sundial, Dawn Tyrant – so Mobilized District's own built-in reduction lowers the base {4} cost by {2}, bringing it to {2} [Mobilized District ruling #0]. Mobilized District itself is not legendary, so it doesn't count toward its own reduction. Next, Zirda, the Dawnwaker's static ability applies: "Abilities you activate that aren't mana abilities cost {2} less to activate. This effect can't reduce the mana in that cost to less than one mana." entries.question: Anderson controls [Quirion Explorer]. Nico controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Anderson taps Quirion Explorer, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Quirion Explorer produces no mana by ignoring Crumbling Vestige's ETB triggered ability, whereas the reference states that triggered abilities count and thus Quirion Explorer can produce any color.
entries.answer:
Tapping Quirion Explorer will produce no mana at all in this situation. Quirion Explorer's ability reads "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." Nico's only land is Crumbling Vestige, which has two abilities: a one-shot triggered ability ("When this land enters, add one mana of any color") and a repeatable mana ability ("{T}: Add {C}"). Under rule [106.7], to determine what a permanent "could produce," you look at what an ability of that permanent would produce if it resolved right now, ignoring whether its costs could be paid. Crumbling Vestige's color-producing ability is tied to it entering the battlefield — it already entered (or, if it is entering right now, that's a separate timing question addressed below) — so that one-shot trigger isn't something that can be made to resolve 'at this time' the way a repeatable activated ability can. The only ability of Crumbling Vestige that can actually be considered as producing mana right now is its repeatable "{T}: Add {C}" ability, and {C} is colorless mana, not a color. Since Crumbling Vestige has no color it could presently produce, there is no color for Quirion Explorer's ability to copy, so by rule [106.5] (an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces no mana instead), activating Quirion Explorer produces nothing. This exact scenario is confirmed by the card's own ruling: 'If the opponent only has lands that produce colorless or no mana, this card's ability can still be activated; it just won't produce any mana' [Quirion Explorer ruling #0]. Note the timing assumption: if instead Crumbling Vestige were entering the battlefield at this very moment (its ETB trigger about to resolve), that delayed/triggered ability [603.7a] could define a color once it actually resolves and a choice is made, but that's a different moment in time than simply tapping Quirion Explorer while Crumbling Vestige just sits on the battlefield as already-resolved land. This ruling applies regardless of how many players are in the game, since it only concerns what Crumbling Vestige itself could produce.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color. Quirion Explorer checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

entries.question: Andi controls [Karn Liberated], which has exiled an [Anvil of Bogardan]. They activate Karn Liberated's -14 ability, and restarts the game. How many cards will they draw during their first turn?

Here's what the given rules do establish. When Andi activates Karn Liberated's −14 ability, the game restarts (727.1, 104.6). The new game begins following normal starting-game procedure, with Andi as the starting player because they controlled the ability that restarted the game (727.1a). As part of starting the new game, each player draws seven cards (727.3) — that draw happens before the first turn even begins, so it isn't 'during their first turn.' Karn Liberated's −14 ability then finishes resolving 'just before the first turn's untap step' (727.4), putting Anvil of Bogardan onto the battlefield under Andi's control at that point — so Anvil of Bogardan is already in play by the time the first turn's untap and draw steps occur. Anvil of Bogardan's own text says 'At the beginning of each player's draw step, that player draws an additional card, then discards a card,' so if Andi actually has a draw step on turn one, that trigger would fire and Andi would draw one extra card (and discard one) in addition to whatever their normal turn-one draw is. The catch is that none of the rules given here state whether the starting player's very first draw step is skipped (a rule that, in a normal two-player game, would mean Andi has no draw step at all on turn one, so Anvil of Bogardan's ability would never trigger and Andi would draw zero cards that turn). Because that draw-step rule isn't included in the provided rules text, I can't say with certainty whether the number of cards Andi draws during turn one is 0 (no draw step at all) or 2 (a normal draw plus Anvil of Bogardan's extra draw, if the draw step isn't skipped). Anvil of Bogardan triggers at the beginning of the draw step, but it doesn't get a chance to trigger if that step is skipped.

entries.question: Nico controls [Drought]. How many Swamps would Ava have to sacrifice in order to cast [Beckon Apparition]?

If Ava controls no Swamps, she cannot pay this additional cost and therefore cannot cast Beckon Apparition at all, per rule [118.3] (a player can't pay a cost without the necessary resources) and [614.17b]-style logic that an unpayable cost can't be chosen. The total cost, once the additional cost is locked in during casting, must be paid in full with no partial payments allowed, per rule [601.2h].

entries.question: Nico controls [Solemnity]. Aimee controls [Vizier of Remedies] and a tapped [Barrenton Medic]. Can Aimee untap Barrenton Medic with its own ability?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the ability can be activated because Vizier reduces the counter placement to zero, but the reference correctly states Solemnity prevents counters being put so the cost cannot legally be paid and the ability can't be activated.
entries.answer:
Yes. Aimee can activate Barrenton Medic's untap ability, and the cost can actually be paid even though Nico controls Solemnity, because Aimee's own Vizier of Remedies changes what the cost does.

Barrenton Medic's ability is "Put a -1/-1 counter on this creature: Untap this creature." The counter placement is the activation cost, paid when the ability is activated (as confirmed for this exact ability by [Barrenton Medic ruling #0]). Solemnity reads "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands." Under rule [614.17b], if an event can't happen, a player can't choose to pay a cost that includes that event -- so normally Solemnity would make this cost impossible to pay, and under [118.3] a player can't pay a cost without the ability to fulfill it, meaning the ability couldn't even be activated.

However, Aimee's Vizier of Remedies has a replacement effect: "If one or more -1/-1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many -1/-1 counters minus one are put on it instead." Barrenton Medic's cost would put exactly one -1/-1 counter on it, and Vizier of Remedies is a creature Aimee controls (Barrenton Medic is too), so the replacement effect applies to that event, changing it from "put 1 counter" to "put 1 minus 1 = 0 counters." Since only one modifying effect (Vizier of Remedies) actually changes the quantity of counters here, rule [616.1] about choosing among multiple replacement effects isn't even needed to resolve a conflict -- Vizier of Remedies simply reduces the event to zero counters before it happens. Putting zero counters is not "putting a counter" at all, so Solemnity's "counters can't be put on... creatures" restriction has nothing to stop -- no counter-placement event occurs for it to prevent.

Because the cost event (as modified) is legal to perform (putting zero counters), Aimee is able to pay the cost, satisfying rule [118.3], and the ability isn't prohibited from being activated under rule [602.5]. The cost is considered paid even though no actual -1/-1 counter ends up on Barrenton Medic, so Barrenton Medic untaps and never accumulates damage from -1/-1 counters, meaning Aimee could repeat this activation as often as she likes.

This is a two-player-neutral interaction (nothing about opponents or turn order is at issue), so the answer is the same whether there are two players or more at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Since Solemnity prevents counters from being put on creatures, Aimee can't activate Barrenton Medic's ability, as its cost cannot legally be paid. Vizier of Remedies's replacement effect won't apply as events that can't happen can only be replaced by self-replacement effects.

entries.question: Aislinn controls [Anointed Procession] and a [Skullmulcher]. They cast [Tempt with Reflections] targeting the Skullmulcher. Can Aislinn apply the devour replacement effect before the Anointed Procession replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Anointed Procession's creation-doubling replacement must be applied first, and each resulting Skullmulcher token's devour choice is applied separately (so one sacrifice can't serve both).
entries.answer:
No. The order is fixed: Anointed Procession's replacement effect on the token-creation event must be applied before Skullmulcher's devour replacement effect on the entering-the-battlefield event, because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating the token(s). Rule 616.1g explicitly works through this exact structure with Doubling Season and Voice of All tokens: "Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order." Anointed Procession works the same way as Doubling Season here — it doubles the number of Skullmulcher tokens Tempt with Reflections creates. Only after that doubling happens do the resulting Skullmulcher tokens actually enter the battlefield, and only then does each one's devour replacement effect (rule 614.12b: a devour choice, like any entering-the-battlefield replacement effect requiring a choice, is made before the permanent enters) get applied — separately, to each token. Since Anointed Procession is doubling the token, Aislinn will end up with two Skullmulcher tokens entering simultaneously (assuming one opponent also copies; if none do, it's still one token from Tempt with Reflections, doubled to two by Anointed Procession). Each of those two tokens has its own independent devour 1 replacement effect that triggers as that specific token enters. A single sacrificed creature can satisfy only one token's devour choice, not both — you cannot reuse the same sacrificed creature for two separate devour effects, since once sacrificed it's no longer on the battlefield to be chosen again. Additionally, the two Skullmulcher tokens can't devour each other, because Skullmulcher's own ruling states devour "can't devour creatures that enter the battlefield at the same time as it" (consistent with the general zone-change rule 614.13a, which bars choosing objects entering the battlefield at the same time as the permanent applying the effect). So to have both tokens enter with a +1/+1 counter, Aislinn would need two separate other creatures to sacrifice (one per token), not just one shared sacrifice — and in any case she cannot choose to apply devour "before" Anointed Procession's doubling, since the doubling effect governs the very act of creating the tokens that devour later applies to.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Skullmulcher: Skullmulcher's own effect and Anointed Procession's effect. Skullmulcher's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Anointed Procession's effect applies to it being created, so Anointed Procession's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Skullmulcher's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Skullmulchers entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

entries.question: Bailey controls [Pandemonium]. Anderson casts [Gray Ogre] and targets Bailey's [Jibbirik Omnivore] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Chelsea casts [Incinerate] targeting Anderson causing them to lose the game. Will Bailey's creature die?
entries.reason: Both conclude the Pandemonium trigger remains on the stack under Bailey’s control and will deal damage equal to Gray Ogre’s last-known power to Jibbirik, which is lethal.
entries.answer:
Yes — Bailey's Jibbirik Omnivore will die. Here's why, given that Bailey, Anderson, and Chelsea make this a three-player (multiplayer) game, so the leaves-the-game rules in 800.4 apply.

The stack, from bottom to top, is: the Pandemonium trigger (targeting Jibbirik Omnivore, dealing damage equal to Gray Ogre's power), then Chelsea's Incinerate (targeting Anderson). Incinerate resolves first and, as stated in the question, causes Anderson to lose the game.

When Anderson leaves the game, rule [800.4a] says all objects Anderson *owns* leave the game with them — that includes Gray Ogre, which Anderson both owns and controls. However, the Pandemonium triggered ability itself is controlled by Bailey, not Anderson, per [Pandemonium ruling #0] ('If player A controls Pandemonium when a creature enters under player B's control, player A controls the triggered ability even though player B chooses the target...'). Since Bailey hasn't left the game, that ability stays on the stack untouched, still targeting Jibbirik Omnivore (which Bailey still owns and controls, so the target remains legal).

When the Pandemonium trigger then resolves, Gray Ogre is no longer on the battlefield (it left the game along with Anderson). Per [Pandemonium ruling #1], 'The triggered ability does not check the creature's power until the ability resolves. If the creature is not on the battlefield when the ability resolves, it does damage equal to the power of the creature right before it left the battlefield.' Gray Ogre is a vanilla 2/2, so it deals 2 damage to Jibbirik Omnivore.

Jibbirik Omnivore is a 3/2 creature. Two damage marked on a creature with toughness 2 is lethal, so once state-based actions are next checked, Jibbirik Omnivore is destroyed.

Note on assumptions: I'm assuming the choice to have Gray Ogre deal damage and the choice of target (Jibbirik Omnivore) were already locked in when the trigger was put on the stack, as the question states Anderson 'targets Bailey's Jibbirik Omnivore with the Pandemonium trigger' before casting Incinerate. If instead that choice were somehow still pending at resolution, the outcome doesn't change here since the target and decision are already given as fixed facts in the question.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The triggered ability of Pandemonium includes a choice to be made upon resolution. However the player that is supposed to make that choice is no longer in the game, therefore the controller of the trigger chooses another player to make that choice. In this case Bailey will choose another player to decide whether Pandemonium's trigger will deal damage to Jibbirik Omnivore. Bailey is the controller of the trigger since they control the enchantment that generated the trigger, even though Anderson is the player making choices about the trigger.

entries.question: Alice controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the token is a 1/1 green Saproling creature land with subtypes Mountain and Saproling that only has the Mountain mana ability "{T}: Add {R}".
entries.answer:
Alice's token ends up as a green 1/1 creature and land with the subtypes Mountain and Saproling, and it only has the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (it loses the Forest-granted "{T}: Add {G}" ability).

Here's why. Life and Limb's static ability says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Because a Saproling token, once it exists, is a Saproling, this effect applies to it the instant it enters the battlefield — continuous effects generated by a static ability apply simultaneously with a permanent entering the battlefield, so the token is never on the battlefield with unmodified characteristics [611.3c]. This gives the token the card type land and the land subtype Forest "in addition to its other types," so it keeps its creature type and its Saproling subtype (per [205.1b] and [Life and Limb ruling #0], each subtype stays tied to its proper card type: Forest to land, Saproling to creature).

Blood Moon's static ability, "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," is also continuously active. Because the token's new land status doesn't carry the supertype "basic" (adding a land subtype/type this way doesn't grant the basic supertype — see [305.7], which states setting a land's subtype to a basic land type "doesn't add or remove any... supertypes"), the token counts as a nonbasic land and is caught by Blood Moon.

Both of these type-changing effects apply in layer 4, and effects within a layer are ordered by timestamp [613.7] (dependency doesn't change the order here, so 613.8 doesn't reorder anything). Life and Limb has an earlier timestamp (it resolved first), so its Forest-and-creature effect is applied first; Blood Moon's Mountain effect, with the later timestamp, is applied afterward. Per rule [305.7], when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land type(s), the abilities generated by its rules text and old land types (i.e., the Forest's "{T}: Add {G}"), and gains the new basic land type's mana ability — here, Mountain's "{T}: Add {R}" ([Blood Moon ruling #2]). This subtype-setting doesn't remove any card types or supertypes, and it only touches the land subtype, so the token's creature card type and its Saproling creature subtype are untouched.

The result: the token is a green (from Life and Limb, layer 5), 1/1 (layer 7b/c, unchanged since it was already 1/1) creature and land, with the subtypes Saproling and Mountain, and its only land-based mana ability is "{T}: Add {R}." (This all works the same whether the game has two players or more than two, since nothing here depends on player count.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 1/1 green Land Creature - Mountain Saproling with "{T}: Add {R}.". Applying Life and Limb's effect would allow Blood Moon's effect to apply to the Saproling and applying Blood Moon's effect first would not affect how Life and Limb's effect is applied or what it does, so Blood Moon's effect is dependent on Life and Limb's effect and waits to apply until afterwards. Since Life and Limb's effect makes the Saproling a nonbasic land, Blood Moon then applies and turns it into a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}." and no other abilities.

entries.question: Anson controls [Mana Reflection] and [Deathrite Shaman]. They activate Deathrite Shaman's first ability, exiling a [Watery Grave] from Nola's graveyard. How much mana is produced?
entries.reason: The candidate treats Deathrite Shaman's activated ability as a mana ability that Mana Reflection doubles to two mana, but the reference ruling states the ability is not a "tap for mana" mana ability and therefore only produces one mana.
entries.answer:
Anson gets 2 mana of a single color of their choice, not 2 mana of two different colors. Deathrite Shaman's first ability reads “{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color,” which is a mana ability because it includes {T} in its activation cost and produces mana. Mana Reflection's text states, "If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead," and this triggers here because Anson is tapping Deathrite Shaman as part of paying that ability's activation cost. Since the ability normally lets Anson choose one color and add one mana of that color, Mana Reflection causes it to instead produce two mana of that same chosen color -- Anson still only picks one color, and both mana produced are of that color, per Mana Reflection ruling #2, which explains that any restrictions the source ability places on its mana (here, that it's a single chosen color) apply to all the doubled mana. The fact that the exiled land card is Watery Grave is irrelevant to the amount or type of mana produced, since Deathrite Shaman's ability doesn't scale off the exiled card's own mana abilities -- it simply requires exiling *some* land card from a graveyard as a cost, and independently grants 'one mana of any color,' which Mana Reflection then doubles to two mana of that chosen color. If Anson controlled a second Mana Reflection, the mana would be quadrupled per Mana Reflection ruling #3, but with just one Mana Reflection in play the result is 2 mana of one color.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just 1. Deathrite Shaman's ability is not a mana ability, and activating it is not "tapping it for mana".

entries.question: Alfredo controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Knight Errant]s with magnet counters on them. Nico controls one [Soaring Drake] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nico's legal blocks?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Soaring Drake is required to block one of the Knight Errants (may choose which) but cannot block both, so the candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Nico's Soaring Drake must block, and it may block either Knight Errant #1 or Knight Errant #2 (Nico's choice) — but it cannot block both, and it cannot decline to block.

Here's why: Magnetic Web reads, "Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able." Both Knight Errant #1 and Knight Errant #2 have magnet counters and are attacking, so each one's attack triggers this ability separately. Each triggered instance creates a requirement that every creature with a magnet counter (here, just Soaring Drake, which also has a magnet counter) must block that specific attacker if able. That gives Soaring Drake two simultaneous requirements: 'block Knight Errant #1' and 'block Knight Errant #2.'

Under the normal blocking rules, a creature can only be assigned to block one attacking creature per declare-blockers step unless something gives it the ability to block multiple attackers — Soaring Drake has no such ability, just Flying, which only affects what can block it, not what it can block. So Soaring Drake is physically unable to satisfy both requirements at once. Rule [509.1c] handles this: the defending player must obey the maximum number of requirements possible without violating any restrictions. Since Soaring Drake can satisfy at most one of the two 'must block' requirements, blocking either Knight Errant satisfies the maximum possible (one requirement), and either choice is legal. If Nico instead had Soaring Drake block neither Knight Errant, that would satisfy zero requirements when one was achievable, making the block declaration illegal under [509.1c], which would send the game back to before blockers were declared per [733.1].

The actual mechanics of declaring the block are governed by [509.1a]: Nico chooses which creatures block and, for each, chooses one attacking creature it's blocking — so he picks Soaring Drake and assigns it to block only one of the two Knight Errants.

Assumption: I'm assuming this is a two-player game (Alfredo attacking, Nico defending) with no other complicating attackers or requirements beyond Magnetic Web's triggers. If Soaring Drake had an ability letting it block multiple creatures, it would be required to block both Knight Errants, satisfying both requirements at once — but no such ability is present here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nico can block either Knight Errant with their Magnetic Web. When declaring blockers, Nico must fulfill the maximum number of requirements, while not violating any restrictions.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alianna announced [Zirda, the Dawnwaker] as their companion. During the game, Alianna cast [Glistening Goremonger] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alianna restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: Karn's −14 restarts the game, both Glistening Goremonger (brought in by Wish) and Zirda end up shuffled into Alianna's library (unless specifically exiled by Karn), and Goremonger cannot be announced as the companion because it violates Zirda's deck restriction.
entries.answer:
The current game immediately ends (no one wins, loses, or draws it), and a new game begins for all players who were still in the game — this is what Karn Liberated's −14 ability does. Both the Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger card that Alianna brought in with Wish and the Zirda, the Dawnwaker card that Alianna is using as their companion end up back in Alianna's library for the new game, because neither of them is one of the specific cards Karn's ability exempts from the restart.

Here's why: rule [727.1] and [104.6] establish that Karn Liberated's −14 ends the old game and starts a brand-new one following the normal starting-the-game procedure in rule 103, with one exception — the exception in [727.5] and Karn's own text, which exempts only the non-Aura permanent cards that are actually still exiled by Karn's ability at the time it resolves; those specific cards skip the library and go straight onto the battlefield under Alianna's control instead ([Karn Liberated ruling #4]). Nothing in the question indicates Glistening Goremonger (the transformed back face of Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger) or Zirda, the Dawnwaker was ever exiled by Karn's −3 ability, so neither qualifies for that exemption.

Rule [727.2] states that every Magic card that was involved in the restarted game — regardless of what zone (or non-zone, in the case of a card sitting outside the game) it was in when the game ended — is involved in the new game, with ownership unchanged. The rule's own Living Wish example is exactly this situation: a card brought into the game from outside the game via a Wish-type effect simply becomes part of its owner's library when the new game begins. By that same logic, the Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger card (brought in via Wish) goes into Alianna's new library, wherever it was and whatever face it was showing when the old game ended.

Zirda, the Dawnwaker is a bit different in that it never entered the game at all — as Alianna's declared companion, it sat outside the game the whole time per [702.139d] and [Zirda, the Dawnwaker ruling #8]/[ruling #9]. But [727.2]'s language ('even if those cards were not originally involved in the restarted game') covers exactly this kind of card too, and since Zirda isn't exempted by Karn's ability, it also becomes part of Alianna's library as the new game's starting procedure begins.

Because the new game follows the full rule 103 procedure, Alianna goes through the pregame steps again, including setting aside any sideboard ([103.2a]) and the companion declaration step ([103.2b]). If Alianna's new starting deck (library) still satisfies Zirda's companion condition — every permanent card in it has an activated ability — Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker again as their companion for the new game; it's not automatic, it has to be redeclared. Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger, having no exemption, just stays in the shuffled library unless later played again.

One timing caveat: I'm assuming Glistening Goremonger was never targeted/exiled by Karn's −3 ability before the −14 was activated. If it had been, it would instead be one of the exempted permanent cards, skipping the library and being put onto the battlefield under Alianna's control at the start of the new game per Karn's own text and [727.5]/[727.1]'s exception.

Finally, note this answer holds regardless of player count for the core restart mechanics, but if this is a multiplayer game, only players still in the game when Karn's ability resolves are carried into the new game — anyone who had already left is not involved (per the Karn Liberated ruling on multiplayer, and consistent with [727.7] regarding range of influence not limiting who's involved).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Glistening Goremonger will be shuffled into Alianna's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Glistening Goremonger violates Zirda, the Dawnwaker's companion restriction, Alianna can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.

entries.question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that Lust for War cannot legally remain as an Aura under Mycosynth Lattice + March of the Machines and ends up in Amos's graveyard without ever providing a lasting enchantment.
entries.answer:
When Lust for War resolves, it will enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel as normal, but it will immediately be turned into a 3/3 artifact creature by the combination of Mycosynth Lattice and March of the Machines, which causes a state-based action to unattach it and then put it straight into Amos's graveyard — so Gilded Sentinel ends up unenchanted and Lust for War never actually has a lasting effect on it.

Step by step: Lust for War is an Aura enchantment (Enchant creature) that targets Gilded Sentinel, an artifact creature. Under normal circumstances it would resolve and enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel per its enchant ability [303.4m]. However, Amos also controls Mycosynth Lattice, whose static ability makes 'All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types,' and March of the Machines, whose static ability makes 'each noncreature artifact... an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value.' Because Lust for War itself is a permanent once it's on the battlefield, Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact, and March of the Machines then makes it into an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value (3, since Lust for War's mana value is 3) — i.e., a 3/3 Aura Artifact Creature — Enchantment. Per the general rule that continuous effects modifying a permanent's characteristics apply the moment it is on the battlefield [603.6b], Lust for War never exists on the battlefield as a non-creature Aura; it is already an artifact creature the instant it arrives, still attached to Gilded Sentinel at that moment.

This is exactly the situation covered by the Mycosynth Lattice ruling: combining Mycosynth Lattice with March of the Machines can make an Aura become a creature, and 'an Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything' [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0]. This matches the state-based action that a creature attached to an object or player becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield [704.5p]. So as soon as state-based actions are checked, Lust for War (now a 3/3 creature) is unattached from Gilded Sentinel but stays on the battlefield as an unattached permanent. Then, because it's an Aura that isn't attached to anything, a further state-based action immediately puts it into Amos's graveyard, as confirmed by the ruling [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0].

Net result: Gilded Sentinel is never actually enchanted by Lust for War in any lasting sense (its triggered ability and 'attacks each combat if able' clause never get a chance to matter), and Lust for War ends up in Amos's graveyard almost immediately after resolving.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Lust for War cannot legally enchant anything, so it will be put directly into its owners graveyard.

entries.question: Avery controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate says Angel becomes a 1/1 with no abilities, whereas the reference says it is a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities (the +3/+3 from Threshold persists), so they reach different final rulings.
entries.answer:
After Turn to Frog resolves, Wayward Angel becomes a blue Frog creature with base power and toughness 1/1 and has no abilities at all — no Flying, no Vigilance, no Trample, no "sacrifice a creature" trigger, and no Threshold ability, even though Avery still has seven or more cards in their graveyard.

Here's why. Wayward Angel's Threshold ability is a static ability that, while the graveyard condition is met, (1) sets Wayward Angel's color to black, (2) gives it +3/+3, and (3) grants it Trample and the upkeep sacrifice trigger. Per rule [113.12], "is black" is a characteristic-setting effect rather than a granted ability, but the +3/+3 boost and the Trample/sacrifice-trigger grants are genuine granted abilities/effects that only exist because the Threshold ability itself is present on Wayward Angel.

Turn to Frog says Wayward Angel "loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1" until end of turn. "Loses all abilities" strips away Flying, Vigilance, and the Threshold ability itself. Once the Threshold ability is gone, it can no longer generate its color-setting, +3/+3, Trample, or sacrifice-trigger effects.

The timing of this within the continuous-effects/layer system matters, and Turn to Frog's own ruling about the Theros Gods spells this out directly: a type- or color-changing effect generated by an ability is computed in an earlier layer than the removal of abilities, so it still "happens" before the ability disappears, but any effect (like a power/toughness boost) that's computed after the ability-removal layer no longer applies once that ability is gone [Turn to Frog ruling #5]. Concretely: Wayward Angel's Threshold-based black color is calculated before the ability-removal step, but Turn to Frog's own instruction to become blue is a newer effect and overwrites it anyway, so the color ends up blue either way. The +3/+3 bonus, however, is a power/toughness-modifying effect computed after abilities are removed, so once Threshold itself has been stripped by "loses all abilities," the +3/+3 no longer applies — Wayward Angel is left at the base power/toughness Turn to Frog sets, 1/1 [Turn to Frog ruling #1]. Trample and the sacrifice trigger are abilities granted by Threshold, so "loses all abilities" removes them along with Flying and Vigilance.

On the type line, Turn to Frog's wording ("becomes a blue Frog") does not say "in addition to its other types," unlike the examples in rule [205.1b] that preserve prior types with that phrasing. So Wayward Angel's prior subtypes (Angel, Horror) are replaced, and it becomes simply a Frog.

If Wayward Angel were to gain a new ability after Turn to Frog resolves, it would keep that new ability [Turn to Frog ruling #3], but that doesn't apply here since nothing else is granting it anything. This scenario doesn't involve more than two players in any way that changes the outcome; the reasoning is the same regardless of table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities. Wayward Angel's last ability begins to apply in layer 5. It's removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply, it will continue doing so in later layers. Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp, so it gives itself trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" before Turn to Frog removes its abilities in layer 6.

entries.question: Aubrey casts [Shahrazad]. As the subgame begins, Aubrey wins the die roll. Can Aubrey choose to play second?
entries.reason: The candidate contradicts the reference by saying the die-roll winner may choose who goes first in the subgame, whereas the correct ruling states the starting player is determined randomly and cannot be chosen.
entries.answer:
Yes. Winning the random determination for the Shahrazad subgame gives Aubrey the choice of who takes the first turn, not an automatic requirement that Aubrey goes first. Rule 729.2 says that as the subgame starts, the game "randomly determine[s] which player goes first," and Shahrazad ruling #3 clarifies what that means in practice: the random method (here, the die roll) determines which player *chooses* to go first or draw first, mirroring the normal procedure in rule 103.1 for starting a game (where the winner of the initial random method chooses who takes the first turn, and that choice need not be themselves). Since Aubrey won the die roll, Aubrey is the one empowered to make that choice, and Aubrey may choose to have the opponent take the first turn instead — effectively 'playing second' in the subgame. The subgame is otherwise run under all the normal rules in rule 103, "Starting the Game" (per rule 729.2), so nothing about being a subgame changes this option. This is a two-player-framed answer since Shahrazad's mechanics and the cited rules here are given in terms of two players; the context doesn't provide multiplayer-specific rules for subgame starting-player determination, so if more than two players were involved in the subgame the procedure might differ.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The starting player in a subgame is determined randomly.

entries.question: Ainsley's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same core ruling—that Ainsley chooses the order the cards are put into their graveyard—so it matches the reference.
entries.answer:
Ainsley (the caster and owner of the cards) gets to choose the order the cards go into their graveyard. When Morality Shift resolves, the entire library is moved into the graveyard as part of the exchange, which counts as multiple cards being put into the same graveyard at the same time. Under rule [404.3], if an effect puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order — and Morality Shift ruling #1 confirms exactly this: "You can choose the order of the cards being placed into the graveyard." So Ainsley decides the stacking order of what is now their graveyard.

By contrast, the old graveyard cards that move into the library as part of the same exchange, and then get shuffled per Morality Shift's own text ("Then shuffle your library"), end up in a fully randomized order — Ainsley does not get to choose or reveal that order, since shuffling randomizes the library regardless of what order the cards arrived in.

Note this ruling and rule 404.3 apply the same way regardless of how many players are in the game, since the choice is made solely by Ainsley as the owner/controller of their own graveyard and library; no other player is involved in ordering their own graveyard or library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In the order of Ainsley's choice.

entries.question: Autumn, Bethany, and Chaim started playing a multiplayer game. Chaim lost the game, and then Autumn restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Autumn draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
