entries.answer:
With the rules provided, this can't be fully settled — here's what we can determine and what's missing. First, because Chaim lost the game before Karn Liberated's ultimate resolved, he is no longer "in the game" and will not be involved in the restarted game — a player who leaves the game before it's restarted isn't included in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. That leaves only Autumn and Bethany in the restarted game. Autumn controlled the ability that restarted the game, so she is the starting player in the new game [727.1a, Karn Liberated ruling #2]. Each player then draws a seven-card opening hand as part of starting the new game [727.4, 103.5, Karn Liberated ruling #2], and may take mulligans as normal [103.5]. However, the question of whether Autumn specifically draws a card during her draw step *on the first turn* of the new game depends on the turn-structure rule about whether the starting player skips their first draw step, and whether that skip applies given that only two players remain. None of the rules given here address the draw step or any first-turn draw skip for the starting player, so I can't confirm or rule out whether Autumn draws during her draw step on turn one. What's missing is the rule governing the starting player's first draw step (and whether it differs between two-player and multiplayer games).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The game began with 2 players, so it is a two-player game.. Autumn will skip their draw step.

entries.question: Addison casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Natalee's [Memnite]. In response, Natalee casts [Resounding Roar] on the Memnite. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Resounding Roar's bonus expires, the permanent -1/-1 counter kills Memnite in cleanup, and Virulent Wound's delayed trigger grants Natalee a poison counter.
entries.answer:
At the end of the turn, Natalee's Memnite dies (from the -1/-1 counter reasserting itself once Resounding Roar's boost wears off), and Natalee gets a poison counter. Here's the sequence: Addison casts Virulent Wound targeting Memnite; in response Natalee casts Resounding Roar, also targeting Memnite. Because a spell cast in response resolves before the spell it was cast in response to (rule 117.7), Resounding Roar resolves first, giving Memnite +3/+3 until end of turn (it becomes a 4/4). Virulent Wound then resolves; Memnite is still a legal target, so under rule 608.2b it checks target legality, finds Memnite still legal, and resolves normally, putting a -1/-1 counter on it. Memnite is now a 3/3 (base 1/1, +3/+3 from Resounding Roar, -1/-1 from the counter) and does not die immediately. Virulent Wound's delayed ability ('When that creature dies this turn, its controller gets a poison counter') is now waiting to see if Memnite dies before the turn ends. At the cleanup step, Resounding Roar's 'until end of turn' bonus expires, but the -1/-1 counter is a permanent modification and does not go away. Memnite's stats revert to its base 1/1 with the -1/-1 counter still applied, making it a 0/0, and it is put into the graveyard as a state-based action. Because this death happens during the cleanup step of the very turn Virulent Wound resolved, it counts as dying 'this turn' for Virulent Wound's delayed trigger. The Virulent Wound ruling confirms the flip side of this: a controller only fails to get a poison counter if the creature is NOT put into a graveyard on the turn Virulent Wound resolved — here it is, so Natalee (Memnite's controller) gets a poison counter. This analysis assumes no other effects intervene between Virulent Wound's resolution and cleanup; if some other effect had removed the -1/-1 counter or otherwise pumped Memnite's toughness permanently before cleanup, Memnite would survive and no poison counter would be granted. This scenario involves only two players' spells, so nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Resounding Roar wears off, but the -1/-1 counter remains. Memnite dies. The delayed triggered ability created by Virulent Wound is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step, and will trigger due to Memnite dying. Natalee gets a poison counter.

entries.question: Amaris, Blaine, and Clyde begin a multiplayer game. In Amaris's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Blaine. Does Amaris draw a card for the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Amaris still draws during their draw step after killing Blaine in upkeep, noting the multiplayer rules don't prevent the active player's draw (aside from the separate first-turn exception).
entries.answer:
Yes. Killing Blaine during Amaris's upkeep doesn't stop Amaris from drawing for the turn — Amaris still draws a card during their own draw step as normal.

When a player loses the game, that player leaves the game (rule [104.5]), and the multiplayer rules govern what happens next (rule [800.4]). But those special-case provisions (like [800.4j], which lets the turn continue without an active player) only matter if the player who left was the *active* player — i.e., if it were Blaine's own turn. Here the kill happens during Amaris's upkeep, and Amaris is the active player the whole time, so Amaris's turn simply proceeds normally: upkeep ends, then the draw step begins and Amaris draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack ([504.1], [703.4d]).

The only thing that would stop Amaris from drawing is the special first-turn rule: if this is the very first turn of the game and Amaris is the starting player, the starting player skips the draw step of their first turn ([103.8c]) — that rule applies in both two-player and multiplayer games, but only in a multiplayer game does 'no player skips the draw step' apply to everyone *except* the starting player's first turn. If this isn't Amaris's first turn as the game's starting player, that exception doesn't apply, and Amaris draws normally. Blaine leaving the game doesn't remove or alter this rule.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The game began with more than 2 players, so it is a multiplayer game, regardless of the current number of players remaining.. Amaris will draw a card during their draw step.

entries.question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
entries.reason: The candidate says the Cauldron will add {C}{C}{C} (including Suppression Field's extra {2}), but the reference says only {C} (just the {X} portion) is noted and later added.
entries.answer:
Allyson adds {C}{C}{C} (three colorless mana), usable only to cast the last card Ice Cauldron exiled. Here's why: Ice Cauldron's second ability - "{T}, Remove a charge counter from this artifact: Add this artifact's last noted type and amount of mana" - is a mana ability, since it's an activated ability whose effect is to add mana and it doesn't target and isn't a loyalty ability [605.1]. Suppression Field's tax ("Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities") explicitly exempts mana abilities, and its own ruling confirms it 'doesn't affect static abilities, triggered abilities, or mana abilities' [Suppression Field ruling #1]. So the second ability costs only {T} plus removing a charge counter - no extra {2}.

The first ability, by contrast, is NOT a mana ability (it lets Allyson exile and later cast a card, it doesn't add mana), so Suppression Field's +{2} did apply to it when Allyson activated it. With X=1, the base activation cost was {1}, {T}; Suppression Field increased that to {1}{2}, {T} = {3} generic plus tapping, per how cost increases are folded into the total cost before it's locked in [601.2f]. Allyson paid that {3} generic requirement entirely with colorless mana, {C}{C}{C}.

Ice Cauldron's own text says its controller must 'note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost' - and per Ice Cauldron's ruling, the Cauldron only cares about what was actually spent, not the value of X and not whatever cost-modifying effects were in play: 'if you spent {C}{C}{R}{R} on X, you get {C}{C}{R}{R} later even if X was 6' [Ice Cauldron ruling #0]. So the noted type and amount here is {C}{C}{C}, exactly what Allyson spent, regardless of the fact that Suppression Field inflated the cost beyond the literal X value.

When Allyson later activates the second ability, it adds that noted {C}{C}{C} to their mana pool, restricted so it can be spent only to cast the specific card most recently exiled by Ice Cauldron [Ice Cauldron ruling #2]. If there had been multiple cards exiled since, only the most recently exiled one could be paid for with this mana.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.

entries.question: Anya activates [Deceptive Landscape]. Before that resolves Nico casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Anya is resolving Deceptive Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Aven Mindcensor's replacement still counts as "searching your library," so Panglacial Wurm can be cast from the library during the restricted search.
entries.answer:
Yes. Anya can cast Panglacial Wurm from their library during this search, even though Aven Mindcensor has changed the search to look at only the top four cards.

Reasoning: Anya activated Deceptive Landscape's ability, whose second mode reads "Search your library for a basic Plains, Swamp, or Forest card, put it onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle." Because Nico controls Aven Mindcensor and Anya is Nico's opponent, Aven Mindcensor's replacement effect applies: "If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead." Under rule 701.23f, when a search of a whole zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to "searching the zone" still apply — the game still treats Anya as "searching her library," just restricted to the top four cards. Panglacial Wurm's ability, "While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library," is exactly such an instruction that keys off "searching your library," so it remains active during this restricted search.

So while Deceptive Landscape's ability is resolving and Anya is looking through those top four cards, she may cast Panglacial Wurm from her library as a special action taken during resolution (per 608.2g, an effect that instructs a search allows casting Panglacial Wurm this way; the Wurm goes on the stack above Deceptive Landscape's ability, and Deceptive Landscape's ability then continues resolving). Per Panglacial Wurm ruling #5, she must cast it before she "finds" any card with the search effect — that is, before she actually selects the basic Plains/Swamp/Forest she's fetching, not merely before revealing the top four cards. Per ruling #4, the Panglacial Wurm she casts this way cannot itself be the card found by Deceptive Landscape's search (it isn't a basic land anyway, so that's moot here). Per ruling #1, casting the Wurm this way follows all the normal rules for casting a creature spell (including paying its full {5}{G}{G} cost) except for the unusual timing and the fact that it's cast from the library instead of the hand.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Anya has not yet chosen/found her basic land when she notices Panglacial Wurm among the top four cards — if she had already completed the search (selected the land) before considering casting the Wurm, ruling #5 says it would be too late to cast it that way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Aven Mindcensor's ability is a replacement effect that replaces searching a library with searching only the top four cards of that library. However for the purposes of Panglacial Wurm's effect, it still qualifies as "searching a library".

entries.question: Aimee controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Noah casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
entries.reason: The candidate says Wayward Angel retains/gains flying, vigilance, and its Threshold ability (keeping all printed abilities), while the reference concludes Turn to Frog strips those printed abilities so it ends up only as a 4/4 black Frog with trample and the upkeep-sacrifice ability.
entries.answer:
Right after Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up, Wayward Angel is a 4/4 black Frog creature (no other creature types) named Wayward Angel, with flying, vigilance, trample, "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature," and its own Threshold ability — all still affected by Turn to Frog's until-end-of-turn duration.

Here's why. While manifested, Wayward Angel was face down, so by rule [708.2a] it had no characteristics other than the default manifest ones: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, abilities, or mana cost. Its Threshold ability did not exist in that state, so it had no effect even though Aimee's graveyard had 7+ cards.

When Noah's Turn to Frog resolved targeting the face-down Wayward Angel, it applied its continuous effect (loses all abilities; becomes a blue Frog; base power/toughness 1/1) to that 2/2 face-down object. Since it already had no abilities, the ability-loss did nothing extra at that moment, but the type (Frog), color (blue), and base P/T (1/1) changes locked in with an early timestamp.

When Aimee then turns Wayward Angel face up, rule [708.8] says its copiable values revert to the printed Wayward Angel values (name, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, type Creature — Angel Horror, P/T 4/4, flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability), while "any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent" — meaning Turn to Frog's effect keeps going. Because Aimee's graveyard still has 7+ cards, Wayward Angel's own Threshold ability becomes active again, granting +3/+3, black color, trample, and the sacrifice-trigger ability [Wayward Angel ruling #0].

Layer by layer: (1) Type/layer 4 — Turn to Frog's "becomes a...Frog" effect is still the only type-setting effect in play, so Wayward Angel is still just a Frog, not an Angel Horror, until end of turn. (2) Color/layer 5 — Turn to Frog set it blue with an earlier timestamp; Threshold's "is black" is regained only once Wayward Angel turns face up, which happens later, so under normal timestamp ordering the later black effect wins, matching how Turn to Frog's own ruling treats things gained after it resolves [Turn to Frog ruling #3]: newly gained abilities/effects that arise after Turn to Frog resolves stick. (3) Abilities/layer 6 — Turn to Frog's "loses all abilities" only stripped what existed at the time it resolved (nothing, since it was face down); flying, vigilance, the Threshold ability, trample, and the sacrifice trigger are all gained afterward (at the moment of turning face up) and are explicitly kept per [Turn to Frog ruling #3]. (4) Power/toughness/layer 7 — Turn to Frog sets base P/T to 1/1 in sublayer 7b; Threshold's "+3/+3" is a modifying (not setting) effect in sublayer 7c, which is always applied after 7b regardless of timestamp [Turn to Frog ruling #1] [613.1], giving a final 4/4.

So until end of turn, Wayward Angel is a 4/4 black Frog with flying, vigilance, trample, "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature," and its Threshold ability (still checking the graveyard count). When Turn to Frog's effect ends at cleanup, if Aimee still has 7+ cards in the graveyard, Wayward Angel will revert to being a 7/7 black Angel Horror with flying, vigilance, trample, and the sacrifice trigger (base 4/4 +3/+3, per its own printed text).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

entries.question: Bobbie has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Angel of Sanctions] that exiled Conrad's [Rotted Hystrix]. Alana casts [Lava Axe], targeting Bobbie. What happens as Bobbie loses the game?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says Rotted Hystrix returns when Bobbie leaves, but the correct ruling is that a phased-out Angel is treated as nonexistent so no leaves-the-battlefield event occurs and the exiled card does not return.
entries.answer:
When Bobbie loses the game and leaves it, Angel of Sanctions also leaves the game with them, and that satisfies the "until this creature leaves the battlefield" duration on its exile effect — so Rotted Hystrix immediately returns to the battlefield under Conrad's control, even though Angel of Sanctions was phased out at the time.

Step by step: This is a multiplayer game (Bobbie, Conrad, and Alana are all named), so when Bobbie loses, Bobbie leaves the game rather than the whole game ending [800.4]. By rule [800.4a], when a player leaves the game, all objects that player owns leave the game as well. Rule [901.10] confirms this happens immediately, not as a state-based action. Because Angel of Sanctions is phased out but still owned by Bobbie, rule [702.26k] specifically says phased-out permanents owned by a leaving player also leave the game (and this does not cause any zone-change triggers to fire).

Angel of Sanctions's own text exiles a nonland permanent "until this creature leaves the battlefield." That's a one-shot, non-stack duration effect, not a triggered ability — Angel of Sanctions ruling #3 confirms the exiled card returns immediately after Angel of Sanctions leaves the battlefield, with nothing happening in between (not even state-based actions). Angel of Sanctions ruling #4 directly addresses this exact scenario: if Angel of Sanctions's owner leaves the game, the exiled card still returns to the battlefield, because the returning effect isn't an ability on the stack and so isn't wiped out along with the leaving player's stack objects under rule [800.4a]. So even though Bobbie (the owner) is leaving the game and taking Angel of Sanctions with them, Rotted Hystrix still pops back onto the battlefield under Conrad's control (its owner) right as Angel of Sanctions leaves the game.

Meanwhile, Alana's Lava Axe has already resolved and finishes doing its job (dealing the 5 damage that put Bobbie's life at -4); Lava Axe itself doesn't care what happens to Bobbie afterward. The game then continues between Conrad and Alana under rule [800.4], since multiplayer games can continue after a player leaves.

One timing note: I'm assuming Bobbie's loss (and thus leaving the game) is processed as a state-based action after Lava Axe fully resolves, which is the normal sequencing — if instead something checked life totals mid-resolution that wouldn't change the outcome here, since Lava Axe has only one effect (5 damage) and nothing else depends on Bobbie's life total before the spell finishes resolving.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All objects owned by Bobbie leave the game. However the game treats phased-out permanents as nonexistent, and does not see the leaves-the-battlefield event happen. Rotted Hystrix will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Natalia controls [Watchwolf] enchanted with [Favorable Destiny]. Aubrey casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Favorable Destiny. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aubrey gains control of Favorable Destiny and it remains attached to Watchwolf (still a legal attachment) rather than falling off.
entries.answer:
When Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability resolves, Aubrey gains control of Favorable Destiny (which is now a legal target because Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact in addition to its other types, so the Aura counts as "an artifact an opponent controls"). Favorable Destiny stays physically attached to Watchwolf — it doesn't move, get bounced, or go to the graveyard — but for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield, Favorable Destiny loses all of its abilities. That means it no longer grants Watchwolf +1/+2 (which only applied "as long as it's white" anyway) and no longer gives Watchwolf shroud. Natalia still controls Watchwolf itself; only the Aura's control changes hands, not the creature's. The "can't attack or block" clause of Opportunistic Dragon's ability is irrelevant here since Favorable Destiny is not a creature (Mycosynth Lattice only makes it an artifact, not a creature), so that restriction does nothing.

Why the Aura doesn't fall off: An Aura is only put into its owner's graveyard by the state-based action in [704.5m]/[303.4c] if it is attached to an illegal object as defined by its enchant ability, or is unattached, or the enchanted permanent no longer exists. Favorable Destiny's enchant ability just says "Enchant creature" — it never required that the Aura's controller and the creature's controller match — so Watchwolf remains a perfectly legal thing for it to enchant even after Aubrey takes control of the Aura. Losing all its abilities (per Opportunistic Dragon's effect) doesn't create an illegal-attachment situation either, since there's no enchant restriction left to violate. So Favorable Destiny simply sits on the battlefield, attached to Watchwolf, controlled by Aubrey, doing nothing, for as long as Opportunistic Dragon survives (per [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #1], the effect only ends if Opportunistic Dragon itself leaves the battlefield, not merely if it changes controller or loses abilities).

If Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield later, its effect ends: Favorable Destiny would return to Natalia's control (it was never a separate control-change event distinct from the Dragon's ongoing effect) and regain its abilities, once again granting +1/+2 and conditional shroud to Watchwolf.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Favorable Destiny will continue to be attached to Watchwolf indefinitely. The "enchant" keyword is a restriction on what an Aura can enchant- without it Favorable Destiny is legally able to enchant anything.

entries.question: Alaia controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Minotaur Warrior] and [Ogre Resister] in their graveyard. They cast [Dance of the Dead] targeting Minotaur Warrior. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Dance of the Dead enters attached and its ETB trigger is doubled (via Panharmonicon + Mycosynth Lattice), returning Minotaur Warrior once and leaving the second trigger with no effect.
entries.answer:
Dance of the Dead's own "When this Aura enters" trigger fires twice, but only one Minotaur Warrior actually comes back to the battlefield — the second instance of the trigger does nothing.

Here's why. Dance of the Dead's printed text says: "When this Aura enters, if it's on the battlefield, it loses 'enchant creature card in a graveyard' and gains 'enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura.' Put enchanted creature card onto the battlefield tapped under your control and attach this Aura to it" [Dance of the Dead ruling #0]. This is a triggered ability that fires when the Aura itself enters the battlefield [614.1c].

Normally Panharmonicon only doubles triggers caused by an *artifact or creature* entering. Dance of the Dead is only an Enchantment — Aura by its own types, so on its own it wouldn't qualify. But Alaia also controls Mycosynth Lattice, whose text says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types." Because that continuous effect is already active, when you check Dance of the Dead's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield (per 614.12, which says to account for continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent), Dance of the Dead is entering as an artifact (and an enchantment). Panharmonicon's ability ("If an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time") explicitly covers a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield triggers, including its own entrance [Panharmonicon ruling #0]. So Dance of the Dead entering as an artifact causes its own "When this Aura enters" ability to trigger an additional time — it triggers twice total, as two separate instances of the same ability (the same pattern by which other doubled triggers, e.g. multiple instances of afterlife or myriad, are treated as separate triggering instances [702.135b][702.116b]).

Both instances trigger at the same moment, referencing the same enchanted creature card — Minotaur Warrior, sitting in the graveyard when Dance of the Dead entered. When the first instance resolves, it changes Dance of the Dead's enchant restriction and puts Minotaur Warrior onto the battlefield tapped under Alaia's control, attaching Dance of the Dead to it. That card, upon moving zones, becomes a brand-new object with no memory of its previous existence as a graveyard card [400.7]. When the second instance of the trigger then resolves, its instruction is still to "put enchanted creature card onto the battlefield" referring to that same original graveyard card object — but that object no longer exists in the graveyard (it already became the new permanent). There is nothing left in the graveyard for this second instance to move, so it has no legal object to act on and simply does nothing; it doesn't create a second Minotaur Warrior or duplicate the permanent.

Net result: Minotaur Warrior enters the battlefield exactly once, tapped, under Alaia's control, with Dance of the Dead attached (now bearing its 'enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura' text), and Ogre Resister is untouched since Dance of the Dead never targeted it.

This is purely a single-player sequence of triggers under Alaia's control, so nothing here differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer game — there's no APNAP ordering needed since no other player has choices to make in this interaction.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Dance of the Dead enters the battlefield attached to Minotaur Warrior and triggers twice. The first trigger will return Minotaur Warrior to the battlefield. The second trigger just does the same things again, so it has no relevant result.

entries.question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Hallow will not prevent the creature's later damage, which directly contradicts the reference ruling that the prevention effect on the spell continues to apply to the damage dealt by the permanent it becomes.
entries.answer:
No. Nico's Hallow will not prevent combat damage dealt later when Keldon Champion attacks. Hallow reads "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn," and it can only target an object that is currently a spell — here, the Keldon Champion creature spell on the stack (rule 117.7 confirms Hallow, cast in response, resolves first). But under rule 400.7a, when the Keldon Champion spell resolves it becomes a new object (the Keldon Champion permanent) with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence as a spell. The only exceptions to that rule are effects that change the characteristics or controller of the permanent (rule 400.7a, rule 112.4) — a damage-prevention effect is neither of those, so it does not carry over to the permanent. Once Keldon Champion is a permanent, any damage it deals (its 'enters the battlefield' triggered ability dealing 3 damage, or its combat damage when it attacks) is dealt by that permanent/its ability, not by 'the spell' Hallow targeted. In fact, a creature spell itself never deals damage as it resolves — it just enters the battlefield — so Hallow's prevention effect ends up with nothing to prevent from the spell, and it has no bearing on the creature's later combat damage. So when Keldon Champion attacks, its combat damage goes through normally and is not prevented by Hallow. (This same reasoning also means the 3 damage from Keldon Champion's enters-the-battlefield trigger is not prevented by Hallow, for the same reason — that damage is dealt by a triggered ability of the permanent, not by 'the spell.')

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Effects that apply to damage from a spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.

entries.question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
entries.reason: The candidate forbids using suspend during Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability, which contradicts the reference ruling that suspend is a special action available while that trigger resolves and thus can be taken then.
entries.answer:
No. Suspending Shivan Meteor is a special action, not casting a spell, so it can't satisfy Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability, which only lets Amelia cast an instant or sorcery spell from her hand without paying its mana cost. Under rule [116.2f], exiling a card using suspend is a special action available any time a player has priority (and only if they could begin to cast it) — it explicitly does not use the stack and is not the act of casting. Rule [702.62a] confirms suspend's first ability lets you 'exile it' rather than cast it. Shivan Meteor's own ruling reinforces this: 'Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting that card. This action doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to' (Shivan Meteor ruling #3). Wildfire Eternal's second ability specifically grants permission to *cast* a spell for free as the trigger resolves — per Wildfire Eternal ruling #1, 'you must cast a spell at that time if you wish to cast one without paying its mana cost.' Since suspending Shivan Meteor is not casting it, choosing to suspend it does not fulfill that ability. Additionally, rule [601.2b] states a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell — Wildfire Eternal's 'cast without paying its mana cost' is itself a cost-substitution, and it can't be combined with Shivan Meteor's Suspend 2—{1}{R}{R} alternative cost even if suspend did involve casting (which it doesn't). So as Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves, Amelia's only options are to cast Shivan Meteor outright for free (dealing 13 damage to a target creature) or decline to cast anything; she cannot use this trigger to suspend it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Shivan Meteor could be cast from Amelia's hand. Normally that's only when Amelia has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)

entries.question: Andrew attacks with [Raiyuu, Storm's Edge], then attacks with it again. Can they activate [Minas Tirith]'s last ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude you cannot activate Minas Tirith because Raiyuu is only one creature even if it attacked in two combat phases, so Minas Tirith's "two or more creatures attacked" condition isn't met.
entries.answer:
No. Minas Tirith's last ability requires that Andrew "attacked with two or more creatures this turn," and in this scenario only one creature — Raiyuu, Storm's Edge — was ever declared as an attacker, even though it attacked twice (once in each of two combat phases). The ability counts distinct attacking creatures, not the number of times attacks were declared, so a single creature attacking in two separate combat phases still only counts as one creature having attacked.

Here's the reasoning: Raiyuu, Storm's Edge's triggered ability reads "Whenever a Samurai or Warrior you control attacks alone, untap it. If it's the first combat phase of the turn, there is an additional combat phase after this phase" (per its printed text, which overrides nothing here but simply grants the extra combat phase). Because Raiyuu, Storm's Edge attacked alone in the first combat phase, it got untapped and an additional combat phase was created; Andrew then attacked with it again (alone) in that second combat phase. Under rule [508.6], a player "has attacked [a player]" if they declared one or more creatures as attackers — this defines whether attacking happened, but the relevant count for Minas Tirith is how many distinct creatures were declared as attackers, and that number is one (Raiyuu, Storm's Edge), used twice. Declaring attackers is a turn-based action governed by rule [508.1], and each declaration in each combat phase only involved the single creature Raiyuu, Storm's Edge. Since Minas Tirith's ability needs two or more creatures, not two or more attack declarations by the same creature, Andrew cannot activate Minas Tirith's card-draw ability this turn unless a different, second creature also attacks (in either combat phase).

Note: this assumes Raiyuu, Storm's Edge was the only creature attacking in both combat phases, as the question states. If any other creature also attacked in either combat phase, then two or more distinct creatures would have attacked this turn, and Minas Tirith's ability could be activated.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Raiyuu, Storm's Edge is only one creature, regardless of how many times it attacked.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Soul Seizer] (back face [Ghastly Haunting])which has been mutated with [Everquill Phoenix]. Everquill Phoenix is the top component. Naomi controls [Axegrinder Giant]. Ariel then attacks Naomi with the merged permanent. Naomi declared no blockers and the merged permanent deals damage to Naomi. What happens when the transformation trigger resolves if Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent and targets Axegrinder Giant?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly says the merged permanent can attach and gain control of Axegrinder Giant, whereas the correct ruling is the transformed component gains the back-face abilities but the merged permanent remains a creature and cannot attach as an Aura, so it does not become attached or gain control.
entries.answer:
When Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent (Soul Seizer/Ghastly Haunting merged with Everquill Phoenix) and targets Axegrinder Giant, the result is: Soul Seizer's component turns face up as Ghastly Haunting, Everquill Phoenix stays as it is, and the whole merged permanent becomes attached to Axegrinder Giant while remaining a creature (not an Enchantment) — and because the Ghastly Haunting ability is now part of the merged permanent, Ariel gains control of Axegrinder Giant.

Here's why. A mutated permanent (the Everquill Phoenix / Soul Seizer merge) is a single permanent represented by more than one card, with 'all abilities of each card and token that represents it,' but its other characteristics (power, toughness, card types, etc.) are derived only from the topmost card — here, Everquill Phoenix [702.140e]. Soul Seizer's triggered ability ('When this creature deals combat damage to a player, you may transform it. If you do, attach it to target creature that player controls') is one of the abilities the merged permanent has, since it comes from the Soul Seizer/Ghastly Haunting component. You chose the target (Axegrinder Giant) when the ability triggered, and you choose whether to transform when the ability resolves [Soul Seizer // Ghastly Haunting ruling #0].

Because Soul Seizer is a double-faced card and is a component of this merged permanent, transforming the merged permanent causes that component to turn so its Ghastly Haunting face is up; Everquill Phoenix, not being double-faced, is unaffected and can't itself transform [730.2i, 712.9]. Transforming is not the same action as an object leaving the battlefield or becoming a new object — the merged permanent doesn't leave the battlefield, and any ongoing effects on it (e.g., it's still attacking, still has any counters, etc.) continue to apply [712.18, 701.27g, 701.27b].

However, since the merged permanent's 'other characteristics' still come from the topmost card, Everquill Phoenix, the merged permanent remains a 4/4 flying Creature — Phoenix; it does NOT become an Enchantment — Aura just because its Ghastly Haunting face turned up [702.140e]. What does carry over is the ability text: the merged permanent now has Ghastly Haunting's ability, 'You control enchanted creature,' as one of the abilities granted by that component [702.140e], and the resolving trigger instructs you to attach it to Axegrinder Giant. So the merged permanent becomes attached to Axegrinder Giant (functioning like an Aura for attachment purposes even though it's still a creature by type), and because it's now 'enchanting' Axegrinder Giant, its 'You control enchanted creature' ability gives Ariel control of Axegrinder Giant.

Note: this is a two-player scenario as described (Ariel attacking Naomi); nothing here depends on multiplayer-specific rules, but with more than two players the same mechanics for merging, transforming, and control-changing would apply per player interactions, only the choice of defending player/opponents would differ, which isn't at issue here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
The component that consists of Soul Seizer is transformed. The merged permanent is still a creature. It is not attached to anything. The merged permanent has the abilities in the text box of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half.

When Ariel chooses to transform the merged permanent, all double-faced components are transformed. The merged permanent now has the abilities of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half. ([702.140e]) The merged permanent is still a creature as Everquill Phoenix is still the topmost card. When the transformation trigger tries to attach the merged permanent to Axegrinder Giant, it can't attach because the merged permanent is still a creature. It remains on the battlefield because the state-based action that puts auras not attached to anything into the graveyard is looking for the "Aura" subtype, not the "Enchant" keyword.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Phyrexian Marauder] in their graveyard. Can Ainsley activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Phyrexian Marauder? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Ainsley may activate the ability and only pay {0}, so the token enters with no +1/+1 counters.
entries.answer:
Yes, Ainsley can activate Back from the Brink's ability targeting Phyrexian Marauder in the graveyard, but they cannot pay more than {0} for its mana cost, and the resulting token will enter with zero +1/+1 counters.

Back from the Brink's activated ability reads: "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost: Create a token that's a copy of that card. Activate only as a sorcery." Since Ainsley controls Back from the Brink and has Phyrexian Marauder in their graveyard, they may exile Phyrexian Marauder and pay its mana cost as the cost of this activated ability (only as a sorcery, i.e., during a main phase with an empty stack and priority).

Phyrexian Marauder's mana cost is just {X} — a variable, generic-mana cost. The catch is that announcing a value for X normally happens as part of *casting* a spell, specifically during the casting process described in rule [601.2b] ("If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it's being cast... the player announces the value of that variable"). Activating Back from the Brink's ability and paying Phyrexian Marauder's mana cost as a cost of that activation is not casting Phyrexian Marauder — rule [601.1] confirms "casting" is specifically the process of taking a card from a zone (usually hand) and putting it on the stack while paying its costs, and rule [601.2f] frames "total cost" determination as part of that same casting process. Phyrexian Marauder is never put on the stack here and is never cast, so there is no step in which Ainsley announces a value for X.

Because there is no announcement step available to Ainsley for X in this context, Ainsley cannot choose to pay any amount for the {X} portion — they cannot pay more than {0}. (Note: the provided rules excerpts don't include the specific general rule that formally sets an unannounced X to a default value of 0 off the stack; that conclusion here is drawn from the fact that rule [601.2b]'s X-announcement step simply doesn't apply to this non-casting cost payment, so no positive value for X can ever be chosen.)

Since X is not chosen to be anything greater than 0, Phyrexian Marauder's own text — "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" — means the token copy created by Back from the Brink's ability enters the battlefield with zero +1/+1 counters.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Ainsley may activate the ability of Phyrexian Marauder paying {0}. He does not have the ability to pay more than {0}. The token will not enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters.

entries.question: Nadia has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Ashley controls a [Peacewalker Colossus] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts a [Clever Impersonator], choosing to have it copy Peacewalker Colossus. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate says the Impersonator enters under Ashley's control (so Gather Specimens doesn't apply), while the reference says Nadia gains control as it enters and gets to choose what it copies.
entries.answer:
Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield under Ashley's control as a copy of Peacewalker Colossus — an Artifact — Vehicle, 6/6, with "Crew 4" and "{1}{W}: Another target Vehicle you control becomes an artifact creature until end of turn." It does NOT enter as a creature, so Nadia's Gather Specimens never applies, and there is no control-swap.

Here's why: Peacewalker Colossus's printed type line is Artifact — Vehicle, not Artifact Creature — Vehicle. The fact that Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus is *currently* a creature is because of a temporary, non-copy effect (its own {1}{W} ability making it a creature until end of turn, or crewing). Clever Impersonator ruling #2 explicitly states that Clever Impersonator "copies exactly what is printed on the chosen permanent... it doesn't copy any non-copy effects that have changed that permanent's power, toughness, types, color, abilities, or so on." This matches rule [707.2], which says a copy uses the copiable values derived from the printed text, and that "other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects)... are not copied."

Under rule [707.5], an object that enters the battlefield as a copy of another object becomes that copy as it enters — it doesn't enter first and then transform. So as Clever Impersonator enters, it is already an Artifact — Vehicle, 6/6, not a creature (the crew/activated 'becomes a creature' effect on Ashley's Peacewalker Colossus is a separate, non-copied effect that doesn't carry over per rule [707.3] and the ruling above).

Nadia's Gather Specimens reads, "If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponent's control this turn, it enters under your control instead." Because Clever Impersonator is entering as a noncreature Vehicle (not a creature), the trigger condition "a creature would enter" is never met, so Gather Specimens simply does nothing here — Ashley keeps Clever Impersonator, which is a 6/6 Artifact — Vehicle named Peacewalker Colossus that isn't currently a creature (it could later become one via its own {1}{W} ability targeting another Vehicle it doesn't have, or by being crewed, since it retains the Crew 4 ability as part of its copied text).

This analysis assumes a standard two-player game between Nadia and Ashley; the outcome (no creature enters, so Gather Specimens is irrelevant) would be the same at a multiplayer table too, since the trigger condition for Gather Specimens still requires an actual creature to be entering.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. As Clever Impersonator begins to resolve, Nadia gains control of it before any other choices are made. Nadia will make the choice of what to copy as it enters the battlefield.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Gaea's Liege], [Rhonas the Indomitable], and 1 [Forest]. Noel controls 5 Forest. Can Aubrey attack with the Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes both creatures can attack, contradicting the reference which states restrictions are checked before creatures become attacking so Rhonas' requirement would not be met.
entries.answer:
Yes. Aubrey can declare both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable as attackers this combat, because once Gaea's Liege is declared an attacker its power/toughness immediately becomes 5/5 (equal to the number of Forests Noel, the defending player, controls), which satisfies Rhonas the Indomitable's attack restriction.

Here's the sequencing: under [508.1a], the active player (Aubrey) first chooses which creatures will attack – she can choose both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable, since both are untapped and have been under her control since the turn began. The act of being declared an attacker is what makes a creature 'attacking' (tapping is merely a consequence of that declaration, per [508.1f], not a prerequisite for the 'attacking' state). Gaea's Liege's own text overrides the default characteristics rule here: 'As long as Gaea's Liege is attacking, its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls.' Since Noel controls 5 Forests, as soon as Gaea's Liege is declared as an attacker it becomes 5/5.

Next, under [508.1c], the game checks restrictions on the chosen attackers. Rhonas the Indomitable's printed text says 'Rhonas can't attack or block unless you control another creature with power 4 or greater.' At this point in the declare-attackers turn-based action, Gaea's Liege is already an attacking 5/5, so Aubrey does control another creature with power 4 or greater, satisfying Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction. [Rhonas the Indomitable ruling #1] confirms that the other power-4-or-greater creature does not itself need to be attacking to satisfy this clause — but here Gaea's Liege only reaches power 4+ because it is attacking (its non-attacking power/toughness would just be 1, from Aubrey's single Forest), so both creatures need to be declared as attackers together for this to work.

If instead Aubrey tried to attack with only Rhonas the Indomitable while leaving Gaea's Liege back, Gaea's Liege would remain at 1/1 (based on Aubrey's own 1 Forest), and Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction would not be satisfied, making that attack illegal under [508.1c] (the whole declaration would be undone per [733.1]). But attacking with both together is legal.

Note: this analysis assumes normal two-player rules as presented; if this is a multiplayer game, Aubrey would still need to choose which defending player each attacker is attacking, but the mechanics of Gaea's Liege's and Rhonas the Indomitable's restrictions work the same way relative to whichever player is being attacked.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. All creatures are declared as attackers at the same time. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Ariyah casts [Stonewood Invocation] targeting [Skeletal Crocodile], and then attacks with the Skeletal Crocodile. Noah blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Phyresis] and indestructible due to their [Valorous Stance]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: The candidate fails to conclude that Skeletal Crocodile dies when the pump ends and therefore misses that Baron Sengir's death-trigger occurs, which disagrees with the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
By the end of the turn, Baron Sengir survives (it's not destroyed despite taking lethal combat damage), and Skeletal Crocodile is left with five permanent -1/-1 counters on it once the Stonewood Invocation pump wears off — whether that actually finishes off Skeletal Crocodile is the one piece I can't confirm from the rules given to me (see the note at the end).

Step by step:

1) Combat damage is dealt simultaneously. Skeletal Crocodile (pumped to 10/6 by Stonewood Invocation's +5/+5) has no infect, so its 10 damage to Baron Sengir is marked normally [302.7], [120.6]. Baron Sengir is a 5/5, so 10 marked damage is well over its toughness — normally lethal — but Baron Sengir has indestructible from Valorous Stance, so it "can't be destroyed" and "ignore[s] the state-based action that checks for lethal damage" [702.12b], [704.5g]. Baron Sengir survives the combat step with 10 damage marked on it but is not destroyed.

2) Baron Sengir has infect (from Phyresis), so its 5 combat damage to Skeletal Crocodile is never marked as damage. Instead, Noah (Baron Sengir's controller) puts five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile [702.90c], [120.3d], [702.90e]. Skeletal Crocodile's shroud (from Stonewood Invocation) only stops it from being *targeted* by spells/abilities — it does nothing to prevent combat damage or the resulting counters, so this happens normally. During combat, Skeletal Crocodile is 10/6 minus five -1/-1 counters = 5/1, which is still alive (toughness 1 > 0, and it has no marked damage triggering the lethal-damage SBA).

3) At the cleanup step, two things happen simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all "until end of turn" effects end [514.2]. This removes Baron Sengir's 10 marked damage (so no lethal-damage check applies to it at all after this point) and ends both Stonewood Invocation's +5/+5-and-shroud and Valorous Stance's indestructible. Phyresis is a permanently-attached Aura, not an "until end of turn" effect, so Baron Sengir keeps infect going forward.

4) The five -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile are counters, not damage, so cleanup does *not* remove them [514.2 only removes damage and "until end of turn" effects; counters persist]. Once the +5/+5 wears off, Skeletal Crocodile reverts to its base 5/1 with five -1/-1 counters still on it, making it a 0/-4.

Here's the gap: whether a creature with 0-or-less toughness is actually put into the graveyard is normally a state-based action, and Baron Sengir's own triggered ability ("Whenever a creature dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn dies, put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir") would matter if Skeletal Crocodile does die this turn — but the specific state-based action for 0-or-less toughness creatures, and the cleanup-step rule about re-checking state-based actions/triggers, were not among the rules provided to me. So I can't cite a rule confirming Skeletal Crocodile is actually put into the graveyard or that Baron Sengir gets its +2/+2 counter, even though the counters clearly drop its toughness below 1.

Summary of what's certain: Baron Sengir ends the turn undamaged (marked damage cleared) and keeps infect permanently; Skeletal Crocodile ends the turn back at its base size plus five permanent -1/-1 counters (net 0/-4 stats), with its actual survival/death not confirmable from the rules given here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Stonewood Invocation wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Skeletal Crocodile remain. Skeletal Crocodile dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Prismari Command], with both modes targeting Nico. Will they be able to copy it with [Chef's Kiss]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Prismari Command targets only a single player (Nico), so Chef's Kiss can target and copy it.
entries.answer:
Yes. Because Ariel chose both modes of Prismari Command ("deals 2 damage to any target" and "target player draws two cards, then discards two cards") and pointed both of them at Nico, Prismari Command has two instances of the word "target," but they resolve to the same single player — Nico. Chef's Kiss ruling #4 explicitly covers this: "If a spell has multiple instances of the word 'target,' but all of them target the same permanent or player, it is a legal target for Chef's Kiss." So Prismari Command qualifies as "target spell that targets only a single permanent or player" for Chef's Kiss's own targeting requirement (Chef's Kiss card text), and Ariel's opponent (or Ariel, per Chef's Kiss ruling #0, which says it can even target a spell you control) can cast Chef's Kiss on it.

When Chef's Kiss resolves, its controller gains control of Prismari Command, copies it (per the general copy rule [707.10], the copy retains the same modes chosen for the original — modes aren't something a targeting change lets you alter, per [115.8] and [700.2e]), and then randomly reselects the targets for both the original spell and the copy. Per Chef's Kiss ruling #4, since Prismari Command has two instances of "target," a new target is randomly reselected for each instance, separately for the original and separately for the copy — and none of those new targets can be Chef's Kiss's controller or a permanent that player controls, per Chef's Kiss's own text.

So the copy is created, but expect the two "target" slots (for the damage mode and the draw/discard mode) to end up pointing at different, randomly chosen legal targets on each of the original spell and its copy, rather than staying on Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When the game checks to see if a spell targets a single permanent or player, it doesn't care how many times that object was targeted, only that it was the only object the spell targeted.

entries.question: Alejandra owns a face-down [Progenitus] in exile. Nicolas uses [Ruin Processor] to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard. Where does Progenitus move to?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly applies Progenitus's replacement effect while it's in exile (face-down), claiming it shuffles into the library instead of going to the graveyard, which contradicts the reference ruling that it has no replacement effect in exile.
entries.answer:
Progenitus does not end up in Alejandra's graveyard at all. Progenitus's own printed replacement effect says, "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." Ruin Processor's ability tries to put the exiled Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard, but that movement is a case of a card being 'put into a graveyard,' so Progenitus's replacement effect intercepts it: Progenitus is revealed (even though it was exiled face down) and is shuffled into Alejandra's library instead of going to her graveyard. Nicolas still gets to choose whether to gain 5 life as part of Ruin Processor's ability, since the ability's instruction to 'put a card... into that player's graveyard' is what's being replaced — the act of attempting it is what triggers Progenitus's replacement, similar to how Ruin Processor ruling #1 describes a replacement effect that changes where a card ends up when something tries to put it into a graveyard from exile. Progenitus's card text overrides the general outcome you'd otherwise expect from Ruin Processor's ability, since a card's own printed rules text always wins over how a general effect would otherwise apply. This is a two-player scenario (Nicolas and Alejandra), and nothing here depends on player count, so the same result would hold at a multiplayer table as well.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The graveyard. Replacement effects must exist before the event in question in order to affect it. Progenitus has no abilities in exile, so there is no replacement effect that would apply to it moving to the graveyard.

entries.question: Aurora controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Snow-Covered Forest. Can Aurora attack with the Gaea's Liege?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion, incorrectly claiming the Liege's power changes upon declaration and is barred by Reverence, while the reference correctly states restrictions are checked before a creature becomes attacking so the Liege is a 3/3 and may attack.
entries.answer:
No — Aurora cannot legally declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against Nico while Reverence is on the battlefield, because the act of declaring it attacking causes its own power to drop low enough to trigger Reverence's restriction.

Here's why: Gaea's Liege's power/toughness are characteristic-defining. While it is *not* attacking, it's a */* equal to the number of Forests Aurora controls (3 Snow-Covered Forests, since Snow-Covered Forest has the basic land type Forest), making it a 3/3. But the moment Aurora chooses to declare it as an attacker, it becomes an 'attacking' creature per the declare-attackers process (rule 508.1), and Gaea's Liege's ability then reads 'its power and toughness are each equal to the number of Forests defending player controls.' Nico, the defending player, controls only 1 Snow-Covered Forest, so as soon as Gaea's Liege becomes an attacking creature it is a 1/1.

Reverence reads 'Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you' — this is a Restriction (see the Restriction definition and rules 508.1c/509.1b). Restrictions on attacking are checked during the declare-attackers step: the active player checks each creature they control for restrictions, and if any restriction is being disobeyed, the whole declaration of attackers is illegal (rule 508.1c). Since Gaea's Liege's power becomes 1 (≤2) the instant it's declared attacking Nico, declaring it as an attacker against Nico violates Reverence's restriction, making the attack declaration illegal. If Aurora tried to do this, the game would treat it as an illegal action and roll back to before the declaration (rule 733.1).

This answer assumes a two-player game between Aurora and Nico, since Nico is the only opponent mentioned. If this were a multiplayer game and Aurora had other opponents within her range of influence (rule 801.3), Gaea's Liege could still be declared attacking one of those other opponents (or their planeswalkers/battles) instead, where its power/toughness would be based on that other defending player's Forests, and Reverence — which only restricts attacks against Nico specifically — would not apply to those attacks (rule 802.3a: restrictions that apply to attacking a specific player only apply to creatures attacking that player).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Ari controls [Village Survivors] and [Vodalian Soldiers] and has 6 life. Nyla controls [Norn's Annex]. If Ari attacks with Vodalian Soldiers, paying 2 life, will it become tapped?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling and reasoning: attackers are tapped before paying attack costs (so Vodalian Soldiers is tapped) and the life payment-triggered vigilance from Village Survivors comes too late.
entries.answer:
Yes — Vodalian Soldiers will still become tapped. Under rule 508.1f, tapping the chosen attackers happens first, before any required attack costs (like Norn's Annex's {W/P} cost) are paid in step 508.1h. So Vodalian Soldiers is already tapped as part of the attack declaration before Ari pays the 2 life to satisfy Norn's Annex's requirement. Only after that tapping does Ari pay 2 life, dropping from 6 to 4 life, which triggers Village Survivors' fateful hour ("other creatures you control have vigilance" once you have 5 or less life). But per the Village Survivors ruling, this vigilance grant comes too late to matter — the tapping already happened, so vigilance has no benefit that combat for Vodalian Soldiers. It attacks tapped.

Note: this is the ruled interaction specifically confirmed for Village Survivors' fateful hour ability — the general sequencing rule (tap first, then pay costs) is what causes the vigilance to arrive after the fact. If Ari's life had already been at 5 or less before declaring attackers (so vigilance was already active from a prior effect), Vodalian Soldiers would NOT become tapped, since vigilance would apply during the initial tapping step. But as described, Ari starts at 6 life and only drops below 6 as a result of paying Norn's Annex's cost during the same declare-attackers action, so the vigilance is granted too late.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Tapping creatures to attack is done before paying any costs to attack.

entries.question: Amari has [Phyrexian Hulk] and [The Mimeoplasm] in their graveyard. Amari casts [Rise of the Dark Realms] to return both to the battlefield. Can they have The Mimeoplasm enter the battlefield as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude The Mimeoplasm cannot enter as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk because Rise of the Dark Realms moves them simultaneously and The Mimeoplasm's replacement effect can't exile an object that is entering the battlefield at the same time.
entries.answer:
No. Because Rise of the Dark Realms puts Phyrexian Hulk and The Mimeoplasm onto the battlefield as part of a single, simultaneous event ("Put all creature cards from all graveyards onto the battlefield under your control"), neither Phyrexian Hulk nor The Mimeoplasm is available to be exiled by The Mimeoplasm's own "As The Mimeoplasm enters, you may exile two creature cards from graveyards" ability. That ability is a replacement effect that modifies how The Mimeoplasm enters the battlefield, and rule [614.13a] establishes that when applying an effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, you can't choose the object that's becoming that permanent (The Mimeoplasm itself) or any other object entering the battlefield at the same time as it (here, Phyrexian Hulk, since both are being moved to the battlefield simultaneously by Rise of the Dark Realms). 

So when The Mimeoplasm's replacement effect is applied, Phyrexian Hulk is no longer sitting in the graveyard available to be exiled — it's leaving at the same instant. If those are the only two creature cards in any graveyard, Amari has no creature cards left to exile at all, so the 'may exile two creature cards' option fails and The Mimeoplasm simply enters the battlefield as itself, a 0/0 Ooze, per its printed characteristics (see [The Mimeoplasm ruling #2] and [The Mimeoplasm ruling #3], which only apply once two cards are actually exiled). A 0/0 creature entering the battlefield is put into its owner's graveyard immediately by the state-based action for having 0 toughness, though that specific state-based action rule isn't in the provided context, so I won't cite a rule number for that last step. 

If there were additional creature cards in other players' graveyards, The Mimeoplasm could still exile two of those (or one of those plus... no, it still couldn't use Phyrexian Hulk since that one is co-entering), and could then copy some other creature, but it cannot use Phyrexian Hulk as one of the two exiled cards under these facts. This is a single-effect scenario handled the same way regardless of how many players are in the game, since the restriction comes from rule 614.13a's 'entering at the same time' rule, not from turn order or APNAP considerations.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The Mimeoplasm has a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield. The game checks for any replacement effects that modify how an object will enter the battlefield before the object has changed zones. So Phyrexian Hulk is still in the graveyard while Amari is making choices for The Mimeoplasm, however they are not allowed to choose an object that is also changing zones at the same time.

entries.question: Autumn casts [Time Stretch]. Can they choose to skip both extra turns with [Time Vault]?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Autumn can skip at most one of Time Stretch's extra turns with Time Vault, while the reference says they can skip both, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
No. Time Vault's ability only lets Autumn skip a turn *if Time Vault is tapped* at the moment that turn would begin, and skipping a turn with Time Vault automatically untaps it. So Autumn can use Time Vault to skip at most one of the two extra turns from Time Stretch, not both.

Here's the sequence: Time Stretch ("Target player takes two extra turns after this one") gives Autumn two extra turns, added one at a time directly after the current turn [500.7]. When the first of those extra turns would begin, if Time Vault is tapped, Autumn may choose to skip that turn instead — and if they do, Time Vault untaps immediately as part of that choice (Time Vault's own text: "If you would begin your turn while this artifact is tapped, you may skip that turn instead. If you do, untap this artifact"; confirmed by [Time Vault ruling #1], which notes the choice is made as the turn would begin, only while Time Vault is tapped, and Time Vault untaps before anything else happens next). Skipping a turn is a replacement effect [614.10a][614.10b][500.11] that simply causes the game to proceed as though that turn never happened.

Because Time Vault untaps the moment the first extra turn is skipped, it is no longer tapped when the second extra turn from Time Stretch would begin. Time Vault's skip ability only triggers off the artifact being tapped at that specific moment, so the condition isn't met for the second turn, and Autumn has no way to skip it with Time Vault (they'd need to tap it again first, e.g. by using its "{T}: Take an extra turn after this one" ability, but that generates yet another extra turn rather than letting them skip the pending one). So at most one of the two Time Stretch extra turns can be skipped this way, never both.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. As their turn ends, they can apply Time Vault's replacement effect, which means the next turn gets skipped and Time Vault gets untapped as part of the next turn that actually happens. Then, since it's still tapped as Autumn's turn is ending, they can choose to skip the next turn again.

entries.question: Averie attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Averie casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Mob]?
entries.reason: Both conclude Cephalid Snitch's effect removes only protection from black until end of turn, so after untapping Pristine Angel still lacks protection from black and can be targeted by Mob.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can legally target Pristine Angel with Mob's "destroy target creature" effect, because the protection-from-black removal from Cephalid Snitch's ability is still in effect and outlasts Pristine Angel's own re-granting of protection.

Here's why: Pristine Angel's own text says "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color." While Pristine Angel was tapped (during combat), it had no protection at all, so when Nico activated Cephalid Snitch's ability ("Sacrifice this creature: Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn.") targeting Pristine Angel, that targeting was legal — Pristine Angel had no protection to prevent it. Cephalid Snitch's ability then resolved, creating a continuous effect that specifically causes Pristine Angel to lose protection from black until end of turn.

When Averie later casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel, Pristine Angel's static ability turns back on and grants protection from artifacts and from each color again — but the effect from Cephalid Snitch's ability doesn't just evaporate because Pristine Angel's characteristics changed back. The rules establish the general principle that an effect created by a resolved ability continues to affect the specific object it identified even after that object's qualities change, as long as it's still the same object (rule 700.7's example: an effect that says "Destroy that creature" still destroys the object later even if it's no longer a creature by then). Applying that same logic here, Cephalid Snitch's "loses protection from black until end of turn" effect keeps suppressing protection from black on Pristine Angel specifically, for the rest of the turn, regardless of Pristine Angel's own static ability re-activating and restoring its other protections (artifacts, and every color other than black).

Mob is a black spell (mana cost {4}{B}). Since Pristine Angel currently lacks protection from black (due to Cephalid Snitch's still-active effect) even though it has regained protection from artifacts and from every other color, Mob's "destroy target creature" can legally target Pristine Angel right now. When Mob resolves, rule 608.2b would again check whether Pristine Angel is still a legal target at that time — and as long as the loss-of-protection-from-black effect (or the fact that Pristine Angel is once again tapped, etc.) still holds, it would remain legal and Mob would destroy it.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players at the table — it's purely about the characteristics of the two permanents/spells involved, so it plays out the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

(The timestamp of Pristine Angel's ability does not change when it becomes untapped.)
